t1-combinatorics: Why Probability Theory Is the Foundation of Texas Hold'em

Texas Hold'em is an incomplete-information game: you can't see your opponent's hole cards or the upcoming community cards. But the deck's composition is fully known — 52 cards, 4 suits, 13 ranks. This means all "luck" can be quantified into precise probabilities. The first dividing line between pro and amateur players is whether you can replace feeling with counting.
Every "feeling" in poker corresponds to a precisely calculable combination count. Master combinatorics and you gain the ability to translate intuition into numbers.
Total Starting-Hand Combinations

Taking any 2 of 52 cards as a starting hand gives C(52,2) = 52×51÷2 = 1326 combinations. These 1326 combos group into 169 classes: 13 "pocket pair" classes (AA-22), 78 "suited" classes (AKs-32s), and 78 "offsuit" classes (AKo-32o).

Any pocket pair (e.g. AA) = C(4,2) = 6 combos
Any suited hand (e.g. AKs) = 4 combos
Any offsuit hand (e.g. AKo) = 4×4−4 = 12 combos

Combination formula and derivation:
C(n,k) = n! ÷ [k! × (n−k)!]
Deriving C(52,2): first count "ordered picks of two" = 52×51; since order doesn't matter, A♠K♥ and K♥A♠ are the same hand, so divide by 2! (the permutations of two cards) → 52×51 ÷ 2 = 1326
Similarly C(4,2) = 4×3 ÷ 2 = 6: order within the pair doesn't count either. (Concepts from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.1-3 combinatorics; Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.2)

These three numbers (6 / 4 / 12) are the atomic units of range analysis. For example, "the opponent's 3Bet range has AA, KK, and AKs" means 6+6+4 = 16 combos. All later range theory (T4) builds on this counting.
Common Starting-Hand Probabilities

Probability of any pocket pair = 78/1326 ≈ 5.9% (about once every 17 hands); of AA = 6/1326 ≈ 0.45% (about once every 221 hands); of AK (including suited) = 16/1326 ≈ 1.2%; of any suited hand ≈ 23.5%.

Example: You've been at a full table for two hours without a big pair. Is that normal? The probability of QQ+ is 18/1326 ≈ 1.36%, about once every 74 hands. Live play deals about 25-30 hands/hour, so ~55 hands in two hours without QQ+ is entirely within normal variance. Understanding base probabilities prevents you from widening your range due to a "card drought".

Example 2 (flop counting): You hold a lone A♠ overcard. The flop deals 3 cards from the remaining 51. The probability at least one A appears = 1 − C(48,3)/C(51,3) = 1 − 17296/20825 ≈ 17%. The difficulty isn't the math but recognizing that "at least one" requires 1 minus the complement event — missing the complement is the most common combinatorics pitfall.

Example 3 (range weighting): An opponent's 3Bet range is marked {AA, KK, QQ, AKs} = 6+6+6+4 = 22 combos. Pocket pairs account for 18 combos (~82%) while AKs is only 4 — "his range is all AK" is often an illusion; the real weight is on pairs. Price ranges by combo count, not class count, so you don't overestimate his air.
Independent Events and Conditional Probability

Every hand is an independent event: if you got AA last hand, the probability of AA this hand is still 0.45%. But probabilities within a single hand are conditional: holding two hearts changes the probability of hearts on the flop — that's the mathematical basis of Blockers, covered later.
The gambler's fallacy — "I've lost five in a row, the next one should win" — is precisely confusing independent events with conditional probability. The deck has no memory, but your chips do.

Counter-intuitive point: 169 classes and 1326 combos are two different counts. 169 is the "equivalent class count" (pair/suited/offsuit types), while 1326 is the "distinguishable actual combo count". Probability math must use 1326 — classes deceive you: suited AK and AA each count as "1 class", but their combo weights are 4 and 6 respectively.

Memorize the 6/4/12 combo counts and the anchor numbers "a pair once every 17 hands, AA once every 221 hands". There's no time to calculate at the table — anchor numbers are your mental-math dictionary.
t1-outs: Outs are the unseen cards in the deck that can make your hand surpass the opponent's. Counting Outs is the first step of postflop math: a flush draw has 9 Outs (13 of the suit minus the 4 you see); an open-ended straight draw has 8; a gutshot has 4; a pair drawing to two pair or trips has 5.
When counting Outs, only count cards that "make you take the lead", not cards that "improve your hand". Improving to second-best isn't an Out — it's a trap.

One card to come (flop→turn or turn→river): equity ≈ Outs × 2%
Two cards to come (flop→river, all-in spot): equity ≈ Outs × 4%

Precise math: after the flop there are 47 unknown cards, so the turn hit rate = Outs/47. With 9 Outs: 9/47 ≈ 19.1%, while the Rule of 2 estimates 18% — error under 1.2 percentage points. The more Outs, the larger the ×4 error (at 15 Outs use the correction: Outs×4 − (Outs−8) ≈ 54%), but within 12 Outs it's accurate enough.

Rule of 2/4 error analysis (flop→river two-card scenario, exact = 1 − (47−Outs)/47 × (46−Outs)/46):
4 Outs: ×4 estimates 16% ｜ exact 16.5% ｜ error −0.5
8 Outs: ×4 estimates 32% ｜ exact 31.4% ｜ error +0.6
9 Outs: ×4 estimates 36% ｜ exact 35.0% ｜ error +1.0
12 Outs: ×4 estimates 48% ｜ exact 45.0% ｜ error +3.0
15 Outs: ×4 estimates 60% ｜ exact 54.1% ｜ error +5.9
Conclusion: for Outs ≤ 9, ×4 error is within 1 percentage point; for Outs ≥ 13 use the correction Outs×4 − (Outs−8), or mentally compute the exact value before a flop shove. (Concepts from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.2 Outs and the Rule of 2 and 4)

Example 2 (practical error significance): On the flop you hold J♥10♥ with board 8♥9♦3♣. An open-ended straight (8 Outs) + backdoor flush, the Rule of 4 shove equity ≈ 32%, exact 31.4% — both beat top pair. But at 15 Outs (flush + straight + overcard combo draw), ×4 overestimates by ~6 points, enough to mislead a "fold" into a "call". Error isn't academic — it's a real decision bias at the table.

Example 3 (turn scenario): On the turn the pot is 200 and the opponent shoves 100; you need 100/400 = 25% equity to call. You hold a 9-Out flush draw: exact 9/46 ≈ 19.6%, Rule of 2 estimates 18% — both below 25%, so pure math says fold unless implied odds are significant (see T2). Remember: on the turn you only count one card — use Outs×2, not ×4.

Example: You hold A♥8♥ on a K♥7♥2♠ flop. The flush draw has 9 Outs, and the 3 remaining Aces may also surpass the opponent (if he only has a pair of Kings) — about 12 "dirty Outs" total. About 24% for one card, 45% for two — that's why a nut flush draw + overcard showdown value can often semi-bluff shove the flop.

Not all Outs are "clean". If your straight Out also completes an opponent's flush, that card must be discounted or not counted. Rule of thumb: on wet boards, non-nut draw Outs typically get a 20-30% discount. For example, if 2 of an 8-Out OESD complete a potential opponent flush, estimate 6 Outs.
Common Outs-counting error: counting all cards that "give you a pair". If the opponent already has two pair, your pairing Outs are zero — Outs are always relative to the opponent's range.
Training method: every time you see a flop, mentally state your Outs count and ×2/×4 estimate before acting. After two weeks this becomes a reflex.
t1-variance: Separating Expected Value from Actual Results

An 80% favorite shove loses on average once every five times. Variance measures how actual results fluctuate around the expected value. Poker's cruelty: in the short term, luck affects results far more than skill; but over the long term, skill is the only determinant. Both facts hold simultaneously.
You can't control the result of a single hand — only decision quality. Always evaluate yourself by the decision process (EV), never by a single result.
Sample Size: How Big Is "Long Run"

For cash games, a winner at 5bb/100 hands typically has a standard deviation of 80-100bb/100. This means even long-term winners have a real chance of losing in a 10,000-hand sample; reliably overcoming variance usually needs 50,000-100,000+ hands. A live player may not reach 30,000 hands in a year — that's why "I won last month" says almost nothing.

Result = expected value (skill) + fluctuation (luck)
Fluctuation's impact ∝ 1/√sample: expanding the sample 100x shrinks luck's relative impact to 1/10

Variance and standard deviation definitions:
σ² = Σ(xᵢ − μ)² ÷ n, standard deviation σ = √σ²
Poker bet-results example: five consecutive bet results +200, −150, +300, −100, +50 (in chips)
Mean μ = (200−150+300−100+50)÷5 = 60
Squared deviations: 140² + 210² + 240² + 160² + 10² = 19600+44100+57600+25600+100 = 147000
σ² = 147000÷5 = 29400, σ ≈ 171
Interpretation: +60 per hand on average, but single results swing ~171 chips around 60 — the standard deviation far exceeds the mean, the mathematical portrait of poker's short-term instability. (Concepts from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.3 variance and standard deviation)

Example 2 (variance and bet size): You get five consecutive shove-able spots, each with 60% equity, with per-hand results as above (σ≈171). Doubling each bet doubles both mean and standard deviation (μ=120, σ≈342) — expectation and fluctuation scale proportionally, but "ruin risk" scales faster. This explains why bankroll management (detailed in T8) must cap bet sizes within variance tolerance.

Example 3 (using standard deviation to judge samples): You tracked 1000 hands, averaging +5bb/100 with σ=90bb/100. "Profitable over 10,000 hands" doesn't prove you played right: 10,000 hands = 100 hundred-hand samples, cumulative σ = 90×√100 = 900bb, while expected profit is only 500bb — the cumulative standard deviation (900bb) exceeds expected profit (500bb), meaning over 10,000 hands luck can still completely overwhelm skill.

Example: AA shoving into KK wins ~81%. Losing three in a row is 0.19³ ≈ 0.7% — but if you play this spot 200 times a year, the chance of a "lost three in a row" window exceeds 60%. Rare events almost inevitably occur over enough trials; that doesn't mean you misplayed.

Understanding variance yields three practical principles: (1) Bankroll management — your bankroll must absorb normal downswings (a common cash standard is 20-40 buy-ins); (2) Emotional control — attributing bad results to variance rather than self-doubt is the first defense against tilt (see T8); (3) Review standards — ask "was this decision +EV" in review, not "did this hand win".

A downswing isn't abnormal — it's a mathematical certainty. Every long-term winner's bankroll curve contains multiple multi-week down stretches. The difference: winners maintain decision quality during drawdowns; losers collapse.

Keep a "decision log" rather than a "win/loss log": record your three hardest decisions each day and your reasoning, then revisit a month later. You'll find progress comes from improved decision quality, and the bankroll curve is just its lagging projection.
t2-ev: Expected Value (EV) = the payoff of each possible outcome × the probability of that outcome, summed over all outcomes. It answers: if this spot repeated infinitely, how much would this decision make (or lose) on average per time. All of poker's strategy theory is essentially "at each decision point, choose the action with the highest EV".

EV = Σ (payoffᵢ × probabilityᵢ)
Call EV = win probability × amount won − loss probability × amount paid

Deriving the EV formula: split a decision into all possible outcome branches, multiply each branch's "probability × payoff", then sum. For "calling an all-in", there are only win/lose outcomes: EV(call) = P(win) × amount winnable − P(lose) × call amount. Note "amount winnable" only counts the current pot + opponent bet, not the call you're about to put in — that part is just returned, not profit. The EV of folding is always 0, so any call with EV > 0 beats folding; a decision is simply comparing branch EVs and taking the max. This split-branch, weight, sum process is the "complete EV derivation chain". (Concepts from: The Theory of Poker Ch.6 EV basics; Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.3)

Example: pot 100, opponent shoves 50, you have 30% equity after calling 50. EV = 0.30×150 − 0.70×50 = 45 − 35 = +10. You lose seven times out of ten, but this is a +EV call averaging +10 each time. "The correct decision that often loses" is poker math's most counter-intuitive yet most important lesson.

Example (bluff branch derivation): river pot 90, you hold unpaired A♣K♣ and the opponent checks. You plan a pure-bluff bet of 60, estimating the opponent folds 60% and calls 40% (you have 0% showdown equity when called). EV = 0.60×90 − 0.40×60 = 54 − 24 = +30. Break-even: required fold rate f satisfies f×90 = (1−f)×60 → 150f = 60 → f = 40%; your estimated 60% far exceeds it, so the +EV holds. Branch breakdown: fold branch wins 90, call branch loses 60, weighted by probability gives the result.

Example (value-bet comparison): river, you hold the nut flush, pot 100. Checking EV = 100 (you win the pot at showdown); betting 50 with an estimated 30% call / 70% fold gives bet EV = 0.70×100 + 0.30×150 = 70 + 45 = +115. 115 > 100, so betting wins — the EV increment of a value bet comes from the extra 50 contributed by the 30% that calls. Note: if the opponent never calls (0%), bet EV degenerates to 100, equal to checking — then betting just gives away free information.
EV Breakdown: Fold Equity and Showdown Equity

A bet's EV has two parts: Fold Equity (winning the pot immediately when the opponent folds) + Showdown Equity (your share of winning at showdown when called). Bluffs rely on the former, value bets on the latter, and semi-bluffs get both — that's why draws are the best bluff candidates (see T6 betting theory).
Bet EV = opponent fold rate × current pot + (1−fold rate) × (equity × new pot − loss rate × bet amount)
A pure bluff's break-even fold rate = bet ÷ (pot + bet). Betting 2/3 pot: if the opponent folds over 40%, the bet is +EV even if your hand always loses at showdown.

In cash games chip value is constant, so chip EV (cEV) equals money EV. But in tournaments chips have diminishing marginal value (doubling chips doesn't double the prize), so ICM converts cEV into $EV (see T9). All calculations in this Level assume cash-game spots by default.
EV is a function of the decision moment, not of the outcome. Once a decision is made, its EV is fixed — whatever cards come after is just variance performing.

The sunk-cost trap: chips already in the pot are dead money — no longer yours. "I've already put 100 in; not calling would waste it" is faulty reasoning — EV only looks at future branches: comparing call EV against fold EV (=0), unrelated to past investment. A pro's folding ability is essentially the discipline of "not chasing sunk costs".
In review, write an EV calculation for every key decision, even a rough estimate. A decision you can write a formula for is a decision you understand; if you can't write one, you're playing on feel.
t2-pot-odds: Pot Odds = the amount you need to call ÷ the total pot after calling. It represents "the price you pay to win the whole pot", and also the minimum equity needed to break even on a call. It's the most frequently used calculation in poker.

Required equity = call amount ÷ (current pot + opponent bet + call amount)
Example: pot 100, opponent bets 50 → required equity = 50÷(100+50+50) = 25%

Deriving the "required equity" formula: let current pot P, opponent bet B, and you call B. If you win (probability E) you net P+B; if you lose (1−E) you net −B. Set the break-even point EV = E×(P+B) − (1−E)×B = 0; expanding: E×(P+B) = (1−E)×B → E×(P+B) = B − E×B → E×(P+B+B) = B → E = B ÷ (P+2B). The denominator is exactly "current pot + opponent bet + call amount". Understanding the derivation matters more than memorizing the formula: once you translate both "price" and "equity" into the same unit (probability), a calling decision becomes a comparison of two numbers. (Concepts from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.3)

Memorize the required equity for common bet sizes: 1/3 pot → 20%; 1/2 pot → 25%; 2/3 pot → 28.6%; full pot → 33.3%; 2x pot → 40%. Note the pattern: no matter how big the bet, required equity is always below 50% — because there's already "dead money" in the pot.
Pot Odds × Outs: The Complete Calling Decision

Example: turn pot 120, opponent bets 60, you hold a flush draw (9 Outs). Required equity = 60÷240 = 25%; your equity ≈ 9×2 = 18%. 18% < 25%, so by pot odds alone you should fold — unless implied odds close the gap (next chapter).

Example (preflop all-in): SB pot including blinds and antes totals 6bb, BB shoves 30bb, you call 30bb. Required equity = 30 ÷ (6+30+30) = 30÷66 ≈ 45.5%. You hold AK: vs BB's shoving range (mostly big pairs + strong high cards) equity ≈ 55%. 55% > 45.5%, so the call is +EV. A preflop all-in has no further betting and zero implied odds — pot odds are the sole judge; it's the cleanest calling-decision exercise.

Example (river bluff-catch): pot 120, opponent bets 80, you hold TPTK (can only beat bluffs). Required equity = 80 ÷ (120+80+80) = 80÷280 ≈ 28.6%. Hand reading (T7 process) estimates his shoving range at ~35% bluffs, 65% value → 35% > 28.6%, call. Against an ultra-tight opponent whose range is almost all value (~15% bluffs), then 15% < 28.6%, fold. A bluff-catching call is always a duel between two numbers: "pot odds vs opponent bluff share".
A calling decision = comparing two numbers: the price the pot offers (required equity) vs your hand's equity. If equity > price, call; otherwise fold or raise.
Pot Odds from the Defensive Perspective

Pot odds also determine how often you "must" defend: the smaller the opponent's bet, the better the price you get and the wider your calling range must be, or the opponent can exploit you by small-betting any two cards. The formalization of this idea is the Minimum Defense Frequency MDF (see T5 game theory).
One of the most common amateur leaks: folding too much to small bets. Facing a 1/4-pot bet you only need 16.7% equity to call — almost any hand with showdown value or a backdoor draw qualifies.

MDF misuse trap: Minimum Defense Frequency (MDF) is the defensive floor "to stop the opponent from small-bet exploiting you with any two cards", not a profit-maximizing calling standard. Against a tight player with an extremely high value share, calling *below* MDF is correct. MDF answers "how often to call", pot odds answer "whether to call this hand" — different purposes, don't mix them (full MDF derivation in T5).
Memorize the "bet size → required equity" table to reflex level: 1/3 pot=20%, 1/2 pot=25%, 2/3 pot=28.6%, full pot=33.3%. This conversion must happen within two seconds at the table.
t2-implied-odds: Implied Odds: An Extension of Pot Odds

Pot odds only count the current pot, but poker is a multi-street game: after you hit your draw, you can usually win extra money from the opponent. Implied Odds factor this "future income" into the decision — it explains why some draws that pot odds say to fold can actually be called.

Implied-odds shortfall = the future winnings needed to break even on a call
Required future winnings = (required equity × total pot − current winnable) ÷ hit probability (rough: call amount ÷ hit rate − current total pot)

Implied odds = (total currently winnable + expected future winnings) ÷ call amount
Example: pot 120, opponent bets 60, expected to win another 100 after hitting → (120+60+100) ÷ 60 = 4.67 : 1
Converted required equity = 1 ÷ (4.67+1) ≈ 17.6%, matching a flush draw's 18% — the formulaic source of the previous example's "call breaks even" (Concepts from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.4 implied odds)

Example: turn pot 120, opponent bets 60, your flush-draw equity is 18% (< 25% required). Call 60; if hitting lets you win another 100+ from the opponent on average, the call turns +EV. The deeper the opponent's stack, the stronger his hand (willing to pay), and the more disguised your draw, the better the implied odds.
The Three Factors of Implied Odds

Evaluate implied odds by three points: (1) effective stack depth — if the opponent has no money left there are no implied odds; at deep stacks (150bb+) small pairs and suited connectors surge in value; (2) opponent type — a calling station gives great implied odds, while tight-passive players won't pay after you hit; (3) draw disguise — a pocket pair flopping a set is the most disguised with the best implied odds; an obvious four-to-a-flush is the worst.

Set Mining rule: calling an opening raise with a small pocket pair, you flop a set ~12% of the time (about 1/7.5), and generally need effective stacks ≥ 15-20x the call to be profitable (accounting for not always collecting fully after hitting).

Set Mining exact probability: holding a small pair, the chance one of the three flop cards is your rank
P = 1 − C(47,2)/C(50,2) = 1 − 1081/1225 ≈ 11.76% (≈ 7.5:1 odds, i.e. about one in 8.5 flops)
Derivation: none of the three flop cards matching = C(48,3)/C(50,3) = (48×47×46)/(50×49×48) = 47×46/(50×49) = C(47,2)/C(50,2). ~11.76% probability, often rounded in textbooks to "about 8:1" (Concepts from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.4)

Example (deep vs shallow stacks): opponent opens CO to 3bb, you hold 55 on the BTN. Effective stacks 150bb: call 3bb, hit 11.76% of the time, needing only ~3×7.5 ≈ 22bb more on average after hitting to break even — 150bb depth gives huge room, call. Effective stacks only 25bb (less than 8.5x): even hitting a set won't collect enough, and you often get your equity denied postflop — fold or 3-Bet is better. Same hand, stack depth directly rewrites the EV.
Reverse Implied Odds: The Second-Best That Bites

Reverse Implied Odds are the mirror image of implied odds: you "hit" but are still behind and end up losing even more. Typical spots: a non-nut flush draw running into a bigger flush; a weak-kicker top pair (like K7 on a K-high board) — you win small pots when ahead and lose big pots when behind.

Example: you hold Q♠J♠ with two spades on the flop. Same flush draw, but if the opponent's range contains A♠K♠, A♠x♠ combos, hitting your flush may run directly into the nut flush — these "hit but lose" branches must be deducted from EV. That's why low suited connectors should chase flushes cautiously in multiway pots.

Judgment mnemonic: easily dominated hands (weak-kicker high cards, low flushes, non-nut draws) have bad reverse implied odds — better to play fewer of them; disguised hands that can make the nuts (pocket pairs, nut flush draws) have good implied odds and are worth paying a little "overprice" for.

The gambler's fallacy: three straight missed flush draws, "the fourth one should hit" — wrong. Every flop is independent; your set probability is always 11.76% and flush draws always ~36%, never accumulating from previous misses. Implied odds and pot odds are computed from the current hand's independent probabilities only; using "my turn to hit" as a calling reason is purely emotional loss-making.

Before convincing yourself to call on implied odds, ask: "after I hit, what hands will the opponent pay me with?" If you can't name specific hand types, you're just finding an excuse for folding fear.
t3-position-value: Position refers to your relative order in the betting sequence. A seat that acts last on every postflop round is "In Position" (IP); otherwise it's "Out of Position" (OOP). The button (BTN) is the only seat that's always in position postflop and has the highest long-term win rate; the blinds (SB/BB) are always OOP and are the only two long-term losing seats — a structural fact confirmed by every tracking database.

(1) Information advantage: the later actor decides after seeing opponents' actions, gaining one more piece of information each round; (2) pot control: the player in position can choose to call and keep the pot small (Pot Control) or raise to inflate it, which OOP players can't do — checking may get bet, betting may get raised; (3) free cards and equity realization: an in-position draw can check to take a free card, while an OOP draw is often forced to decide at unfavorable prices.

The essence of positional advantage is "Equity Realization": with the same 50% raw equity, in position you can realize 100%+ while OOP you often realize only 80-90%. Position directly discounts or boosts your equity.

Actual equity = raw equity × realization rate (R)
In position (IP): R is typically 100%+; Out of position (OOP): R is typically 80-90%
Example: same 50% raw equity, IP ≈ 50%×105% = 52.5%, OOP ≈ 50%×85% = 42.5%

Equity-realization magnitude references (common modern estimates): BTN calling an open ≈ 105-110% (over-realization — not just keeping raw equity but squeezing out a bit more from position); CO ≈ 100-105%; BB defense ≈ 85-92% (last to see a free flop, but OOP postflop); SB flat ≈ 80-88%. Three main factors affect R: (1) position — IP realizes high, OOP low; (2) hand type — nut flush/straight draws realize high, middle and weak pairs low (often driven off by later opponent bets); (3) opponent aggression — the more aggressive the opponent, the more often you're forced to forfeit equity, the lower R. Plugging R into "actual equity = raw equity × R" is the quantitative form of position value. (Concepts from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.5 position and equity discussion)

Example: holding the same 8♠7♠ facing an opening raise. Calling on the BTN: you act last every postflop round — hit a draw and control the pot to chase, hit a pair and thin-value, miss and steal after seeing the opponent show weakness. Calling in the SB: you act first postflop — checking gets half your weak hands bet off by a C-Bet, and betting exposes your range. Same hand, wildly different EV by position — that's why each position's starting range must differ.

Example (OOP realization loss): you're in the BB with A♣9♣ calling a BTN open, flop 9♠7♦3♣ (top pair weak kicker). You check and BTN bets 2/3 pot — already painful: if you call and the turn brings Q/K/J, BTN's range is full of Qx/Kx and you'll be forced to fold again. Turn Q♥, he bets again, and you fold a hand "you would have won on the BTN". The same hand on the BTN: check or small-bet the flop to control, check the turn for a free card, and no loss if you miss. Being OOP slashes medium-strength realization — the intuitive source of that ~85% R.

Example (position difference in value betting): river, you hold K♥Q♥ having hit a Q-top-pair (board Q♠8♦4♣2♥9♠). In position: opponent checks → you thin-value bet 1/3 pot, fold safely if raised, capturing the thinnest value; out of position: you check → the opponent may bet, reducing your top pair to a passive "call or fold" choice; if you bet, you may get raised and can't get away. Same hand — position demotes it from "active thin value" to "passive bluff-catch". That's positional value showing directly at the showdown street.

Standard Raise First In (RFI) range widths approximate: UTG tightest (~15% or so), widening as position moves back, reaching 40-50% at the BTN. The logic chain: the later the position → fewer opponents to get through behind + more likely to have position postflop → higher marginal-hand EV → wider range. The range-trainer module's positional ranges are exactly this principle in practice.
The biggest structural leak of beginners is "playing the same set of hands from every position". Playing K9o in UTG burns money; folding K9o on the BTN burns opportunity.

Dilution of positional advantage: in 3+ way pots, the information value of "acting last" drops — you must guess three ranges at once, and pot control is compressed (you can only call/fold when others bet, and raising faces multiway responses). Being IP still beats OOP, but the edge shrinks significantly. So tighten your participation range in multiway pots and don't take heads-up positional advantage for granted.
A self-check habit: before entering a pot, state your position and whether you'll have position postflop. If OOP postflop, cut your intended entering range down a notch.
t3-starting-hands: The Value Dimensions of Starting Hands

Starting-hand value comes from four dimensions: (1) high-card strength — AK-type hands that win with a pair; (2) pairing potential — pocket pairs that win big pots with sets; (3) connectivity — connected cards that make straights; (4) suitedness — suited cards that make flushes. What truly decides entry isn't "does this hand look good", but its EV in the current position, stack depth, and opponent structure.

Hand strength roughly splits into three classes: made-hand types (big pairs/big high cards, prefer small heads-up pots), speculative types (small pairs/suited connectors, prefer cheap multiway deep-stack entry), and garbage (neither high-card strength nor potential). The same hand can move between classes at different stack depths.

Starting-hand EV tiers (illustrative magnitudes for 100bb cash, unopened pot): Tier 1 "auto-enter" — AA, KK, QQ, JJ, AK-type, +0.6~+1.5bb per hand; Tier 2 "situational enter" — TT-77, AQ, KQs, etc., EV depends on position and opponents; Tier 3 "conditional speculation" — small pairs, suited connectors, positive when entering cheap deep, negative shallow or expensive; Tier 4 "negative EV" — dominated hands like K9o, Q8s, losing to open from any position (except special steal spots). Replace the "pretty/ugly" binary with "this hand's EV tier in this position, stack, and opponent context". (Concepts from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.5 starting-hand groupings)

Starting-hand entry EV = showdown value + made-hand potential × implied odds + positional bonus × equity realization − domination-risk penalty
Example (100bb cash, unopened): AA ≈ +1.2bb/hand; 77 ≈ deep +0.2bb, shallow −0.3bb; K9o in UTG ≈ −0.3bb
Core: the same hand's EV shifts continuously with position, stack depth, and opponent strength — the mathematical basis for "tiers" replacing "fixed tables"

David Sklansky's Gap Concept: the hand strength needed to call someone's opening raise is higher than what you need to open-raise yourself. Two reasons: (1) the raiser has already shown strength — you face a stronger range; (2) opening carries Fold Equity (opponents may fold and you win the blinds), while calling doesn't — you lose one winning path.

Example: A9o can open-raise from the CO (has Fold Equity + position), but after a UTG open you should fold the same A9o in the CO — A9o is severely dominated vs the UTG range (mostly AQ/AK/big pairs): hitting an A can even lose big money, which is reverse implied odds (T2) manifesting preflop.

Gap Concept's modern theoretical basis (why calling a raise needs stronger hands): (1) range filtering — the raiser's range has already removed its weakest part, so you face an upgraded strength distribution; (2) equity-realization loss — a passive caller has no postflop initiative and may be driven off by later bets, realizing less with the same strength than the aggressor (linking to this chapter's position theory); (3) reverse implied odds — calling with marginal hands builds yourself a "win small, lose big" structure. Modern solvers show the Gap's size flexes with position and stacks, but the direction always holds: facing shown strength, your entry bar must move up. (Concepts from: The Theory of Poker Ch.2-3; Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.5)

Example (preflop tiering): BTN opens 2.5bb, you're in the SB. The 3Bet range splits into two piles: the value pile QQ+, AKs/AKo (~2.5%, ahead of BTN's calling range); the bluff pile A5s, KQs-type (~4%, choosing combos with A or K blockers so BTN struggles to re-raise with AA/KK or call with Ax). The calling pile is JJ-22, AQs, 87s, etc. (speculative, relying on implied odds). This is Gap logic applied preflop: against BTN's wide open, you both re-raise harder and give every bluff 3Bet a blocking rationale.

Example (stack depth changes tiering): shallow 25bb — speculative tier (55, 76s) EV collapses: no depth to cash in sets and straights, and postflop often forced all-in without pot control; made-hand tier (big pairs, AQ+) rises, showdown value dominates. Deep 200bb — roles reverse: speculative tier's value doubles, marginal suited connectors upgrade from "fold" to "call". Same 77: at 25bb vs a 3bb open it's 3Bet-or-fold; at 200bb it's an easy call to mine a set. Stack depth is the second variable in starting-hand tiering.

Modern preflop theory's consensus: when first into an unopened pot, raise rather than limp. Raising keeps Fold Equity, builds initiative, and avoids multiway equity dilution. The problem with limping is it only has one winning path (making a hand) and announces to everyone "my hand isn't worth raising". The same logic applies to 3Betting: against an open, a "3Bet or fold" structure usually beats wide flat-calling (except BB defense, since you've posted a blind and closed the action).

Modern revision of the Gap Concept: as position and stack depth change, the "gap" size flexes — BTN can 3Bet/call very wide vs a CO open, while UTG+1 must be extremely tight vs a UTG open. The principle stands: facing shown strength, your bar must move up.

The "pretty hand" trap: QQ is a pretty hand, but in a 4Bet-then-5Bet shove spot against a Nit who only 5Bets AA/KK, QQ is a -EV "bad hand". Starting-hand value isn't an absolute label — it's the joint result of current position, stack depth, and opponent range. Tiered thinking requires repricing every hand in every context.

To judge whether a hand can call an open, don't ask "how pretty is it", ask three questions: Am I dominated? Do I have position? Are stacks deep enough to cash in the potential? Fold if two answers are "no".
t3-fundamental-theorem: David Sklansky's Fundamental Theorem of Poker (The Theory of Poker): every time an opponent plays differently from "how he would play if he could see your hole cards", you profit; every time you play differently from "how you would play if you could see the opponent's hole cards", the opponent profits.
Poker's profit doesn't come from good cards but from opponent errors — your whole strategy (bets, sizing, bluffs, slowplay) essentially creates situations where opponents are more likely to err.

The theorem's quantitative form: your profit = Σ expected money from each opponent decision error
Profit = opponent error probability × EV each error gives up on average
Example: river value bet 50, opponent calls with a beaten hand 30% → profit = 0.30 × 50 = +15
Exploitation direction: opponent calls too much → increase value-bet sizing; folds too much → increase bluff frequency

Example: you flat-call preflop with AA and the opponent sees a free flop with T9o and flops two pair. The opponent seeing the flop with T9o was an error (he'd fold if he knew you had AA), but your limp turned that error into a free or even correct play — you fixed the opponent's error for him. That's the mathematical explanation for why "over-slowplaying" violates the theorem.

Example (value-bet direction): river, you hold the nut flush, pot 100. By the theorem, the opponent holding JJ (which you beat) should fold if he could see your cards; but he can't, and calls your 50 bet — the opponent is making a "call too much" error, exactly your value bet's profit source. Zoom out: every time your strong hand gets called by a weak hand, the opponent is donating via an error, and your job is to keep creating those spots.

Example (bluff direction): river, you hold unpaired A♠K♠ on board 8♦6♦4♣3♥2♣, pot 100, you shove 80. If the opponent could see your cards he should call with any pair (you're only high cards); but he can't, and you estimate 70% fold — the opponent is making a "fold too much" error, and your bluff profits. The two opposite examples show: identifying which direction the opponent deviates from the theorem decides whether you value-bet more or bluff more (the starting point of T7 exploitation).

Opponent errors split into two classes: calling too much (paying too much against your value bets) and folding too much (folding too much against your bluffs). No opponent can avoid erring in both directions simultaneously — if he calls a lot, value-bet more and bluff less; if he folds a lot, bluff more and thin your value. Identifying which direction an opponent errs is the entire starting point of exploitative strategy (T7, T9).

Initiative is the narrative right gained by the last preflop raiser: postflop he can bet first representing the strongest range (Continuation Bet), forcing opponents to decide first without information. Initiative is a kind of "structural bluff license" — on the same flop, a bet with initiative carries far more credibility than one without. This is also the deeper reason Gap Concept favors raising over calling: a raise buys not just the current pot but the initiative on every subsequent street.

Note: the Fundamental Theorem has exceptions in multiway pots (one player's "correct" call can hurt both you and a third party), so its strictest application is heads-up pots. This is also an important lesson in theory study — every theorem has an applicability boundary.

Results-oriented bias: getting called and losing on a shove ≠ wrong decision; the opponent folding and you winning ≠ right decision. The theorem's unit of measurement is "is the decision correct", not "did this hand win". A single hand's win/loss is variance performing; the theorem's profit comes from accumulating repeated correct decisions long-term — judge the decision first in review, then talk about results (the core claim of Thinking in Bets, detailed in T8).
Before every action, silently ask: "if the opponent could see my cards, would he want me to do this?" If the answer is "yes", you're probably making an error.
t4-range-thinking: A range is the set of all hand combos a player can hold at a given decision point. "What cards does he have?" is the wrong question — you can never know a single hand for sure. "What is his range, and how much weight does each part carry?" is the answerable question. Range thinking is the key step that turns an incomplete-information game into a computable problem.

Three levels of hand reading: Level 1 only looks at your own cards; Level 2 guesses the opponent's "one hand"; Level 3 builds a range for the opponent and updates it with every action. All serious strategy discussion happens at Level 3.
The Narrative of a Range: Actions Are Filters

Every action filters the opponent's range: a UTG open narrows it to roughly the top 15%; a flop C-Bet keeps the betting range and removes the folding range; a turn check removes most strong value... By the river, a logically consistent player's range has been compressed to something very specific. Reading isn't telepathy — it's set operations along the action sequence.

Example: A tight-aggressive player opens UTG, the BTN calls. Flop K♠7♦2♣, UTG C-Bets, BTN calls. Turn 3♥, UTG fires again, BTN calls again. River 2♦, UTG shoves — his range narrative is "claiming K+ strength on all three streets": AK, KK, AA, and 77 dominate, with an occasional AQ bluff. Your KQ becomes a bluff catcher, and the decision shifts from "I have a pretty big pair of K" to "does his shoving range bluff enough to cover 25%?"

Example 2 (preflop range construction): You open ~40% on the BTN and BB 3Bets to 3x. His action filters his range into {QQ+, AK, some AQo, a few A5s-A4s balancing 3Bets} — of your 40% opening range, only the top 8-10% has the right to continue (4Bet or call) right now. Range thinking starts preflop: opening width directly determines your fold-to-3Bet rate, and that fold rate is precisely where the opponent's 3Bet profit comes from.

Example 3 (street-by-street range updating): Flop Q♠8♦3♣, you bet and the opponent calls; his range is mainly {Qx, 88, 33, small/medium pairs, two-overcard draws}. The turn 2♥ is a blank — his range narrative barely changes, so you can keep firing to represent Q+. But if the turn were 9♠ (completing draws like 89s/97s in his calling range), the combos that "suddenly got strong" multiply and your double-barrel frequency should drop — range updating is a set operation done street by street, not a one-shot guess.
Range vs Range, Not Hand vs Hand

Every one of your own actions also declares a range to the opponent. High-level play is "my range vs his range": evaluating a bet isn't asking "is betting this hand good" but "how does my whole range build its bet/check mix at this node, and which part does this hand belong to?" This is the mindset prerequisite for GTO strategy (T5).

Quantitative tool for range vs range: your overall equity = Σ(share of each combo × that combo's equity vs the opponent's range)
Example: your range = {AA 6 combos, KK 6 combos}, opponent's range = {AK 16 combos}
AA vs AK is about 93%, KK vs AK about 70% → overall equity = 0.5×93% + 0.5×70% ≈ 81%
This weighted calculation replaces "my hand" and answers whether the whole range should commit at this node (concept from: MSSA Ch.1-4 range-construction methodology)

Range consistency: if your action sequence can't tell a self-consistent range story (e.g. check the flop and turn, then suddenly overbet-shove the river for nuts), observant opponents will snap-call your bluffs.

Practice with "range snapshots" in review: at the end of every street, write down three tiers of the opponent's range (value / medium / bluffs) with rough weights, then verify after showdown which street your snapshot drifted on.
t4-combinatorics: The quantitative tool of range analysis is the combinatorics you learned in T1: a pair has 6 combos, a suited hand 4, an offsuit hand 12, and any two unpaired ranks 16. When the opponent shoves the river and you must judge the "value:bluff" ratio, counting combos on both sides one by one is the only rigorous method.

Pocket pair = C(4,2) = 6 combos; when one card of that rank is on board = C(3,2) = 3 combos
Suited hand (e.g. AKs) = 4; offsuit (AKo) = 12; total (AK) = 4×4 = 16
Bluff ratio = bluff combos ÷ (value combos + bluff combos), compare with the required equity for the answer

Example: Board K♠9♦4♣2♥7♠, the opponent shoves the river and you read his value range as {KK, 99, 44, K9s} and bluffs as {A♠Q♠, A♠J♠ class missed backdoors}. Value combos = KK 3 (one K on board) + 99 3 + 44 3 + K9s 2 = 11; bluffs about 6. Bluff ratio 6/17 ≈ 35% > required 25% equity (facing a pot bet), so the call is correct — notice the conclusion comes entirely from counting, not feel.
Every card on the board trims related combos: with one K on board, KK drops from 6 to C(3,2)=3 and AK from 16 to 12. You must count combos "looking at the board".

A blocker is a card you hold that reduces the count of specific opponent combos. When you hold A♠, the opponent's nut-flush combos like A♠X♠ drop to zero — you "block" it. Blockers turn your hole cards from mere hand strength into information about the opponent's range.

Two classic blocker applications: (1) bluff selection — bluff when holding a nut-flush blocker (e.g. a lone A♠ on a three-spade board), because the opponent's strongest calling hands are blocked and your fold equity rises; (2) bluff-catching / over-folding — when your hand blocks the opponent's bluff combos, his range skews more toward value and you should lean fold (only call when you unblock bluffs).

Example: A three-heart board and you hold A♥ (but no flush). Against a big shove, you happen to block every A♥X♥ nut-flush combo — half of the "claimed" strongest hands are falsified, boosting the credibility and success rate of both your raise-bluff and hero call.

Example 2 (preflop 4Bet spot): You hold A♠K♣ and read the opponent's 4Bet range as {AA, KK, QQ, AK}. Without a blocker the total is 6+6+6+16 = 34; holding AK: AA drops to C(3,2)=3, KK to 3, QQ stays 6, AK drops to 3×3=9 → 21 total. QQ (where you're ahead) rises from 6/34 ≈ 18% to 6/21 ≈ 29% — blockers turn "ahead/behind weight" into precisely computable inputs, giving preflop all-in EV a foundation.
The blocker effect is marginal: it adjusts combo ratios, not rewrites the whole range. Before letting a blocker talk you into a wild play, confirm the base range analysis supports the direction.

Off-the-table drill: set up a random board, assign the opponent a range, and time yourself counting value and bluff combos. Once fluent, you only need to count the key branches in play — you can get the ratio in under 10 seconds.
t4-range-advantage: Range advantage: on a given board, one side's overall average equity is higher. Nut advantage: one side's range contains more of the strongest combos (sets, big two pairs, nut flushes, etc.). They often point the same way but not always — distinguishing them is the key to modern postflop strategy.

Example 1: A♠K♦7♣ board, UTG opener vs BB caller. UTG's range is full of AK/AQ/AA/KK, while most of BB's strong Ax already 3Bet out of range — UTG holds both range and nut advantage and can C-Bet small and frequently with his entire range.

Example 2: 6♥5♥4♠ board, again UTG vs BB. UTG's big pairs still have overall equity (range advantage shrinks but persists), but combos like 87s, 53s, and 22 (straights/sets) live almost exclusively in BB's defense range — BB has the nut advantage. UTG's C-Bet frequency must drop sharply, while BB earns the license to check-raise and lead.

Example 3 (3Bet pot and turn flip): In a 3Bet pot you're IP on J♠T♠4♦. BB's defense range holds plenty of Jx/Tx, straight draws, and flush draws, but your range (the 3Better) has overpairs, AJ/KJ/QJ, and nut draws — double advantage on your side, so bet frequently. The turn 9♣ completes QT straights — QT is far more common in your range than BB's (his defense range barely contains pure QT), and the nut advantage tilts further toward you; you can even overbet directly.

Quick judgment: high boards (A/K high) favor the preflop raiser; low connected boards (small/medium connectors) favor the preflop caller (especially BB, whose defense range keeps all the small cards). The wetter the board, the more important nut-advantage ownership becomes.

Quantitative framework (compute per flop):
Range advantage = your overall range equity vs the opponent's (you have it when your range-vs-range equity > 50%)
Nut advantage = the density of your "top 5% strongest" combos ÷ the opponent's same density (> 1 means you own more nuts)
Evaluate both dimensions independently, then synthesize: double advantage → bet small and often; nut advantage alone → overbet license; neither → check frequently (concept from: Applications of NLHE Range Construction board-ownership analysis)

Range advantage sets betting frequency: the bigger your advantage, the more often you can bet (even small bets with your whole range). Nut advantage sets the sizing ceiling: only the side with more nuts earns the right to apply oversized (overbet) pressure, because the opponent's strongest hands can only respond passively. With neither advantage, the standard play is to check frequently and control the pot.

The same framework explains turn/river "board changes": when the turn completes draws in the caller's range (e.g. a low connected board makes a fourth connected card), nut advantage changes hands and the aggressor should contract; when the turn is a blank, the existing advantage persists and you can keep firing.

Common mistake: treating "I have top pair" as a reason to bet. The correct order is to first decide whose range the board belongs to, then decide what role your specific hand plays under that strategy.
Before every flop, spend two seconds asking: "whose range does this board hit, and who holds more nut combos?" The answers basically determine this hand's frequency and sizing framework.
t5-game-theory: Game theory studies strategic interaction between rational decision-makers. Heads-up poker (ignoring rake) is a classic two-player zero-sum game: one side's gain is exactly the other's loss. Von Neumann's 1928 minimax theorem proves such games always have an "optimal strategy pair" — when both sides play their respective strategies, neither can profit by changing unilaterally.

Nash Equilibrium: a set of strategies where no single player can improve by deviating unilaterally. John Nash proved it exists in an extremely broad class of games — poker's GTO strategy is precisely poker's Nash equilibrium.

Zero-sum math: heads-up U₁(a,b) + U₂(a,b) = 0 (one side's gain is the other's loss)
Minimax theorem: there exists a game value v such that max_a min_b U₁(a,b) = min_b max_a U₁(a,b) = v
An equilibrium strategy guarantees your expectation ≥ v, and the opponent can't unilaterally push it lower — this is the mathematical source of being "unexploitable" (concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.2 basic game theory)
What Equilibrium Means — and Common Misreadings

The equilibrium strategy is "unexploitable": no matter how the opponent plays, your expectation is never below the game value. It doesn't promise to "win the most" — against a maniac donating money, the equilibrium strategy earns less than a targeted exploitative one. Equilibrium is the floor, exploitation is the ceiling; this tension runs through all advanced theory (unified in T9).

Example: Rock-paper-scissors' equilibrium is randomizing each 1/3. If the opponent always throws rock, the equilibrium strategy still breaks even (expectation 0), but the exploitative "always paper" wins every round. However, if you always throw paper you become exploitable yourself (he switches to scissors) — deviating from equilibrium to exploit necessarily opens your own leaks. Poker is exactly isomorphic.

Example 2 (minimax in a toy game): You write 1 or 2, the opponent guesses; if he guesses right you lose 1, if wrong you win 2. When you mix 50/50, his expectation guessing 1 = 0.5×1 + 0.5×(−2) = −0.5, and guessing 2 = 0.5×(−2) + 0.5×1 = −0.5 — both sides equal, so you lock in +0.5. Any deviation lets him pick the favorable side and push your expectation down. Poker solvers do exactly the same thing: at each node find the mixing ratio that makes all opponent responses indifferent.

If your strategy is deterministic (same spot, same action forever), observant opponents will eventually decipher and counter it. An equilibrium strategy therefore must include mixed components: the same hand at the same node splits across actions by certain probabilities (detailed in this level's chapter 4). Randomizing isn't indecisiveness — it's a mathematical weapon that makes any opponent guess unprofitable.

Important multiway warning: the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee strictly holds only for two-player zero-sum games. In pots with three or more, even if everyone plays "equilibrium", coalition effects can damage one side. Theoretical tools all have applicability boundaries.

Think of equilibrium as a "bulletproof vest", not a "weapon": wear it against strong and unknown opponents for safety, take it off and switch to a knife (exploitation) once you identify weaknesses — knowing when to wear it and when to take it off is the real skill.
t5-gto-concept: GTO (Game Theoretically Optimal) refers to poker's Nash equilibrium strategy. Solvers approximate it through massive iteration: given preflop ranges, stack depth, and available sizings, they output each hand's action frequency at every node. GTO is the "origin of the coordinate system" for strategy — not an answer to copy verbatim, but the benchmark for measuring every deviation.

Intuitive features of GTO: every bet is composed of value and bluffs in a specific ratio; every calling range makes the opponent's bluffs exactly break even; every sizing choice makes all opponent responses indifferent. It is "exactly right" everywhere — no more, no less.

Value:bluff ratio derivation (pot P, bet bP, opponent has a bluff catcher):
Opponent call EV = f×(P+2bP) − (1−f)×bP, set = 0 (indifferent) → f = b/(1+2b) (f = your bluff share of the betting range)
Example: full pot b=1 → bluffs 1/3 (value:bluff = 2:1); half pot b=0.5 → bluffs 25% (3:1) (concept from: Modern Poker Theory Ch.2-3 GTO structure)

This ratio exactly equals the pot odds the opponent needs to call — making his call and fold EV with a bluff catcher identical (indifferent). The bigger the bet, the more bluffs it can carry: the mathematical root of "big size = polarization" (detailed in T6). On the turn and flop, because more streets remain, bluff share can be higher (some bluffs later give up or convert).

Example: On the river you full-pot bet; your range should be about 2/3 value + 1/3 bluffs. If you actually "only bet nuts" (0% bluffs), the opponent can exploit you by folding everything to your bets; if you bluff more than half, he exploits you by calling everything. The equilibrium ratio is the only construction that leaves the opponent helpless either way.

Example 2 (minimum necessary deviation): You observe an opponent who only calls big river bets 30% of the time (equilibrium ~50%). Based on this you can raise your river overbet bluff frequency overall — but cap the adjustment at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 40%", keeping room to return to baseline anytime. This is exactly the executable example of "using GTO as baseline, making directed, disciplined deviations from observable biases".
The Correct Relationship Between GTO and Exploitation

The mature framework in practice: use GTO as the baseline to understand what each node "should" look like, then make minimal necessary deviations based on the opponent's observable biases (Maximally Exploitative in direction, Minimally Exploitative in magnitude). The baseline gives you invincibility; the deviations give you profit. Exploitation without GTO is running naked; GTO without deviation is self-shackling.

Common misreading: "GTO is playing tight" or "GTO is balancing to the point of boredom". In fact solver strategies are full of high-frequency bluffs, overbet shoves, and thin value — it just keeps all of it at ratios the opponent can't counter.

When studying solver outputs, don't memorize frequencies; ask three whys: why this sizing on this board? Why does this hand go into the betting range and that one into the checking range? Why did the frequency change on the turn? Understand the structure and the frequencies will remember themselves.

When studying solver output, don't memorize frequencies — ask three whys: why this sizing on this board? Why does this hand enter the betting range and that one check? Why did the frequency change on the turn? Understand the structure and the frequencies will remember themselves.
t5-mdf-alpha: MDF answers: facing a bet, what minimum share of my range must I continue with (call or raise) so the opponent's "any-two-card bluff" is unprofitable? If your defense is below MDF, the opponent needs no hand strength at all — every bet itself is a money printer.

MDF derivation (P = pot, B = bet, b = B/P, f = your fold rate):
Opponent pure-bluff EV = f×P − (1−f)×B, set = 0 → f = B/(P+B) = b/(1+b)
Your minimum defense frequency MDF = 1 − f = P/(P+B) = 1/(1+b)
Example: half pot b=0.5 → 67%; full pot b=1 → 50%; 2x pot b=2 → 33% (concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.5-6 bet-fold subgame)
Alpha: The Bluff's Break-Even Fold Rate

Alpha (α) = bet ÷ (pot + bet) = b/(1+b) = 1 − MDF
Example: a half-pot bluff needs the opponent to fold ≥33% to break even; full pot needs ≥50%

MDF and Alpha are two sides of the same coin: when the defender's fold rate exactly equals α, the attacker's pure-bluff EV is zero — neither side can profit by changing frequency, which is the equilibrium point of this "bet-fold" subgame.

Example: Pot 100, opponent bets 50. MDF = 100/150 ≈ 67%, so you need to continue with roughly your strongest 67%. Choose which hands to continue by ranking hand strength + improvement potential: made hands and good draws first, pure garbage goes into the folding 33%. If you actually only defend 40%, the opponent instantly profits 0.60×100 − 0.40×50 = 40 on every 50 bluff.

Example 2 (overbets and MDF): Pot 100, opponent shoves 200 (b=2). MDF = 100/300 ≈ 33%, greatly reducing your defense burden; meanwhile the overbet's equilibrium bluff share b/(1+2b) = 2/5 = 40%, i.e. his range should be 60% value + 40% bluffs. Judging whether his "value:bluff" matches 3:2 matters more than mechanically memorizing MDF: if he's actually 90% value, your defense should drop below 33% — this is the correct combination of MDF and exploitation.

Defense isn't only calling: raises also count toward defense frequency. Against high-frequency bluffers, substitute some calls with raises to both defend and collect value; against tight-passive value bettors, over-folding (below MDF) is the exploitation. First compute the total, then allocate.

MDF is the floor against "balanced bluffing opponents", not a universal prescription: (1) against opponents who almost never bluff (many low-stakes players' big river bets), folding well below MDF is actually optimal exploitation; (2) in multiway pots the defense burden is shared — not everyone needs to hit MDF; (3) with a raise option, defense can be built from calls plus raises. Remember: equilibrium frequencies are the bulletproof vest when you lack opponent information; exploit first when you have information.
Memorize three practical anchors: defend 75% vs 1/3-pot bets, 67% vs half-pot, 50% vs full-pot. Whatever sits below the anchor is automatic profit you're handing the opponent.

The easiest leak to self-audit in review: track your actual fold rate against big turn/river bets. The vast majority of players fold far above equilibrium — which is why the opponent's big bets always seem to "just happen" to make you fold.
t5-mixed-strategy: Mixed Strategies and the Indifference Principle

Open any solver and you'll see: the same hand at the same node is often split across multiple actions (e.g. 70% bet / 30% check). The foundation is the Indifference Principle: in equilibrium, a hand is mixed only when all its actions have exactly equal EV; and the purpose of that mixing is to make the "opponent's" marginal hands (like bluff catchers) also exactly indifferent between calling and folding.

Indifference principle proof sketch (mixed hand H):
Let H's bet EV = V_b and check EV = V_c. If V_b > V_c, a rational strategy bets 100%; if V_b < V_c, it checks 100%
→ Mixing exists ⇔ V_b = V_c (by contradiction: any imbalance gets exploited by the opponent)
Similarly, the opponent's bluff catcher is indifferent between call/fold in equilibrium — the two indifferences jointly lock in the frequencies (concept from: Modern Poker Theory Ch.3 mixed strategies and indifference)

Division of labor between two hand types: "pure-strategy hands" in the range (unique clearly-best action, e.g. betting nuts, folding garbage) contribute most of the EV; "mixed hands" sit at the tipping point, and their frequency allocation is the glue that keeps the whole system unexploitable.

Example: On the river you hold a bluff catcher facing a full-pot bet. In equilibrium the opponent bluffs 1/3, and your required equity is exactly 33% — call and fold have identical EV. The solver might output something like "call 50% / fold 50%". Practical meaning: the single-decision cost of getting these wrong is ≈0, so don't agonize; the real EV differences hide in range construction on earlier streets.
How to Execute Mixing in Practice

Humans can't be truly random; use external random sources (watch the second hand, use dealt suit) or "simplify to pure strategies": split the mixed frequency by readable features (suited hands bet, offsuit check). For most players the more pragmatic path is: accept that choosing either side at a mixed node costs almost nothing, and invest practice time in decision points with high EV differences.
Node Locking: The Bridge From Equilibrium to Exploitation

Node locking is an advanced solver feature: "lock" the opponent's strategy at a node to the real tendency you observed (e.g. "this opponent never bluffs the river" or "folds to C-Bets 60%"), then re-solve your optimal response. The output is the maximally exploitative strategy against that leak.

Example: After locking "BB folds to turn double-barrel 55% (equilibrium ~45%)" and re-solving, the solver immediately pushes your turn bluff frequency higher, even adding weak hands that originally checked into the betting range — it precisely shows "how much you should deviate for every 1% the opponent deviates" to harvest. Node locking turns exploitation from intuition into calculation.

Example 2 (five-step node-locking workflow): ① collect enough HUD samples to confirm the leak (e.g. "BTN folds to 3Bet 65%"); ② lock that node to a fixed frequency in the solver; ③ re-solve your response and compare to baseline; ④ mark the specific hands whose frequencies and sizings got pushed up; ⑤ execute in play, re-checking the sample roughly every 500 hands to see if it still holds. A "lock" without data support is just exploitation on paper.

Node-locking discipline: the locked tendency must come from real observation over a sufficient sample, not single-hand impressions. Using imagined leaks for maximum exploitation is like swapping a bulletproof vest for a paper shirt.

Learning path suggestion: first use solvers to understand equilibrium shapes (the why), then use node locking to study "standard harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate in live play — close the three-step loop and theory becomes profit.
t6-bet-purpose: The Two Fundamental Purposes of Betting

The first principle of modern betting theory: every bet must answer "do I want worse hands to call (value) or better hands to fold (bluff)?" A bet that does neither is burning chips. The classic counterexample is the "probe bet" with medium-strength hands: worse hands all fold (no value collected) and better hands all call (nothing bluffed) — a loss on both ends.

The standard for a value bet isn't "I might be ahead" but "more than half of the opponent's calling range is worse than me". If a bet doesn't meet this standard, the calls it collects lose money on average — such marginal value is called "thin value" and needs precise range judgment to back it.

Value-bet break-even formula (pot P, bet B, win rate w when called):
EV = w×(P+B) − (1−w)×B > 0 → w > B/(P+2B)
Half pot (B=0.5P) only needs w > 25%; full pot needs w > 33%
So "more than half your calling range is worse" is the conservative textbook version; the exact version loosens with sizing — the mathematical basis for why thin value can profit (concept from: The Theory of Poker betting and value)

"Protection" (making the opponent's live hands pay or forfeit equity) is a real but secondary betting reason: it only matters when the opponent has meaningful equity to deny AND your hand fears being outdrawn (e.g. a pair on a wet board). Beware of bets justified mainly by protection — if the opponent either has no equity (garbage) or dominates you (made hands), protection is a false premise.

Example: On a dry K♠7♦2♣ board, betting KQ is value (worse Kx, 77-JJ, 7x call); on a wet 9♥8♥7♠ board, betting A9 is mainly protection + thin value (lots of two-overcard draws with 25-40% equity — getting them to fold or pay is both fine); the same A9 becomes a bluff catcher against a three-street shove — one hand's betting reason drifts with board and node, and must be re-answered every time.

Example 2 (river thin value): Board J♦8♦4♣2♠6♠, you hold A♣J♣ and bet 3/4 pot. If the opponent's calling range has more worse hands (weak Jx, busted diamond draws) than better ones (88, 44), this is thin value; if the opponent knows you never bet thin value at this node, your betting range is only strong hands and he'll fold almost all marginal hands to you. Thin value not only makes money directly — it also gives your strong hands and bluffs credibility.

The strategic value of checking is often underestimated: (1) pot control — keep the pot at a size medium hands can afford; (2) inducement — let the opponent's bluffs build the pot for you (check-raise / check-call); (3) protecting your checking range — if all your good hands bet, your checking range is only garbage and the opponent can attack at full force whenever you check. In equilibrium, strong hands mix into the checking line at some frequency precisely to make your checks unattackable.

A semi-bluff is the intermediate state on the value-bluff spectrum: behind now (bluff component) but with meaningful improvement equity (future value component). It has one extra winning path over a pure bluff, which is why draws are always first on the bluff-candidate list.

Build the "complete the sentence before betting" habit: "I'm betting to get ____ to call, or ____ to fold." When you can't fill either blank with a specific hand type, checking is almost always better.
t6-sizing-theory: A polarized range consists of "strong value + bluffs" with the middle missing — either nuts or air. A linear/merged range runs continuously from strongest to medium hands with almost no pure bluffs. These two structures map to radically different optimal sizings.

Core theorem: polarized ranges prefer large sizings (full pot, overbet, even all-in); linear ranges prefer small-to-medium sizings (1/4-1/2 pot). Sizing is both the leaker and the amplifier of range structure.

The math behind size↔structure (pot P, bet bP):
① Bluff capacity f = b/(1+2b) rises monotonically with b: big bets can carry more bluffs, serving polarized ranges
② Break-even win rate when called w = b/(1+2b): small bets need very low win rates to profit, serving linear ranges
→ Polarized = big (value doesn't fear calls + high bluff capacity); linear = small (cheap rent-collection + low break-even line) (concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.9-10 sizing and equilibrium)

The value part of a polarized range doesn't fear calls (the more you call the better for us), and the bluff part needs maximum fold pressure — big sizing serves both ends at once. And per the T5 formula b/(1+2b): the bigger the sizing, the more bluffs it can carry, which is exactly the capacity a polarized range needs. Conversely, mixing medium hands into big bets is a disaster: hands worse than you are scared off by the size and only better hands call.

Linear ranges (e.g. full-range C-Bets on range-advantage boards) use small sizing: the goal isn't maximum fold rate but collecting rent at minimum cost from the opponent's entire continuing range — forcing his many marginal hands to choose between "folding loses" and "calling also loses", while preserving a cheap showdown path for your own medium hands.

Example: A♠K♦7♣ dry board (raiser's range crushes): standard is a full-range 1/4-1/3 pot small bet — linear rent collection. When the turn brings Q♠ and your range's nut density rises further, you can switch to a polarized 2/3-to-full-pot bet, pushing AQ/KQ/77 and bluffs into a big pot together. In the same hand, sizing evolves with range structure.

Example 2 (river overbet): Board A♠8♦4♣2♥J♥, you hold AJ and judge the opponent has many Ax that won't fold to a standard bet, so you shove 1.5x pot. Value {AJ, AA, 88, 44, A8s} + bluffs {Q♥T♥ class busted nut draws}. The overbet extracts payment from Ax while maintaining balance with b/(1+2b)=0.75/2.5=37.5% bluff density; if your range is actually linear (lots of medium Ax), the overbet is a disaster — sizing must be issued by range structure.

Example 3 (blocking bet in play): On the turn OOP with K♠J♠ (top pair + backdoor flush), pot 200, effective 900. Checking would face an 80%-pot bet, so you lead 50 (~1/4 pot): medium hands see the showdown at a self-chosen price, and the opponent's weak hands can't see a free card. If you never mix strong hands into this line, the opponent starts raising to strip you — equilibrium requires the top of your blocking range to carry some strong hands (e.g. slow-playing some strong Kx in the same line) so raises are unprofitable.
Blocking Bets: The Defender's Sizing Weapon

A blocking bet is a ~1/4-pot small lead by the OOP player to "set the price first", seeing showdown cheaply or collecting thin value with medium hands, avoiding facing the opponent's big bet after checking. It's the linear-small-bet logic applied OOP — but must avoid being exploited by raises once recognized, so the equilibrium blocking range also needs some strong hands mixed in.

Blocking bet pricing (pot P, you bet 0.25P):
Opponent's required call equity = 0.25/(1+2×0.25) ≈ 17%, your small bet makes his marginal hands "a shame to fold, unprofitable to call"
If he raises to 3x (0.75P), his bluff EV = f×1.25P − (1−f)×0.75P; once your fold rate f exceeds 37.5% he profits automatically
→ Equilibrium requires your blocking range to defend ≥ 62.5%, so it must include enough strong hands (concept from: Modern Poker Theory Sizing blocking-bet equilibrium)

The amateur sizing-leak pattern: big bet = strong hand, small bet = weak probe. An opponent who reads this pattern can respond almost perfectly. The fix isn't "do the opposite" — it's making every sizing supported by a structurally complete range (value and bluffs in proportion).

Sizing selection order: first judge whether my range at this node is polarized or linear (determined by range/nut advantage), then let this specific hand obey the range's sizing — not the other way around, letting the sizing obey this hand's mood.
t6-geometric: SPR (Stack-to-Pot Ratio) = effective stack ÷ flop pot. It measures "how deep the pot is relative to the stacks", directly deciding which hand strengths are worth fighting for all the chips: at SPR ≤ 3 (shallow pots), single pairs (top pair good kicker, overpairs) can usually get all-in without letting go; at SPR 6-13 (medium-deep), single pairs need caution and only two pair+ / sets are willing to play for stacks; at SPR 20+ (very deep), nut-tier hands (straights, flushes, big sets) are the all-in candidates.

SPR is shaped preflop: 3Bet pots are naturally low-SPR (favoring single-pair hands like AA/KK), while limp-called pots are high-SPR (favoring nut-potential hands like suited connectors and small pairs). When choosing sizings preflop, strong players are already setting up the postflop SPR.
Geometric Sizing: The Art of Uniform Scaling

Geometric sizing: when you plan to get the effective stack in across three streets, use the same pot percentage each street so the pot grows geometrically and the river shove lands exactly. This is the mathematical solution to value maximization: uniform pressure makes the opponent's calling price identical at every call, with no cheap "brake" on any street.

Three-street geometric sizing derivation (pot P, effective stack S, SPR = S/P, bet fraction x of pot each street):
The pot scales by (1+2x)³, and a three-street all-in requires P(1+2x)³ = P + 2S → x = ((1 + 2·SPR)^(1/3) − 1) / 2
Example: SPR=7.5 → 16^(1/3) ≈ 2.52, x ≈ 0.76 (about 76% pot each street)
Bet 76 on the flop → pot 252; bet 191 on the turn → pot 635; shove the remaining 483 on the river — exactly cleared (concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.9 geometric planning of multi-street betting)

Example: You flop a set in a 3Bet pot at SPR ≈ 4. Geometric planning only needs ~60-70% pot each street to shove by the river — no overbet scare on any street needed. Conversely, if you only bet 1/3 pot on flop and turn, the river will have 1.5x pot left, forcing an abrupt overbet shove that instantly tightens the opponent's calling range.

Example 2 (low-SPR quick clearing): Flop pot 200, effective 400 (SPR=2). With two-street geometric x = ((1+4)^(1/2) − 1)/2 ≈ 62%: bet 124 on the flop → pot 448, shove the remaining 276 (about 62% pot) on the turn — exactly cleared. Compare the wrong line: betting only 1/3 pot on the flop leaves the turn pot at ~330 with 267 behind, needing an abrupt ~80% pot bet to clear — in low-SPR pots the discipline of "enter the geometric line directly" matters more than the sizing itself.
The Link Between Frequency and Sizing

The multi-street view also reveals frequency decay: the flop betting range contains many "one-shot" semi-bluffs and equity-denial bets; the range that keeps firing on the turn naturally narrows and strengthens (the industry's "turn is the watershed"), and the three-barrel river range is the most polarized. Understanding this decay lets you read the sudden attack window when "opponent calls the flop, then checks the turn" — his range just exposed its ceiling.

Planning starts on the flop: the first thing when you see the flop isn't deciding "bet or not" but asking "if I'm playing three streets, is the goal all-in or pot control?" The answer back-solves this street's sizing. A bet with no destination is a random walk.

Heuristic geometric sizings to memorize: SPR≈2 → about 60% pot on the flop, shove the turn; SPR≈4 → about 55% pot each street; SPR≈7 → about 3/4 pot each street (exact via x = ((1+2·SPR)^(1/3) − 1)/2). Remember the anchors and apply the nearest one in play.
t7-stats: Single-hand impressions are full of noise (the opponent who bluffed you once with 72o isn't necessarily a maniac). Statistics compress large-sample behavior into a stable portrait. The core four metrics established by the online HUD era — VPIP, PFR, AF, WTSD — combine to infer almost a player's entire strategic skeleton. Live, there's no HUD, but the same dimensions can be accumulated manually through observation.

VPIP (Voluntarily Put $ In Pot): share of hands you voluntarily put money in — measures looseness. Table reference: <18% tight, 22-28% standard, >32% loose. PFR (Preflop Raise): preflop raise percentage — measures aggressiveness. The gap between VPIP and PFR is the key signal: a small gap (like 24/20) means raise-when-entering, the hallmark of discipline; a big gap (like 40/8) means lots of passive limping — the fingerprint of a typical fish.

AF (Aggression Factor) = (bets + raises) ÷ calls, measuring postflop style: <1.5 passive, 2-3 standard aggressive, >4 high-pressure. WTSD (Went To Showdown): share of hands that reached showdown — measures stickiness: >32% signals a calling station (bluffing him = burning money; value bet thin and thick); <22% folds too much (a golden bluff target).

The fifth key metric, 3Bet%: share of reraises after facing a preflop raise. <2% means he only re-raises super-strong hands (a NIT fingerprint); 3-5% is the standard balanced value; >7% raises often with a polarized range (including many bluff 3Bets). Combining 3Bet with VPIP/PFR distinguishes two superficially similar loose players: "38/18 + 3Bet 6%" (loose-aggressive, actively pressures) vs "38/18 + 3Bet 1%" (loose but passive, only calls) — without the 3Bet dimension, the counter-plans for these two are completely different. (Concept from: Poker HUDs analysis; Applications of NLHE Ch.7)

VPIP = hands with voluntary money in ÷ total hands (<18% tight / 22-28% standard / >32% loose)
PFR = preflop raise hands ÷ total hands; VPIP−PFR gap = passive limp frequency
AF = (bet count + raise count) ÷ call count; WTSD = showdown hands ÷ flop-seen hands

Metrics must be read in combination + with sample-size awareness: VPIP/PFR become basically reliable within dozens of hands, while AF/WTSD need hundreds. With insufficient samples, metrics are hypotheses, not conclusions.

Example: Opponent 45/12, AF 0.8, WTSD 38%. Translation: extremely loose preflop, barely raises, passive postflop, calls everything down — a textbook calling station. The counter-plan auto-generates: value bet down to the river, bigger sizes, stop bluffing entirely, and believe him when he suddenly raises (a passive player's aggression = real strength).

Example (combined-reading comparison): Player A: VPIP 24, PFR 20, AF 2.8, WTSD 27, 3Bet 6% — VPIP≈PFR means raise-on-entry, high AF postflop aggression, moderate WTSD: a well-trained TAG/LAG, not worth fighting head-on. Player B: VPIP 38, PFR 6, AF 1.2, WTSD 35, 3Bet 1% — lots of limping, passive postflop, shows down everything: a textbook calling station. The "opponent plans" for these two are completely opposite, derived from the five-metric combination, not any single number.

Example (sample-size trap): A certain opponent's first 35 hands show VPIP 38%, PFR 34% — a wild LAG elite. But look closely: in those 35 hands he was dealt QQ+/AK about 12 times in a row — the "loose-aggressive" was just an illusion propped up by card luck. Extended to 120 hands, the data settles at a 24/20 TAG truth. If you treat those 35 hands as real and immediately adjust your play, you're making a systematic response to one random fluctuation — the most typical cost of "treating a small sample as a conclusion".

The live "manual HUD": count how often the opponent enters a pot per orbit (VPIP), whether entry is a raise or a limp (PFR gap), and postflop whether he bets or calls (AF). Three orbits of observation produce a rough but usable portrait.

Sample-size warning lines: VPIP/PFR need about 50-100 hands to stabilize; AF/WTSD need 300+. Below the threshold, metrics only support "directional hypotheses" — mark confidence and revise after more hands. Better to hold conclusions one session late than define an opponent by the numbers of one random event.

X-ray yourself first: export or recall your own VPIP/PFR/WTSD. Most losers' problems aren't in reading others but in their own 38/10 or a 15% river WTSD — the first application target of exploitation theory is always your own leaks.

HUD discipline (practical Poker HUDs advice): read the hand count before reading metrics; only trust the most recent 300-500 hands (opponents adjust; all-time averages lag); put a question mark on low-sample metrics in notes; clear "expired portraits" after each session and leave trusted hand counts for the next table.
t7-player-types: Using VPIP (looseness) and aggressiveness (PFR/AF) as two axes, players fall into four classic quadrants: tight-aggressive TAG (like 22/18, AF 2.5), loose-aggressive LAG (like 32/26, AF 3.5), tight-passive NIT/rock (like 12/8, AF 1), and loose-passive calling station (like 45/10, AF 0.8). Types aren't a labeling game — each quadrant maps to a clear leak list and harvest plan.

TAG: strong range, good discipline; fighting head-on is unprofitable. The leak is "over-honesty": he gives up easily when his C-Bet meets resistance, and big bets = real hands. Plan: use float and turn attacks more from position, and respect his three barrels. LAG: creates errors with wide ranges and constant pressure — the most dangerous and the most testing for you. Plan: tighten entry ranges but refuse to be pushed around — trap with strong hands so he builds the pot for you, and widen your bluff-catching threshold.

NIT: only nut-tier starting hands; entry is an alarm. Plan: steal his blinds constantly preflop, and retreat when he shows interest postflop — folding top pair to a NIT is no shame. Calling station: a fish that refuses to fold. Plan: as the previous chapter gave — value to the river, zero bluffs. Of the four, the calling station is the most stable profit source; TAG play is your own default starting point.

Type dynamics: the same player drifts across quadrants depending on deep/shallow stacks, winning/losing (Tilt), and fresh/tired states. Keep updating the portrait, especially watching for "NIT turning LAG after losing a big pot" — Tilt is the #1 driver of type drift.

Player portrait = f(VPIP, PFR, AF, WTSD, 3Bet)
Quadrant judgment: VPIP−PFR gap (passivity), AF (postflop aggression), WTSD (stickiness)
Example: 42/8/0.8/38/1% → loose-passive calling station; 24/20/2.8/27/6% → trained TAG
Dynamic drift: portrait(session) ≠ portrait(long-term) — win/loss states shift metrics short-term and require continuous re-estimation

Example: The TAG to your right, after losing two big pots, raises his open frequency from 2 to 5 per orbit and showed down a wild J6s bluff. This is no longer that 22/18 — switch immediately: counter with 3Bets/calls from medium-strong hands you'd normally fold, harvest through the type-drift window until he cools down and returns.
