Example (losing-type drift): A calling station starts at 42/8/0.7/36; after losing three big pots it enters "win it back" mode: WTSD climbs to 44%, fewer bluffs, more showdowns, top pair calls you to the river. Your value bets should get thicker and bigger — his "win-it-back" mindset makes harvesting easier. Watch the reverse too: he may occasionally bluff in desperation, but a station's bluff outbreaks usually subside after one or two, not worth changing the main plan.

Example (winning-type drift): A rock NIT (11/7), after winning two big pots, sees VPIP climb to 18% and starts stealing blinds with A9o from the CO — the classic House Money Effect ("playing looser with winnings"). During the window his blind-steal profit drops, but his 3Bet frequency also rises (trying new lines), and his "new moves" are easier to catch bluffing than usual. Recognize winning drift — don't over-fold to the stale "he never bluffs" portrait.

Don't forget the mirror: opponents are profiling you too. Your bluff success rate is higher under a tight-aggressive image, and your value bets get called more after being caught in one big bluff — image is an asset; spend it at the right moments.

The static-label trap: labeling an opponent TAG and playing him as TAG forever is the biggest death in type theory. Within one session, stack depth, win/loss state, and fatigue all drift players 1-2 quadrants. A label is a snapshot, not an identity — every 30 minutes re-verify with recent behavioral evidence; better to update half a beat late than play the whole table with an expired portrait.

Homework to finish in the first 15 minutes even without big hands: assign each opponent a four-quadrant initial label plus one concrete behavioral evidence. A table with portraits and a table without are two different games.
t7-hand-reading: Hand Reading Is a Process, Not Intuition

TV makes hand reading look like staring into the opponent's pupils. Real hand reading is a trainable pipeline: (1) starting range — set by position and preflop actions (UTG open ≈ top 15%, BB defense ≈ very wide); (2) street-by-street filtering — each action deletes illogical combos; (3) board crossover — re-estimate the strength distribution of the remaining range with board structure; (4) combo counting — count the value:bluff ratio when a precise decision is needed (T4 Ch.2).

The four-step hand-reading process:
①Starting range (position × preflop action) → ②street filtering (action elimination) → ③board crossover (strength re-estimate) → ④combo counting
Bluff share = bluff combos ÷ (value combos + bluff combos)
Call if and only if: bluff share ≥ pot-odds required equity (example: 14 value vs 5 bluffs → 5/19 ≈ 26% ≥ 30% then call)

The golden filter question: "if he held X, would he play it this way?" Note two-way elimination: a bet eliminates "hands he'd usually check", and a check also eliminates "hands he'd usually bet" — passive actions are information too.

Example: A tight-aggressive opponent opens CO, you call on BTN. Flop Q♠T♠6♦ he C-Bets (range still wide: overpairs, Qx, Tx, draws, air). Turn 2♣ he double-barrels (range narrows: mostly AQ+, KK+, strong draws — 2♣ changes nothing, anyone still firing has a real plan). River A♦ he stops and checks — the golden question fires: "would he check AQ/AK? No." His range ceiling was just cut off by his own check; your QJ can confidently bet thin value and easily fold to a raise.

Example (refining step four): 3Bet pot, board K♠8♦5♣2♥3♥, opponent shoves, you hold QQ. Process: starting range (UTG 3Bet defense is tight, mostly 77+, AQ+, KQs) → flop/turn action filtering → river shoving range = {KK, 88, KQ, a few missed-draw bluffs}. Count: KK 3 + 88 3 + KQ 8 = 14 value; bluffs (QJ, T9 missed) about 5. Bluff share 5/19 ≈ 26%, facing a 0.75-pot bet needing 30% → 26% < 30%, fold. This "fold" comes from combo counting and pot odds, not "I feel beaten".

Example (the starting range decides everything): You hold 99, flop 9♥7♠2♦ (top set). Scenario 1: opponent opens BTN, you call BB — his range has plenty of 9x/7x/structured hands; your set is strong but the board needs straight protection. Scenario 2: you open BTN, opponent calls BB — his defense range is very wide (any two cards), your set is close to the nuts and you can confidently bet for value. Same flop, same hand, different starting range → completely different follow-up strategy. Hand reading always starts with "how did he enter the pot preflop".

Reliable hierarchy of live tells (consensus research of Mike Caro and Zachary Elwood): hesitation length before betting, chip-handling manner, and changes in willingness to talk are far more reliable than "nose-touching, eye-blinking". Two validated baselines: strong hands tend toward relaxation (willing to chat, natural movements); bluffs tend toward rigidity (holding breath, stillness, deliberate staring). A quick instant call often signals a draw/medium hand (no raise consideration process). Online, watch the timing: snap bets are often preset actions; small bets after a long think are often struggling weak hands.

Tell discipline: it only deserves "the tie-breaking vote on a balanced decision" and can never overturn range analysis. When range says fold and the tell says call, trust the range — tells have noise, math doesn't.

Over-confident hand reading: "I must finish by naming one hand (he must have AA)" is the biggest mistake of beginner reading. The correct output is a weighted range + confidence — locking one hand means abandoning filtering; any single hand is just one sample in the range, and the set of possibilities is the actionable answer.

Training method: when watching pro hand livestreams, pause on every street, write down your range judgment before watching commentary and showdown. Don't fix wrong answers — record "which filter step went off" — all progress in hand reading hides in the deviation log.
t7-exploit: Exploitation = making a directed deviation opposite to the opponent's deviation from equilibrium. The four most used mappings: opponent folds too much → bluff more; calls too much → add value, remove bluffs; bluffs too much → widen bluff-catching range and use inducing checks; bluffs too little → over-fold to big bets. Each is a direct application of Sklansky's Fundamental Theorem (T3).

The four exploitation mappings:
Folds too much → raise bluff frequency; calls too much → add value, remove bluffs
Bluffs too much → widen bluff-catching range, inducing checks; bluffs too little → over-fold to big bets
Counter-exploitation monitoring: when exploitation profits decay or counter-attack frequency rises → pull back the deviation, restore equilibrium (arms-race loop)

Maximal vs moderate exploitation: against opponents who don't adapt (the vast majority of low-to-mid-stakes players), go straight to maximal exploitation (e.g. 100% stop bluffing a calling station); against strong opponents who watch you, make smaller deviations while keeping the ability to return — exploitation intensity is inversely proportional to the opponent's adaptability.
The Cost of Exploitation: You Open Leaks Too

Every deviation from equilibrium makes you exploitable (the T5 rock-paper-scissors lesson): your strategy of high-frequency blind stealing against tight-passives gets counter-harvested by an opponent who starts defending wide and light-3Betting. So the complete exploitation loop is four steps: observe and profile → directed deviation → monitor whether the opponent adapts → retreat or counter when adaptation appears. Exploitation is a perpetual arms race, not a one-time answer.

Example: You notice the BTN bets 100% when you check in the BB. Step 1 exploitation: double your check-raise frequency (harvesting his automatic C-Bets). Two orbits later he only bets real hands — adaptation appears. Step 2: pull your check-raises back to equilibrium frequency while starting to check-call wider to catch his shrunk value bets. Every step steps on the opponent's last adjustment.

Example (over-folding under population tendencies): Statistical consensus of low-stakes pools — river big bets are under-bluffed. You hold TPTK facing a tight-passive's 2x-pot overbet: pure GTO wouldn't fold all top pairs, but in this pool this player's overbet is almost nut-tier strength, so you over-fold — statistically correct exploitation. Log it too: if he starts overbet-bluffing at some point, he's adapting, and you must dial "over-folding" back into a calling range. Exploitation always carries a retreat plan.

Example (signals of being counter-exploited): Your C-Bet's check-raise encounter rate climbs from 12% to 30% — the opponent (or table population) is targeting your "bets 100% on check" leak. Fix: lower your automatic betting frequency on check, add a checking range (including strong traps and medium-hand pot control), so his check-raises face a balanced betting range and fail. The arms race is turn-based: he adjusts, you adjust again, there's never a final answer.
Population Tendencies: Default Exploitation Without Data

Against an unknown stranger, the best prior isn't pure equilibrium but "the average leaks of this stake's player pool" (Population Tendency): acknowledged tendencies of low-to-mid-stakes pools include — river big bets are under-bluffed (can over-fold), facing 3Bets folds too much (can widen bluff 3Bets), small bets defended too little (can collect rent with frequent small bets). Defaulting to population tendencies and overlaying individual profiles is the most efficient information architecture in practice.

Exploitation priority: first exploit "big and stable" leaks (loose-passive preflop, never-bluffing river), then "small and volatile" ones (a specific hand's tendency). The former is the vein; the latter is just gold dust.

Sunk-cost counter-exploitation: "he's already counter-exploited me for two big pots; this hand I must win back" is the most expensive comeback mindset. The first question of an exploitation audit isn't "how do I win it back" but "where did my strategy open a leak and has the opponent already adapted" — focus on fixing the strategy itself, not recovering past losses.

Do an "exploitation audit" every 30 minutes: what deviation am I making against whom? Does the evidence still hold? Is anyone exploiting me in reverse? — the third question is the most ignored and the most expensive.
t8-tilt: Tilt Is the Most Expensive Leak

Tilt is the collapse of decision quality when emotion overrides reason. Jared Tendler's core claim in The Mental Game of Poker: most players produce 80% of their losses in 20% of their Tilt time. No matter how good the technique, a tilting player executes his worst version of strategy — one psychological leak can cancel all technical advantages.
The Seven Types of Tilt (Tendler's Classification)

(1) Bad-luck Tilt — ignited by a Bad Beat, "why does it always happen to me"; (2) Injustice Tilt — believing the game is targeting you; (3) Revenge Tilt — locking onto an opponent you must win back against; (4) Can't-lose Tilt — escalating risk to recover losses; (5) Mistake Tilt — self-attack over your own errors, spiraling; (6) Entitlement Tilt — "I play well so I deserve to win", most likely when a winner loses; (7) Despair Tilt — giving up after a long downswing. Identifying which types you have is the prerequisite for intervention: different triggers and antidotes.

Type-by-type breakdown (trigger → response): (1) Bad luck — triggers: river outdraw, AA losing to a fish; response: recite "this landed in the 20% branch", use T1's variance language, no excuses, no complaints. (2) Injustice — triggers: consecutive coolers, three Bad Beats; response: leave the table 10 minutes, tell yourself with data that the distribution is uniform and the deck has no memory. (3) Revenge — triggers: humiliating bluffs or slow-rolls by a specific player; response: change tables or leave directly, clear that "winning back from him is a byproduct, not the goal". (4) Can't-lose — trigger: starting to size up near the stop-loss line; response: execute the preset stop-loss, the line is non-negotiable. (5) Mistake — trigger: self-blame after misclicking a raise or an erroneous call; response: accept on the spot that "the error happened", leave the fix for review, don't punish yourself at the table. (6) Entitlement — trigger: thinking you're better than the opponent yet losing to a fish; response: remind yourself variance doesn't know skill — winners get Bad Beat too. (7) Despair — trigger: giving up resistance after days of downswing; response: preset a "downswing battle plan" (move down, reduce volume, reinforce basic training), turning despair into an action plan. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker seven-type Tilt classification and intervention)

Almost every Tilt type shares the same cognitive fuse: mistaking variance for injustice. T1's variance theory closes the loop here — those who truly internalize "correct decisions also lose in streaks" see Bad Beats as statistical noise; those who don't light a match every time.

Tilt has physiological and behavioral precursors that appear before the decision collapse: heart racing, jaw tightening, leaning forward; faster actions (calling without thinking), starting to play hands you'd normally fold, bet sizes suddenly losing logic, wanting to "teach someone a lesson". Build yourself a "precursor checklist" and catch the signal 10 minutes before the collapse — that 10 minutes is the stop-loss window.

Example: After AA gets outdrawn by T9s on the river, you catch yourself raising K4o from UTG the next hand. This isn't strategy; it's a standard revenge-Tilt symptom — the goal has drifted from "make +EV decisions" to "win it back right now". Players with a checklist execute their plan (leave the table 10 minutes); players without one lose three buy-ins 30 minutes later.

Example 2 (mistake-Tilt cascade): On the turn you miscalculated pot odds, called a bet you shouldn't have, and lost the river. The next three hands are all decided with a "I'm so stupid" mindset — entering with 97o preflop, snap-calling raises. Mistake Tilt's horror is that it's motivated by "punishing myself", and the punishment is playing more bad poker. Response: admit the error on the spot and switch the self-blame switch to "next hand, fresh start".

Tilt's expected loss ≈ Tilt hourly rate × duration
Example: A-Game rate +8bb, Tilt rate −15bb, lasting 1 hour → relative loss (8−(−15))×1 = 23bb
If you intervene within 10 minutes of the precursor (leave the table, cool down), duration drops to 0.1h → loss about 2.3bb
Conclusion: the "investment return" of intervention isn't a feeling but quantifiable chips — every minute the precursor checklist saves translates directly into money saved. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker A-Game state management)

The standard intervention sequence: recognize the precursor → physical interruption (leave the table, 10 deep breaths, water) → recite the preset script (like "variance is performing; my EV hasn't changed") → if you haven't hit the calm line, end the session. The value of interruption isn't relaxation; it's wresting decision authority back from the limbic system to the prefrontal cortex.

Write your own Tilt file: your 2 most common types, 3 precursor signals, 1 intervention plan. Tape it by the screen or keep it on your phone — when Tilt hits you won't have the ability to design a plan on the spot; you can only execute one.
t8-session: Your decision quality isn't constant: focus, patience, and emotional stability are resources consumed over time. Divide your state into A/B/C tiers (A = best decisions, B = okay, C = leak-ridden). Session management has exactly one goal: play as many hands as possible in A/B, and compress C time to zero. One extra hour of C-Game often costs more than three hours of A-Game profit.

Pre-table warm-up: enough sleep? Any residual emotion (life stress, last session's bad results)? What's today's strategic focus? Pros warm up like athletes; entering the table with residual emotion is like bringing your own fuse.

Session expectation = Σ(tier hourly rate × tier duration)
Example: A tier 3h×+10bb + B tier 1h×+3bb + C tier 0.5h×−20bb = 30+3−10 = +23bb
If you end before entering C tier (cutting the 0.5h): +33bb — cutting half an hour of C-Game earns 10bb more
Conclusion: state stop-loss isn't "quitting" — it's the arithmetically optimal exit time. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker session management)
The Truth About Stop-Loss Lines and Taking Profits

Purely mathematically every hand is independent; "stop when down X" doesn't change EV. But the stop-loss line manages you, not the cards: after consecutive losses, Tilt probability spikes and decision quality drops — the stop-loss line (commonly 2-3 buy-ins) is essentially a "state stop-loss", forcing exit before C-Game. Conversely "quit early when winning" has no mathematical basis: when the table is good (fish present) and your state is good, a winning session should actually be extended. Stay or leave depends on exactly two variables: table quality × your own state, unrelated to the day's profit or loss.

Example: 4 hours into the session, you're up 2 buy-ins, but you've miscalculated pot odds twice and started checking your phone. The textbook answer is to leave — state has slipped into B-/C tier, and continuing is paying for C-Game with A-Game earnings. "It's a shame to leave while winning" is entitlement psychology, not strategy.

Example 2 (executing the state stop-loss): Your rule is "leave when down 2 buy-ins". Tonight you're down 1.9, then win an AA all-in, back to −1.2. The thought "one more orbit and I'm even" surges — but your heart rate is already up and you keep glancing at the clock. Per the formula: at this moment your state has slipped into B-/C tier, continuing has negative EV, and the point of the stop-loss is precisely not letting "so close" hijack decisions.

Example 3 (table-quality assessment): You're up 3 buy-ins, but the 5 remaining players are all tight-aggressive regulars and the one or two fish just left. Using the "table quality × state" formula: table quality dropped (EV down), so continuing is just donating to tougher games. The correct move is to take profit or move to a softer table — stay/leave always depends on the two variables, unrelated to today's profit.
Review: The Session's Second Profit Source

Within 24 hours of the session, do a structured review: mark the 2-3 hardest hands (not the biggest pots), write down your reasoning at the time, verify with range analysis or a solver; also review the psychological side — which moment your state dropped a tier and what the trigger was. Technical review improves strategy; psychological review shortens C-Game — together their long-term value is no less than the table itself.
Fatigue is invisible Tilt: research repeatedly shows sleep deprivation damages judgment comparably to alcohol. The late-night "one more hour" decision is almost never made by your A-Game.

Write down three hard rules for yourself: a fixed pre-session warm-up checklist, an explicit state-exit signal (like two consecutive calculation errors), and a fixed review time. Rules only bind when written; rules kept in your head get rewritten by emotion on the spot.
t8-bankroll-psych: The Dual Function of Bankroll Management

Bankroll management's mathematical function is bankruptcy prevention: even long-term winners can see variance create 10-20 buy-in downswings, and insufficient funds turn "bad luck" into "permanently out". Common benchmarks: 20-40 buy-ins for cash games, 100+ for tournaments because variance is larger. But its equally important second function is psychological: only when a single buy-in's win/loss "doesn't hurt" can you execute correct but high-variance decisions.

Playable stake limit: cash bankroll ≥ 20-40 buy-ins; tournament bankroll ≥ 100 buy-ins
True floor = max(mathematical benchmark, psychological tolerance benchmark), take the stricter
Loss-aversion coefficient ≈ 2: the pain of losing 100 ≈ the pleasure of winning 200 (Kahneman's prospect theory)

Kelly criterion (brief): f* = (bp − q) / b
b = net odds (win b when winning, lose 1 when losing), p = win probability, q = 1 − p
Example: win rate 55% (q=0.45), odds 1:1 (b=1) → f* = (1×0.55 − 0.45) ÷ 1 = 0.10, i.e. optimal bet fraction = 10% of bankroll
Practical conclusion: even a clear 55% edge, Kelly suggests only 10% of funds — and it assumes no psychological wear during downswings, so in reality people use half-Kelly (5%) or more conservative. It gives the mathematical ceiling; psychological tolerance gives the floor. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker bankroll quantification; Kelly 1956)

Risk-tolerance check (three steps): (1) would losing 3 buy-ins in one session affect tonight's sleep and tomorrow's judgment? (2) would losing 10 buy-ins in a row distort your strategy? (3) after a 50% bankroll drawdown, can you still play per plan? If any answer is "yes", your psychological bankroll floor is above the mathematical one — decide stakes by the psychological floor.

The Scared Money mechanism: when stakes exceed psychological tolerance, loss aversion (the pain of losing 100 is about twice the pleasure of winning 100 — Kahneman's prospect theory) systematically distorts decisions: draws you should call get folded, bluffing spots go timid, thin river values get checked. The opponent needs no hand reading — just pressure.

Example: A player with a 10-buy-in bankroll sits at a +EV table and faces a flop all-in coin flip (52% equity, slight favorite). Math says call, but losing would break him — he folds. One hand doesn't cost much, but "systematically abandoning thin edges out of fear" accumulates and turns a winner into a loser. A fully bankrolled opponent makes the same decision with no burden — that's bankroll as fighting power.

Example 2 (Kelly in practice): You estimate a real edge of 3bb/100 at 2/5; half-Kelly converts to an affordable buy-in count of about 30-40. But psychologically you start agonizing over single-bet sizing after losing 8 buy-ins. So your true floor is the psychological 8, not the mathematical 30 — staying at 2/5 means every decision carries a Scared Money discount. The correct move: drop stakes until "8 buy-ins feels like 30-40".

Example 3 (moving down IS profit): Your bankroll drops from 40 buy-ins to 18; the mechanical rule requires moving down a level. You execute — three months later you're back to 60. Meanwhile the opponent who held the original level went from 18 to 6 and busted. Moving down lets you keep running your complete strategy (protecting +EV); holding means every decision is discounted by fear. Moving down isn't admitting failure; it's protecting the environment where +EV can run.
Discipline for Moving Up and Down

Healthy take-a-shot posture: try the higher level with an explicit budget (like 3 buy-ins), drop back immediately when gone, no re-buying. The psychological hurdle of moving down is harder: dropping feels like admitting defeat, so many players cling to the original level after drawdowns until bust. Writing promotions/demotions as mechanical rules (move up at X, down at Y) and executing unconditionally is the only way to strip ego out of financial decisions.

Another high-frequency psychological trap is "spending winnings" (the bankroll version of Winner's Tilt): after a win streak you feel like you're "playing with house money" and risk appetite surges. Accounting-wise there is no "house money" — all chips are equivalent; winnings join the total bankroll and obey the same rules.

Bankroll and life must be physically separated: table bankroll is earmarked funds; living expenses go in a separate account. Someone playing with rent money has every decision distorted by Scared Money — you've already lost the psychological war before sitting down.

Self-test: if you lost 3 buy-ins right now, would you sleep tonight? If not, your stakes exceed your psychological bankroll — the true bankroll floor is the stricter of the mathematical benchmark and psychological tolerance.
t8-mindset: The Four Major Cognitive Biases at the Poker Table

(1) Resulting: judging decision quality by the result — a lucky misplay gets remembered as "bold genius", a correct call that lost gets remembered as "a lesson". This is the biggest contaminant of the learning curve. (2) Confirmation bias: remembering only evidence that supports your judgment ("he always bluffs" — when he was caught only once). (3) Availability bias: recent or most painful memories get overweighted — just got outdrawn by a flush, so you overestimate every draw's threat. (4) Sunk-cost fallacy: "I've already put so much in the pot" — invested chips no longer belong to you; calls should only be based on current odds.

Complete cognitive-bias checklist (8+, for self-audit):
① Resulting — judging decisions by single results
② Confirmation bias — collecting only evidence supporting existing judgments
③ Availability — recent memories over-weighted
④ Sunk cost — keeping chips you've already invested alive
⑤ Gambler's fallacy — "five losses in a row, I'm due" (confusing independent events)
⑥ Overconfidence — overestimating the precision of your reads and judgments
⑦ Hindsight — "I knew he had AA" after showdown, contaminating review
⑧ Anchoring — locked onto the first piece of information (like an opponent label)
Each has a counter: ① judge EV not results; ② actively seek counterexamples; ③ replace recent memory with long-term frequency; ④ ask "considering only now, is the money still mine"; ⑤ reread T1 independent events; ⑥ test confidence with evidence; ⑦ write the decision first, the result after; ⑧ delay judgment and re-evaluate. (Concept from: Thinking in Bets Ch.1-4 decoupling decisions and results)

Annie Duke's antidote in Thinking in Bets: "decouple decisions from results". To evaluate any hand, only ask: given the information available at the time, what was this decision's expected value? Results are only for calibrating probability estimates, never for judging decisions.

The relationship between decision quality and results (Duke's decoupling quantified):
Single result = EV + variance noise
Long-term result of correct decisions = Σ EV (noise shrinks with sample size, proven in T1)
Bayesian calibration: P(correct decision | lost) ≠ 1 − P(lost | correct decision)
Example: a 55%-equity call lost; P(lost)=45% — but this doesn't change P(correct)=55%.
Review formula: only update the "probability estimate" (is 45% accurate?), not the "decision quality" (is the 55% call right?). (Concept from: Thinking in Bets Ch.2 correcting result-orientation)

Example: On the river you correctly called a 2:1 pot-odds bluff catch (his range bluffed 40%); this time he showed the nuts. A result-oriented review writes "shouldn't have called"; a probability-thinking review writes "was the 40% bluff-frequency judgment justified? Yes — so the call was correct; this just landed in the 60% branch". Two review styles, two different skill levels three months later.

Carol Dweck's mindset theory mapped to poker: a fixed mindset treats losing as evidence of "I can't do this", thus avoiding review and strong opponents; a growth mindset treats losing as data for locating leaks, actively seeking discomfort. Combined with the three elements of deliberate practice — focused training on weaknesses (not repeating comfort zones), immediate feedback (solver/coach/review), and spiraling difficulty — the skill gap is fundamentally a practice-quality gap.

The last piece of the long-term mindset is process goals: result goals (win X this month) are contaminated by variance and uncontrollable; process goals (review 3 hands daily, zero C-Game in a session, learn one theory module weekly) are fully controllable. Watch the process; results are the byproduct — in a variance-dominated game this isn't chicken soup, it's math.

Beware "fake learning": repeatedly watching entertainment hand videos, only reviewing winning hands, bookmarking tutorials without ever practicing — these activities provide the feeling of learning, not learning itself. There's only one test: did it change your next decision?

Turn this chapter's four biases into a review checklist and run it every review: "Am I judging decisions by results? Am I ignoring counterexamples? Am I magnifying fear with recent bad memories? Am I clinging to sunk costs?" — the best tool against bias is a checklist, not willpower.

Example 2 (hindsight contamination): On the river you fold top pair to an all-in and the opponent shows a bluff. In review you write "I knew he was bluffing" — but at the decision moment you didn't have that certainty; hindsight is rewriting the record. Counter: write down your judgment and reasoning at the decision moment (even mentally), compare after showdown, and you'll know your true reading precision.

Example 3 (anchoring and overconfidence): Your first impression labels the opponent "tight-passive", and after three consecutive big bluffs you still respond with the tight-passive model — anchoring makes you ignore counterexamples. Meanwhile you're fully confident in your reading precision, yet stats show your river hero-call win rate is only 30%. Fix: add "invalidation conditions" to every opponent label (re-evaluate if X counterexamples appear), and calibrate confidence with actual win rates.
t9-mop: Bill Chen and Jerrod Ankenman's The Mathematics of Poker (2006) is the intellectual source of the solver era. Its methodology: rather than studying complex real poker directly, construct precisely solvable "toy games", and distill structural regularities that still hold in real hands. The bluff ratio b/(1+2b), MDF, and indifference principle you learned in T5 all originate from this line.
The [0,1] Game and the AKQ Game

One classic toy game is the AKQ game: the deck has only A, K, Q, each player gets one card in a single-street showdown. The equilibrium solution reveals three timeless roles: A (the nuts) always value-bets; Q (air) bluffs at a precise frequency; K (the medium hand) never bets — it can only be a bluff catcher, calling at an indifferent frequency. Every real hand at every node plays one of these three roles; this is the theoretical prototype of the "three-tier range structure" (value / medium / air).

AKQ equilibrium solution (fixed bet B, pot P; A always bets, Q bluffs at frequency f, K calls at frequency c):
① K's call EV = f×P − (1−f)×B; set equal to fold EV(=0): f×P = (1−f)×B → f = B/(P+B)
② Q's bluff EV = c×P − (1−c)×B; set equal to check EV(=0): c×P = (1−c)×B → c = B/(P+B)
③ Equilibrium: f = c = B/(P+B) — bluff frequency and call frequency are equal, both equal to the bet's share of "pot + bet"
Example: bet = pot (B=P) → f = c = 1/2; betting 1/3 pot → f = c = 1/4
This is the isomorphic source of MDF and Alpha in the minimal model (T5): defender call frequency and attacker bluff frequency share the same formula. (Concept from: The Mathematics of Poker Ch.5 toy games and the AKQ equilibrium)

Example 2 (mapping AKQ to real hands): On the river you hold medium strength (the K role) and the opponent bets one pot. In equilibrium his bluff frequency f = 1/2, so you should call with K-type hands at c = 1/2 (with MDF, fully derived in T5). If the opponent is observed to never bluff (f far below 1/2), lower your call frequency accordingly — the toy game provides the baseline for adjustment; real hand reading provides the deviation direction.

Example 3 (the preflop version of the three roles): Preflop BTN opens, BB defends. BB's calling range against the open has three classes: strong hands (A role, continue 3Betting or slow-play), medium hands (K role, only call to showdown), bluff candidates (Q role, occasionally 3Bet-bluffing). MOP's three-tier structure is the skeleton of range construction — for every hand preflop you must first ask: "is this hand an A, K, or Q in this spot?"

The deepest conclusion of the AKQ game: the correct strategy for medium strength is passivity (check/call); betting belongs to the two poles. This conclusion cuts through every level — "betting medium hands" remains the most common amateur leak (T6 argued the same thing from a sizing angle).
The Stratification of Strategy and Tactics

MOP also establishes the levels of analysis: the tactical layer solves "how to play this hand", the strategic layer solves "how to construct my whole range". The book's famous insight: the weak think about single hands, the strong think about ranges, the strongest think about the rules of range construction. Modern solvers are the engineering of this idea: they never tell you "what to do with this hand" — they output the whole range's allocation over the game tree.

Example: MOP's risk-aversion theory also answers a practical question: when you have a significant technical edge, you can moderately avoid small +EV all-ins with high variance (preserving the opportunity to realize your edge); conversely, as the weaker side you should actively embrace variance. This gives a rigorous mathematical statement for "good players avoid big-coinflip pots with better players" — not just street wisdom.

The right way to read MOP: don't derive every page; grasp what variable each toy game isolates and what the conclusion is. Toy games are to poker what inclined-plane experiments are to physics — simplification isn't distortion, it's developing the image.
Self-test your depth: can you use the AKQ game to explain to a friend "why medium hands shouldn't bet" and "why bluffs must exist"? If you can explain both clearly, you've grasped MOP's essence.
t9-icm: In cash games, 1 chip is always = 1 unit of money. In tournaments it isn't: the prize ladder (e.g. 30% first, 20% second...) makes chip marginal value decrease — double your chips and your prize expectation is far from double; losing your chips costs all remaining expectation. ICM (Independent Chip Model) is the standard model converting "chip counts" into "prize expectation ($EV)": it recursively computes the probability of finishing each place by chip share, and weights the prizes for true value.

ICM's core corollary: an all-in that is "cEV-neutral or even slightly positive" in tournament chips can be significantly $EV-negative. Survival itself has value — this is the root of tournament strategy diverging from cash-game strategy.

ICM recursive algorithm (simplified 3-player SNG, prize 50/30/20, chips A=5000/B=3000/C=2000):
Step 1 (first-place probability = chip share): P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.3, P(C)=0.2
Step 2 (recursive second place): P(A 2nd) = P(B wins)×A/(A+C) + P(C wins)×A/(A+B) = 0.3×5000/7000 + 0.2×5000/8000 ≈ 0.339
P(B 2nd) = 0.5×3000/5000 + 0.2×3000/8000 = 0.375
P(C 2nd) = 0.5×2000/5000 + 0.3×2000/7000 ≈ 0.286
Step 3 (third = 1 minus the first two): P(A 3rd) ≈ 0.161, P(B 3rd) = 0.325, P(C 3rd) ≈ 0.514
Step 4 (weighted prizes): $EV(A) = 0.5×50 + 0.339×30 + 0.161×20 ≈ 38.4
$EV(B) = 0.3×50 + 0.375×30 + 0.325×20 ≈ 32.8
$EV(C) = 0.2×50 + 0.286×30 + 0.514×20 ≈ 28.9
Check: 38.4+32.8+28.9 ≈ 100 (prize conservation), and A's $EV share 38.4% < chip share 50% — decreasing marginal value visualized. (Concept from: ICM Theory independent-chip-model recursive definition)

Example 2 (the intuition of recursion): Step 2's recursion — "A finishes second" decomposes into "if B wins first, A competes with C for second" + "if C wins first, A competes with B for second". Each step asks "after removing the winner from the table, the rest compete by chips for the next place". Real ICM calculators repeat this recursion at higher dimensions (6-9 players), done by program when many players remain.

Example 3 (using the computed results): In the example above, A has 50% of the chips but only 38.4% of the prize pool. If A shoves on B at the bubble with 55% equity: after the call A becomes 8000 ($EV rises to ~46), busting makes it zero; expectation = 0.55×46 ≈ 25.3 < folding's 38.4 — the quantified demo of "winning mathematically, folding on ICM": it's not that 55% is insufficient; it's that chips' marginal value is compressed by the tournament prize structure.

Example: On the bubble (one more elimination and everyone gets paid), you're medium-stacked and a big stack shoves on you. Even if you judge 55% equity (clearly +cEV), calling may still be a $EV disaster: winning adds limited chip value, losing zeroes 100% of your prize expectation; and the opponents the big stack can't eliminate are waiting for you two to collide. Conversely this is precisely the big stack's weapon — ICM pressure lets him push every medium stack with an extremely wide range: you "know he's stealing", yet mathematically you can only fold.

(1) The bubble and money-jump stages are the most distorted: medium stacks play tightest, big stacks most aggressively, and small stacks can play almost normally (they're about to be gone anyway); (2) push/fold charts in shallow stacks (<15bb) are almost entirely determined by ICM and math — memorizable away from the table; (3) the fair baseline for final-table deals is the ICM value — those who don't know ICM lose once at the negotiating table.

Know ICM's boundaries too: it ignores position, technical edge, and blinds rising (assumes equal skill and immediate settlement), so technically superior players may slightly deviate from ICM's conservative solutions (future edge still realizable), and it also undervalues the big stack's bullying value early in the FT. The model is a map, not the territory.

The most common ICM disaster isn't miscalculation but disregard: playing the bubble with cash-game intuition, "I have AJo, why should I fold" — because of the prize structure. Every tournament decision must run two books: one cEV, one $EV, and the latter governs.
Training order suggestion: first memorize the sub-15bb push/fold base charts, then review your own bubble decisions with an ICM calculator — these two are the highest-ROI homework for tournament ROI.
t9-multiway: Each additional opponent dilutes your showdown equity once: AA is about 85% heads-up but falls to ~55% four-way; for "ranges" it's crueler — heads-up top pair weak kicker is a good hand, but in a four-way pot it's often just a paying second place. The first law of multiway pots: the made-hand threshold rises across the board, and nuttiness trumps everything — hands that can make the nuts (suited connectors, pocket pairs) appreciate, while dominated hands (weak Ax, KJo class) crash.

Multiway showdown equity table (typical starting hands vs N random opponents):
AA: 1 opponent ≈85%｜2 ≈73%｜3 ≈64%｜4 ≈56%｜5 ≈49%
KK: 1 ≈82%｜2 ≈69%｜3 ≈59%｜4 ≈51%
AKs: 1 ≈67%｜2 ≈50%｜3 ≈40%
87s: 1 ≈41%｜2 ≈30%｜3 ≈24%
Pattern: each extra opponent drops equity about 8-12 percentage points; big pairs dilute slowest and suited connectors resist best — because the latter's value comes from nut potential rather than current made strength. (Concept from: Multiway Theory multiway equity allocation)

Example 2 (using the equity table): You open AA from UTG and three callers make it a 4-way pot. Per the table AA showdown equity is still about 56%, but note this is "showdown" equity — every time a street threatens a straight/flush/set from one caller, your "realizable equity" drops further. Conclusion: even AA in multiway pots should bet fast to build the pot and control variables, not slow-play and give free cards.

Example 3 (87s counterintuition): In the table, 87s heads-up is only 41% — looks weak, yet in 3-4-way pots it still holds about 30% — because its value comes entirely from making straights/flushes postflop. This is the quantitative support for "multiway rewards nut potential": weak Ax is 55% heads-up but may drop below 25% in a 4-way pot (dominated), while 87s decays much more gently.

Bluffs depreciate sharply in multiway pots: a bluff needs everyone to fold, and success drops exponentially with player count; plus each extra opponent is another chance someone has hit the board. Multiway fundamentals: cut bluff frequency sharply, while value bets get called more easily — "play value in multiway, play pressure heads-up".

The most important theoretical change (warned in T5): the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee only holds for two-player zero-sum games. In multiway games, even if everyone plays "equilibrium", two players' strategic interaction can objectively squeeze a third (without collusion); one player's error can also happen to hurt another rather than benefit. So there's no "copy-and-safe" GTO multiway — solid fundamentals (tight, value-oriented, position) and reads on specific opponents weigh far more than equilibrium dogma.

Example: BTN limps behind CO's open, and you're in the BB with A5s facing 2.5bb. Heads-up this is a standard 3Bet-bluff candidate (blocker + nut potential), but now you're squeezed in the middle: a 3Bet must get through two ranges at once, and once called your A5s can't continue on most flops in a 3-way 3Bet pot. Multiway dynamics turn a "beautiful equilibrium play" into lighting fireworks — the correct answer retreats to call or fold.

In multiway pots the "protection" value of betting rises (the more live hands, the more valuable making equity fold), and the cost of slow-playing rises too — giving three opponents free cards is giving three chances to outdraw. On defense, responsibility is shared: facing a bet, MDF doesn't need to be met by you alone; the player with the best position/hand structure takes more of the defense; in the sandwich spot (between the bettor and yet-to-act players), your calling range must be much tighter than heads-up.

Multiway discipline checklist: starting hands favor nut potential, bluff less postflop, fast-play strong hands instead of slow-playing, pot-control medium hands, and play tight in the sandwich position. Violating any one of these costs more than heads-up.

Low-stakes multiway pots are the profit home: opponents bring heads-up mindsets and play top pair weak kicker for all three streets in four-way pots. You need only one thing — be there with a nut-oriented range waiting for them.
t9-alpha:
Alpha = bet ÷ (pot + bet) — the break-even fold rate the opponent needs for your bluff

Example: when you bet 1/2 pot (bet=0.5pot)
- Alpha = 0.5/(1+0.5) = 33%
- The opponent's fold rate must exceed 33% for your bluff to profit

This is the "price tag" from the attacker's perspective, answering: "what minimum share of hands must the opponent fold for my bluff to break even?"

MDF and Alpha are the two sides of the same game tree, revealing the essence of game theory:
- MDF = pot/(pot+bet) — **your defense frequency** (defender's view)
- Alpha = bet/(pot+bet) — **the fold rate the opponent needs** (attacker's view)
- **Key finding**: MDF + Alpha = 1 (they are complements)

This duality shows that one side's optimal strategy exactly cancels the other side's exploitation space. The defender's MDF determines the attacker's Alpha, and vice versa. They share the same denominator (pot+bet) mathematically, differing only in numerator (pot vs bet).
Proof of MDF + Alpha = 1: pot/(pot+bet) + bet/(pot+bet) = (pot+bet)/(pot+bet) = 1

Alpha's core value is providing a **quantitative view** to evaluate whether the opponent's bluff frequency is high enough to justify calling. Concrete steps:
1. **Compute Alpha**: calculate Alpha from your bet size and current pot
2. **Observe the opponent's fold rate**: via stats like C-Bet fold rate, big river bet fold rate
3. **Compare Alpha with his fold rate**: if his fold rate exceeds Alpha, calling profits; otherwise fold

This quantitative view lets you decide more objectively rather than by intuition or experience.

Example: You bet 1/3 pot, Alpha = 1/4. The opponent's C-Bet fold rate is 30%, below Alpha. This means his bluff frequency isn't high enough — you should fold. Conversely, if his fold rate is 40%, above Alpha, you should call.
Example 2: You bet 1/2 pot, Alpha = 1/3. The opponent's big river bet fold rate is 25%, below Alpha. You should fold. If his fold rate is 35%, above Alpha, you should call.
Example 3: You bet 1/4 pot, Alpha = 1/5. The opponent's C-Bet fold rate is 20%, below Alpha. You should fold. If his fold rate is 25%, above Alpha, you should call.
Alpha's application principle: **quantitative comparison**, not intuition. Through Alpha you can more objectively evaluate the opponent's bluff frequency and make more accurate decisions.
Self-test your depth: can you use Alpha to explain to a friend "why you should fold in certain situations"? If you can explain this clearly, you've grasped Alpha's essence.
t9-unified: The End of the False Dichotomy

"GTO camp vs exploitation camp" is a false dichotomy of the learning stage. In the complete framework both are two modes of one system: equilibrium is optimal without information (bulletproof vest against unknown opponents / strong players / insufficient samples), exploitation is optimal with information (harvest knife when leaks are confirmed). Every decision answers the same question: what my knowledge of the opponent supports — how much deviation, in what direction?

Decision = equilibrium baseline + f(information quality) × directed deviation
Zero information → pure baseline; complete information and non-adapting opponent → maximal exploitation; in between → scale deviation by confidence (concept from: Applications of NLHE equilibrium-exploitation unified framework)
The Knowledge Map Across Nine Levels

Looking back: T1-T2 gave you the measuring system (probability, EV, odds) — the units of all judgment; T3-T4 gave you the coordinate system (position, range) — where you are and what you fight against; T5-T6 gave you the equilibrium baseline (GTO, MDF, sizing theory) — the correct shape without information; T7 gave you the information system (stats, types, hand reading, exploitation) — turning observations into deviation evidence; T8 gave you operational safeguards (psychology, bankroll, state) — keeping the system stable on a real human; T9 assembles everything and annotates each tool's applicability boundary (multiway, ICM, model limits).

The framework's operating loop: start from the equilibrium baseline → accumulate information through observation → deviate with evidence (exploitation) → monitor opponent adaptation → retreat or counter → escorted throughout by psychology and bankroll systems. This loop has no endpoint — poker is never "finished", only versioned.

Example: One river full-pot bet decision, all nine levels show up — pot odds says you need 33% equity (T2); range filtering + combo counting says he bluffs about 25% (T4/T7); equilibrium says "should" be 33% bluffs here (T5); his WTSD and river AF say this player never bluffs big on the river (T7); you just lost a big pot, and the checklist reminds you not to comfort yourself with "he always bluffs" (T8) — fold. A decision's quality equals the number of theories correctly invoked behind it.

Example 2 (confidence-driven deviation): You collect 200 hands and find an opponent folds to C-Bets 65% (far above equilibrium ~45%) — high confidence. Your deviation: raise C-Bet frequency and bluff share, specifically firing at him. But if the sample is only 15 hands, 65% may be noise — at low confidence, return to baseline. Same observation, two different-magnitude decisions; the difference is entirely information quality.

Example 3 (the adaptation-monitoring loop): Three times in a row you fold bluff catches using the read "he never bluffs big on the river". The fourth time he shoves, you fold, and he shows pure air — an adaptation signal. This isn't discarding the read but downgrading it to "usually true", returning to the equilibrium baseline while waiting for new samples. Exploitation is a dynamic game: you adjust others, and others adjust you.

Suggested reading order: The Theory of Poker (Sklansky, intellectual awakening) → The Mental Game of Poker (Tendler, psychological system) → Applications of No-Limit Hold'em (Janda, equilibrium application) → Modern Poker Theory (Acevedo, solver-era synthesis) → The Mathematics of Poker (Chen & Ankenman, mathematical foundation). Toolchain: solver + database + this platform's training modules — theory closes the loop into muscle memory here.

The final warning is the same as the first principle: theory has value only when executed. Knowing MDF yet over-folding under pressure, understanding variance yet tilting after a Bad Beat — the gap between knowing and doing is the distance between you and your ceiling.

Graduation assignment: after finishing this level, go to the Strategy Academy and training modules to practice each theory at least once (range training → T3/T4, odds quizzes → T1/T2, GTO simulator → T5/T6). The Theory Academy gives you the map; the training ground lets you walk the path.
t1sd-combinatorics: From 52 Cards to 36: The Reshuffling of the Combo World

Short Deck (6+ Hold'em) uses 36 cards: the 2, 3, 4, and 5 are removed, leaving only 9 ranks (6-A) per suit. The smaller deck means combo counts plummet, starting hands shrink, and "draw density" rises sharply. Understanding these combinatorial changes is the first step to mastering short-deck probability — you no longer face the familiar 52-card world.

The key to the short-deck combo world: the smaller the deck, the rarer the strong hands and the more common the draws. Starting hands drop from C(52,2)=1326 to C(36,2)=630, and the relative value of every two-card hand is reshuffled — the same hand has a completely different win rate in short deck than in full-ring.

Short-deck combo basics (36 cards, 9 per suit):
Total starting hands = C(36,2) = 36×35÷2 = 630
Pocket-pair combos = 9 ranks × C(4,2) = 9×6 = 54
Any two unpaired ranks (e.g. AK) = 4×4 = 16

Compared with full ring (52 cards): 1326 starting hands, 78 pocket pairs, AK still 16

Key difference: the "pair share of starting hands" rises from 78/1326 ≈ 5.9% to 54/630 ≈ 8.6% — pairs are more common, but their relative strength changes due to the hand-ranking reshuffle (detailed in T3). (Concept from: Short Deck Hold'em: The Ultimate Guide / 6+ Hold'em rules)

The more important combinatorial difference is in flop structure: short deck has only 9 ranks, so the "connectivity" of flops hitting straight/flush draws is far higher than full ring. For example, a 9-8-7 flop is extremely wet in short deck (TJ, T6, 65 all make straights), as in full ring but with a bigger combo base. The key — "connected flops" occur more often in short deck because you draw from a smaller rank pool.

Example: In short deck you hold A♠K♠ and read the opponent's range as {pocket pairs, AK, AQ}. Counting combos: 54 pocket pairs, AK 16 (after your A♠, AK drops to 3×3=9), AQ 16. The AQ you beat is 16 of (54+9+16) ≈ 20%. But note — in short deck AK is the strongest non-pair, running about 43%-45% against any pocket pair preflop all-in (full ring ≈ 43%), and the rule "pocket pairs > AK" (trips > straights, plus high pair density) makes this comparison even more subtle.

Example 2 (outs density): Short-deck flop 9♥8♣3♠, you hold 7♣6♣. You draw to 5 or T for a straight: about 8 outs accounting for seen cards. Compare full ring's same 8 outs — but only 31 cards remain unknown in short deck after the flop (36−2 hole−3 flop), so single-street hit rate is about 8/31 ≈ 26%, noticeably above full ring's 8/47 ≈ 17%. Short-deck "draws get there more often" is mathematical necessity, not illusion.

Counterintuitive point: in short deck AK is the "strongest non-pair" but usually trails any pocket pair preflop all-in (about 43%-45%). The correct reading of "AK is strong" is "it dominates other non-pairs", not "it beats pairs". Directly transplanting the full-ring memory "AK is the strongest under pairs" overestimates AK's preflop value.

Short-deck combo quick reference: 630 starting hands, 54 pocket pairs (8.6%), 4 suited / 12 offsuit per unpaired pair. When counting "how many pairs are in his range" at the table, remember short-deck pair density is higher — this directly affects your calling and bluffing frequencies.
t1sd-outs: Outs Recalculated: Only 9 Cards Per Suit

The definition of outs doesn't change — unknown cards that let your hand overtake the opponent. But short deck must recalculate the outs base on a 36-card deck: only 9 cards per suit, so a flush draw's outs are no longer full ring's 9, but 9 minus the seen cards of that suit. This "subtraction" is the core of short-deck outs math; directly applying the standard hold'em outs table systematically overestimates your equity.
Short-deck outs rule: flush draw outs = 9 − seen cards of that suit. Holding 2 hearts + 2 hearts on board → flush outs = 9 − 4 = 5, not full ring's 9.
Short-Deck Equity Calculation and the 2/4 Rule Correction

Short-deck flush draw outs recalculated (holding 2 hearts, 2 hearts on board, 4 seen):
Flush outs = 9 − 4 = 5

Unknown cards after the flop = 36 − 2 (your hole cards) − 3 (flop) = 31
Single-street hit rate (turn): 5 ÷ 31 ≈ 16% (full ring same line 9÷47 ≈ 19%)
Two-street hit rate (flop to river): 1 − (26/31)×(25/30) ≈ 1 − 0.699 ≈ 30%

The 2/4 rule (5×4 = 20%) systematically underestimates in short deck:
the denominator shrinks from full ring's 47/46 to 31/30, so the same number of outs hits more often than in full ring
(full ring 5 outs two-street: 1 − (42/47)×(41/46) ≈ 20%; short deck 5 outs two-street ≈ 30%).

Key conclusion: the reason short-deck draws have "lower absolute equity" is that the outs count itself shrinks (flush 5 vs full ring 9),
not because each out carries less weight — quite the opposite, each out hits more often with a smaller denominator.
Re-evaluate draw EV on three factors: fewer outs × higher per-out hit rate × higher made-hand value. (Concept from: 6+ Hold'em math framework and Short Deck Poker outs recalculation)

But "lower absolute equity" doesn't mean "lower value" — in short deck, when draws get there they are usually nuts or near-nuts (straight/flush value rises due to the hand-ranking reshuffle). So short-deck draws have excellent implied odds and semi-bluffs are amplified. In practice the key is: don't do mental math with the full-ring outs table; recalculate on 36 cards, then judge whether to chase based on the high value of short-deck made hands.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♥K♥ on a 9♥7♥2♣ flop. You draw to the flush: seen hearts A♥K♥ + 9♥7♥ = 4, so flush outs = 9 − 4 = 5. Plus A/K each have 3 overcard outs (counting backdoors). The opponent bets 2 ante into a 6-ante pot; you need 25%. Your 5 flush outs are about 16% on one street, plus 4-6 overcard outs → about 30%+ on two streets, and a made flush is nut-tier. Calling is +EV, and a raise-semi-bluff is worth considering (short-deck flush value is huge).

Example 2 (straight outs): Short deck, you hold T♠J♠ on an 8♦9♣2♥ flop. You draw to 7 or Q for a straight: 4 each = 8 outs (8/9 already on board). Only 31 cards remain unknown after the flop, single-street 8/31 ≈ 26%, two-street about 46% — short-deck straight draws are very strong, and a made straight beats the opponent's two pair but not trips (in short deck trips > straight, so be careful).

Counterintuitive point: short-deck flush draws have only 5 outs (full ring 9) and lower absolute equity — but a flush is a super-strong hand in short deck (beats full houses), basically locking the pot once made. So "few outs" doesn't mean "weak draw"; the key is the relative strength once made. Using the full-ring intuition "more outs = stronger draw" misjudges short-deck flush draws.

Short-deck outs quick math: flush = 9 − seen cards of the suit; straight = connecting ranks ×4 (minus seen); single-street hit rate approximated by "outs ÷ 31" (after flop) or "outs ÷ 30" (after turn). Memorize 5 outs ≈ 16% single-street, 8 outs ≈ 26% — faster than counting at the table.
t1sd-variance: Short Deck: A Game of Amplified Variance

Short-deck variance is significantly higher than standard hold'em for three structural reasons: (1) higher flop rate — with 36 cards, hitting the flop is easier and more hands see one; (2) more common draws — connected flops appear often, outs hit rates are relatively high, and all-ins/chases are frequent; (3) bigger pots on average — ante structure plus more calls. Combined, these make short-deck's "single-result uncertainty" far exceed full ring.
High short-deck variance isn't a flaw; it's the game's structure. Understand it, accept it, and ride it with more conservative bankroll management — rather than doubting your skill mid-variance.

Short-deck variance magnitude (typical bb/100 values):
Full-ring hold'em: winner 5bb/100, standard deviation 80-100
Short-deck 6-max: winner 8-15bb/100, standard deviation 150-220

Short-deck all-in equity often lands in 45%-55% (draws vs made hands colliding constantly), making single results more uncertain.

Bankroll advice (more conservative):
Standard hold'em cash: about 50-100 buy-ins
Short deck: suggest ≥ 150 buy-ins (higher standard deviation)

Derivation: if single all-in σ≈55, N-hand cumulative variance = σ×√N. Short deck needs a larger sample for expectation to converge, hence a higher bankroll bar. (Concept from: 6+ Hold'em variance research and bankroll frameworks)

Handling short-deck variance is also psychological: because the flop rate is extreme and nearly every hand sees a flop, your hourly "win-loss alternation" is far denser than full ring. Losing 10 all-ins in a row is more common in short deck (since all-in equity often lands in 45%-55%). Treating consecutive losses as mathematical normalcy rather than a skill problem is a survival skill for short-deck players.

Example: Short deck, you shove 8 hands in a row at 50% equity (draws vs made hands colliding), and the probability of losing all 8 is 0.5^8 ≈ 0.4% — seemingly rare, but short deck has frequent all-ins per hour, so a session may contain one. Your mind knows "EV neutral" but your emotions want "to get even". The right move: recognize the revenge impulse → pause → restart with "what is this hand's EV".

Example 2 (bankroll simulation): Short deck, your standard deviation per hundred hands is about 180 with an expectation of 10bb/100. With 50 buy-ins, a 50-buy-in (5000bb) downswing is not unlikely; with 150 buy-ins, the same variance consumes only ~30% of the bankroll. Short deck's higher deviation demands a more conservative bankroll bar than standard hold'em.

Counterintuitive point: in short deck, "losing many hands" almost never proves you're "playing badly". The hourly sample is packed with 45%-55% equity all-ins and draw chases; losing streaks are mathematical normalcy. Review with a decision log (recording the reasoning of each key decision) instead of a win/loss log, or you'll make your worst strategic adjustments during the most violent variance.

Short-deck session management triad: (1) preset a variance budget — pause and review after losing 40-50BB, as a stop-and-restart rather than a chase; (2) stand up every 100 hands to break losing-streak inertia; (3) review only EV, never results.
t2sd-potodds: Short-Deck Pot Odds: The Unique Ante Structure

Short deck usually uses an ante structure: everyone posts the same ante, and the BTN posts an extra ante. This means no traditional SB/BB blind structure — the pot is built from fixed antes. The pot-odds formula is unchanged (required equity = call ÷ pot), but short deck's specifics matter: pots are usually bigger (ante + more calls) and draw hit rates must be recalculated on 36 cards.
Pot odds are just numbers, not emotions. Short-deck pots are big and call prices relatively cheap, but you must judge with short-deck-corrected equity (on 36 cards), not the full-ring equity table.

Pot-odds required-equity formula:
Required equity = call ÷ (current pot + opponent bet + call)

Short-deck example (ante structure, pot 8 ante, opponent bets 4 ante, you need to call 4):
Required equity = 4 ÷ (8+4+4) = 25%

But your equity must be short-deck corrected:
Flush draw 5 outs → about 15% single-street, 28% two-street
Straight draw 8 outs → about 24% single-street, 44% two-street

Only call when equity ≥ required equity (or with implied odds). (Concept from: Short Deck Poker pot odds and the 6+ math framework)

Key practical point for short-deck pot odds: because pots are usually larger and call prices cheap, more marginal hands are worth calling; but because draw hit rates are absolutely lower than full ring, you must lean on "the high value of short-deck made hands" (flushes/straights are often nuts) to justify calls. Understanding the balance of these two forces is the core of short-deck odds decisions.

Example: Short-deck pot 10 ante, you (BTN) hold A♥K♥ on a 9♥7♥2♣ flop. The opponent bets 5 ante (half pot); you call 5 into a 20 pot. Required equity = 5/20 = 25%. Your flush draw (5 outs) plus overcards ≈ 8 combined outs, about 35%+ on two streets. 25% odds vs 35% equity → call is +EV; and a made flush is nut-tier with excellent implied odds, so a raise-semi-bluff is even available.

Example 2 (marginal call): Short-deck pot 6 ante, you hold Q♠J♠ on a 9♣8♦2♥ flop, drawing to a T straight (8 outs, but 9/8 seen). The opponent bets 3 ante (half pot), required equity 25%. Your single-street ≈24% (8/33) is slightly below 25%, but two-street ≈44%, and a T straight can beat the opponent's two pair. With implied odds the call turns +EV — short-deck straight draws carry high implied value.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck pots are big and odds cheap, but "cheap" doesn't mean "free". You must judge with short-deck-corrected equity — a flush draw has only 5 outs (15% single-street), seemingly not enough to call, but once made it's a super-strong hand. Combining "cheap odds" with "corrected equity" is the right short-deck odds posture.

Short-deck odds quick math: half-pot bet needs 25%, 1/3 pot 20%, full pot 33.3%. Memorize these, then combine with "flush 5 outs ≈ 15% single-street, straight 8 outs ≈ 24% single-street" to judge whether you qualify.
t2sd-implied: Short-Deck Implied Odds: The Polarization of Made-Hand Value

Implied odds ask "how much more can I win in the future after calling now". Short-deck implied odds are polarized: on one hand, flushes (beating full houses) and straights are super-strong once made, with excellent implied odds; on the other, sets (trips) have worse implied odds because their hand rank is below full houses and flushes. Understanding this polarization is the core of short-deck implied-odds decisions.
Short-deck implied-odds rule: chasing flushes/straights → excellent implied odds (nut-tier when made); chasing sets → worse implied odds (trips lose to full houses/flushes).
Set-Mining Threshold: Why Short Deck Demands More

Short-deck set-mining threshold derivation:

Probability of flopping trips with a pocket pair:
Each rank has 4 cards; you hold 2, leaving 2 in the deck; at least 1 of your rank appears among the 3 flop cards
= 1 − C(31,3)/C(33,3) ≈ 1 − 4495/5456 ≈ 17.6%
(full ring ≈ 12%)

But short-deck trips drop in value: trips < full house < flush

So although the hit rate is higher (17.6% vs 12%), the required payoff ratio is higher:
Short-deck set mining needs a ≥ 15-20× call-amount recovery threshold
(full ring ≈ 10-12×)

Logic: after making trips you lose to full houses/flushes more often, discounting implied odds, requiring a bigger multiple to compensate. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker set mining and 6+ math)

Why are the implied odds of chasing flushes/straights good in short deck? Because once made they're nuts or near-nuts: a flush beats full houses, a straight only loses to trips/full houses/flushes. When the opponent's range contains big pairs or strong hands, making your flush/straight extracts lots of chips. Chasing sets is the opposite — after making trips you can still lose to full houses/flushes, and opponents fold easily too (they know trips aren't the nuts).

Example: Short deck, you hold 7♥8♥ on a 6♦9♣2♠ flop (open-ended straight draw, 7 outs: 5 and T). The opponent bets half pot; you call 5 ante to see the turn. Your implied odds: if T or 5 makes your straight (7-8-9-T or 5-6-7-8-9), it's a strong short-deck straight that can beat the opponent's two pair or anything below trips. If his range has pairs/strong hands, you can win 10+ more ante when you get there. The call's implied odds are excellent.

Example 2 (set mining comparison): Short deck, you hold 5♠5♦ and call 2 ante preflop. Flop 5♣9♥K♦ — you make trips. It looks like a huge advantage, but in short deck trips lose to full houses (opponent's 99/K9) and flushes. And combos like 99/K9 are more common in short-deck ranges (higher pair density). So even making trips, you must watch for outdraws — exactly why short-deck set implied odds are poor.

Counterintuitive point: "making trips" in short deck is nowhere near as happy as in full ring. Full-ring trips are hidden nuts; short-deck trips only beat straights and lose to full houses and flushes. On wet boards the opponent's stronger made hands can outdraw you at any time, heavily discounting trips' implied odds.

Short-deck implied-odds quick memory: chasing flushes/straights → nut-tier when made, chase freely; chasing sets → needs a higher threshold (15-20× the call), and stay alert for full houses/flushes after hitting. Always ask first "is what I make the nuts".
t2sd-reverse: Reverse Implied Odds: Short Deck's Hidden Trap

Reverse implied odds (RIO) ask "after calling now, how much more might I lose in the future". Short-deck RIO is amplified: because of the hand-ranking reshuffle (flush > full house, trips > straight) and high pair density, marginal made hands (top pair, two pair, straights) are more easily dominated by stronger hands. Slow-playing marginal hands or chasing cheap draws can cost you the entire pot on the river.

Short-deck RIO rule: marginal made hands (top pair, two pair, straights) lose value on wet short-deck boards and are easily dominated by stronger hands. RIO awareness prevents "winning small pots and losing big ones".

Three classes of high-RIO spots in short deck: (1) top pair weak kicker — losing big pots to the opponent's two pair/straight/flush; (2) marginal straights — dominated by bigger straights, full houses, flushes; (3) slow-playing strong hands and getting outdrawn — short-deck draw density is high, so slow-playing hands the opponent free draws. After recognizing these spots, use "pot control + timely stop-loss" to avoid RIO.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♠K♦ on a K♣9♦8♥ flop. You flop top pair with an A kicker, but the board is wet (98 connected — the opponent can make straights/two pair). He bets half pot and you call. Turn 7♣ completes the TJ straight. Your top pair now loses to many straights and two pairs — this is RIO: you're ahead now but can lose a big pot on later streets. The right move is flop pot control or cautious calling, not slow-playing all the way.

Example 2 (slow-play trap): Short deck, you hold A♥A♣ on an A♦9♣3♠ flop, making trips of Aces. Looks like the nuts, but in short deck trips < full house < flush, and the board has heart-flush potential. If you slow-play and check, the opponent chases a flush draw for free and makes it on the turn to outdraw you. Short-deck draw density is high — strong hands must bet to protect, avoiding slow-play RIO.

Counterintuitive point: "I have top pair / two pair" is not a reason to slow-play in short deck. The wetter the board and the higher the draw density, the more dangerous your marginal made hand. Fast-playing strong hands for protection plus pot-controlling marginal hands is the core of avoiding RIO.

Short-deck RIO three questions: (1) is my made hand the nuts? (2) what stronger combos can the opponent have? (3) does slow-playing hand him a free draw? After three questions: fast-play the nuts, pot-control marginal hands, and avoid slow-plays on wet boards.
t3sd-rankings: Short-deck starting-hand strength differs fundamentally from standard hold'em, from two rule changes: (1) hand-ranking reshuffle — trips > straights, flushes > full houses; (2) pair density — pocket pairs rise from 5.9% to 8.6% of starting hands. Result: pocket pairs rise in value (easier to make trips, and trips is one of the strongest made hands), while big high-card hands like AK shift subtly in relative value.
Short-deck starting-hand rule: any pocket pair > any A-K. AK is the "strongest non-pair" but doesn't beat pairs. AA/KK are still top tier, but small pairs rise because trips outrank straights.
AK vs Pocket Pairs in Short Deck

Short-deck AK vs pocket-pair preflop all-in comparison (36-card deck):

AK vs any pocket pair (e.g. 22): about 43%-45% (AK trails)
AK vs AK: about 50% (split or suited clash)
AK vs KK: about 25% (KK dominates)

Why pocket pairs rise in value:
1. Trips > straights in short deck, so making trips is a very strong hand
2. High pair density means flopping trips is more likely (about 17.6%)
3. Big pairs (AA/KK) dominate AK more easily

AK's value: still the strongest hand dominating other non-pairs, and it can flop top pair postflop. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker starting-hand strength and 6+ rules)

Practical meaning of the short-deck reshuffle: preflop all-in, AK usually trails a pocket pair (43%-45%), so "AK all-in vs pair" is no longer full ring's "slight coin-flip favorite". Meanwhile, suited connectors (JTs, 98s) are playable because straights/flushes are valuable, but they belong to a secondary tier — they can win big pots (make nuts) yet are weaker preflop than pairs and AK.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♠K♠ and the opponent 3Bets all-in preflop. Your hand is the "strongest non-pair", but against a pocket pair (e.g. 88) you have about 44%. The decision depends on pot odds: if you need 45% and have 44%, marginal fold; if only 40%, call is +EV. The key is using the short-deck-corrected equity (AK vs pair 43%-45%), not the full-ring 43% intuition.

Example 2 (small-pair value): Short deck, you hold 7♠7♦ facing a raise preflop. In short deck 77 flops trips about 17.6% of the time (full ring 12%), and trips is a strong made hand (only loses to full houses/flushes). So small pairs (22-77) rise significantly in short-deck value — set mining still needs a higher threshold (T2), but the strength and frequency of made trips both support more calls.

Counterintuitive point: "AK is strong" in short deck needs the right reading. AK dominates all non-pairs and can flop top pair, but trails any pocket pair preflop all-in. Transplanting the full-ring memory "AK is a slight coin-flip favorite" into short deck overestimates AK's preflop value.

Short-deck starting-hand quick memory: AA/KK top tier, other pairs next (trips value), AK strongest non-pair, suited connectors (JTs+) playable but secondary. For preflop all-ins, use "43%-45%" for pair vs AK, not full-ring intuition.
t3sd-suitedness: Short Deck: The Rise of Flushes

In short deck, a flush beats a full house — the fundamental difference from standard hold'em (where full house > flush). The relative value of flushes rises sharply, making them one of the top made hands in short deck. This changes starting-hand strategy: suited connectors (JTs, 98s, etc.) and suited Ax become significantly more playable — they can make both flushes (nut-tier) and straights.

Short-deck flush rule: flush beats full house — a top-tier made hand. So "suited hands" are worth far more in short deck than in full ring — chasing flush draws has excellent implied odds, and once made they basically lock big pots.

Short-deck suited-connector preflop equity (vs random range):

JTs: about 42%-44%
98s: about 40%-42%
76s: about 38%-40%

Slightly lower than the same hands in full ring (high pair density), but short-deck made-hand value is high:
1. Making a flush (beats full house) → nut-tier
2. Making a straight (connecting across ~8 ranks) → strong hand

Excellent implied odds: chasing flushes/straights deep-stacked pays hugely.

Strategic status: suited connectors are playable but not top tier (AA/KK/QQ/JJ/AK are), so know when to let go against strong preflop resistance. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker flush value and 6+ starting hands)

Suited Ax also rises in short-deck value: A♠K♠, A♠Q♠, etc., can make a flush (beats full house), flop top pair of Aces, and carry an A blocker. But note — suited Ax's value comes from "flush-draw nut potential + top pair", not "AX itself", because short-deck pair density is high and Ax gets dominated by pairs more often.

Example: Short deck, you hold J♠T♠ facing a BTN raise preflop. JTs is playable in short deck: the flop can give a flush draw (high value), a straight draw, or top pair. Though weaker preflop than pairs, its postflop potential is huge. Deep-stacked, actively call or 3Bet-semi-bluff to exploit flush-value implied odds.

Example 2 (flush chase): Short deck, you hold A♥9♥ on a K♥8♦3♣ flop. You draw to the flush (seen A♥9♥K♥ = 3 hearts, flush outs = 9 − 3 = 6). The opponent bets and you call. If the turn brings a heart, your flush is nut-tier (beats full houses) and extracts lots of chips. Short-deck flush draws have few outs (6) but enormous made value — chasing has excellent implied odds.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck suited connectors being "playable" doesn't mean "top-tier strong". They win big pots (making nut flushes/straights) but are weaker preflop than pairs and AK. Treat them as "high-reward speculative hands", not "steady value hands", to use them correctly.

Short-deck flush quick memory: flush beats full house → chasing flush draws is hugely valuable; JTs and above suited connectors are playable; suited Ax has both nut potential and top pair. When facing strong preflop resistance (big 3Bet), suited connectors should let go — they're speculative hands.
t3sd-position: Short-deck position value is amplified because draw density is high, decisions are more frequent, and pots are bigger. Being in position (BTN/IP) means you act after seeing the opponent's action, can realize equity more cheaply, and can control pot size. Out of position (BB/OOP) hurts more in short deck — more draws, easier to be outdrawn, and forced into more tough decisions.

Short-deck position rule: with position on the BTN, chase more draws (cheap equity realization); in the BB without position, tighten marginal calls to avoid high-RIO spots. Position in short deck is both an advantage and a risk regulator.
BTN and BB Positional Strategies in Short Deck

BTN (IP) strategy in short deck: open wider and chase draws more aggressively — position lets you realize equity and control pots. BB (OOP) strategy: defend a reasonable range against BTN's wide opens, but pot-control marginal draws (easily outdrawn) to avoid RIO. The core of short-deck OOP play is "pot control + timely stop-loss".

Example: Short deck, you're on the BTN holding 7♠8♠ on a 9♦6♣2♥ flop (open-ended straight draw). IP, betting or calling realizes equity cheaply — make a straight on a 5/T turn, or see a free river/fold when missing. In the BB (OOP) with the same hand, you act first and get squeezed when raised. Position makes the same draw's value completely different.

Example 2 (OOP pot control): Short deck, you're in the BB holding Q♦J♦ on a Q♣9♦8♠ flop (top pair + gutshot). OOP, you act first. Top pair on a wet board has high RIO and you can't realize equity without position. The right play is pot control (small bet or check) — avoid building a big pot then getting outdrawn by straights/flushes. An in-position BTN can instead bet thin value.

Counterintuitive point: out of position in short deck, "aggressively betting to seize the initiative" can backfire. Because draw density is high and you act first OOP, aggression tends to build a big pot and then land in a high-RIO spot. In short deck position is more a "pot control and stop-loss" tool than mindless aggression.

Short-deck position quick memory: BTN/IP → wide opens + aggressive draw chasing (cheap equity realization); BB/OOP → tighten calls + pot control/stop-loss (avoid RIO). Ask "do I have position" for every hand before deciding between aggression and control.
t4sd-range-construction: Short-Deck Ranges: Different Structure, Same Logic

The basic logic of range construction is unchanged in short deck (divide by hand strength into value/medium/bluffs), but the structure differs: pair density is higher (8.6% vs 5.9%), flush value rises, and the AK-vs-pair relationship shifts. Result: "pairs and suited hands" weigh more in short-deck ranges, while "pure big high cards (offsuit AK/AQ)" fall in relative value.

Short-deck range feature: pairs and suited hands are more valuable; offsuit big high cards relatively devalue. When constructing ranges, allocate more combos to pairs/suited connectors and reduce reliance on "offsuit AX".

Short-deck preflop range tiers (adjusted from standard hold'em):

Top: AA / KK / QQ (pairs are valuable and dominate AK)
Secondary value: JJ-TT / AK (strongest non-pair) / big pairs
Speculative tier: 99-22 (set mining, trips value) / suited connectors JTs+ / suited Ax

Versus standard hold'em:
In hold'em AK is upper-secondary value; in short deck AK is still secondary but below pairs
In hold'em suited connectors are the speculative tier; in short deck, with flush value up, they stay speculative but pay better

Polarization: short-deck betting ranges are more polarized (nut pairs + flush draws/bluffs) because draw density is high and made-hand value is large. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker range construction and 6+ structure)

Short-deck range practice differs: because draw density is high and made-hand value is large (flushes/straights), short-deck ranges can be more "polarized" — bet value with strong made hands (pairs/two pair/flushes), semi-bluff with strong draws (flush/straight draws), and check-control medium hands. Some "medium hands" in standard hold'em are better checked in short deck because their RIO is high.

Example: Short deck, BTN opens and you (BB) hold T♠9♠. T9s belongs to the speculative tier in short-deck ranges: it can make a flush (beats full houses) and straights. Chase draws actively postflop. Holding A♠K♦ (offsuit) instead, it's secondary value — can make top pair, but with high pair density on the flop, top pair is worth less than in standard hold'em.

Example 2 (polarized range): Short-deck flop 8♦7♣3♠, you (BTN IP) hold two pair (87) and a flush draw (A♥9♥). Two pair bets value (not the nuts in short deck but strong), the flush draw semi-bluffs. Medium hands (like 99) have high RIO on wet boards and are better checked. Short-deck range polarization makes the opponent hard to play against.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck ranges being more polarized doesn't mean "more aggressive into chaos". Polarization means strengthening "value/bluffs" and checking "medium hands" — because medium hands have high RIO on wet short-deck boards. When both extremes of the range are strong and the middle is empty, the opponent finds you hard to play against.

Short-deck range quick memory: top pairs + secondary AK + speculative pairs/suited connectors. Betting ranges are polarized (value pairs + semi-bluff draws); medium hands check-control. For every hand, first build your bet/check ratio by "which boards does my range dominate".
t4sd-equity: Short deck is a 6-max game, but with high draw density, multiway pots dilute equity (Equity) significantly. In multiway pots your top pair/two pair face multiple opponents' draws and the win rate gets carved up; the risk of a flush/straight draw's "one of my outs gives another opponent a stronger hand" rises. Understanding equity dilution is the foundation of short-deck multiway decisions.

Short-deck multiway equity rule: every extra opponent dilutes your made-hand equity. Top pair/two pair drop in value multiway, and draws lose "cleanliness" (may feed a stronger hand) — tighten and pot-control in multiway pots.

Multiway equity dilution example (short deck):
