Heads-up: you hold top pair vs a single range, about 60%-70%
Three-way: add one more opponent, your top pair may drop to 35%-45%

Draw out "cleanliness":
Multiway, your flush-draw outs may be held by another opponent / make a bigger flush, losing value

Equity sums: heads-up U₁+U₂=100%, three-way U₁+U₂+U₃=100%
Your share falls as opponents increase

Conclusion: multiway, the thin value of made hands (top pair/two pair) is diluted and draws' reverse implied odds rise. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker multiway equity and 6+ math)

Short-deck multiway practice: because pots are usually big and entry rates high, multiway pots are common. In multiway pots: (1) tighten marginal calls (top pair weak kicker's value is diluted); (2) fast-play strong hands (avoid giving multiple opponents free draws); (3) chase draws more cautiously (outs cleanliness drops, RIO rises).

Example: Short deck, you hold A♠K♠ on an A♦J♣8♥ flop (top pair top kicker) three-way. You have top pair of Aces but two opponents. Heads-up your top pair is strong (about 65%); three-way it may drop to 40%. One opponent holds a J, another an 8 or a draw — either can overtake you. The right play is to bet for protection (fast-play), but realize the bigger the pot, the more your thin value is diluted — control or reassess on the turn and river.

Example 2 (draw RIO): Short deck, you hold 7♥8♥ on a 9♦6♣3♠ flop, drawing to an open-ended straight (5/T), three-way. Your straight-draw outs get "diluted" multiway: if another opponent also draws 5/T, you split the pot or he makes a bigger straight. And if the turn brings the opponent two pair/trips, your straight can lose to bigger hands too. Chase draws more cautiously multiway.

Counterintuitive point: in short-deck multiway pots, "I have a strong draw so I chase" can become donating money. Because outs cleanliness drops (may feed a stronger hand) and RIO rises, your draw equity gets divided among many. Multiway pots are for "fast-playing strong hands + tightening draw chases", not "aggressive draw chasing".

Short-deck multiway quick memory: each extra opponent dilutes equity about 10%-20%. A heads-up 60% top pair is about 40% three-way. Multiway: fast-play strong hands for protection, tighten marginal calls, and judge draw chases by outs cleanliness.
t4sd-blockers: Short-Deck Blockers: A New Dimension of Hand Reading

A blocker is a card you hold that reduces specific opponent combos. Blockers have special value in short deck: because flush value is enormous (beats full houses) and pair density is high, blocking the opponent's flush/pair combos affects bluffing and calling decisions more. When you hold A♥, the opponent's A♥X♥ nut flush is completely blocked — extremely valuable in short deck.

Short-deck blocker rule: holding an A blocks the nut flush (opponent's A♥X♥ combos = 0); holding a pair blocks the opponent's pairs. Short-deck flushes/pairs are valuable, so blocking them massively impacts bluff success.
The Triple Application of Short-Deck Blockers

Short-deck blockers have triple value: (1) blocking flushes — holding A♠ zeros out the opponent's A♠X♠ nut flush, raising bluff success; (2) blocking pairs — holding a K drops the opponent's KK from 6 to 3 combos; (3) unblocking value — not holding a suit means the opponent is more likely to have a flush and pay your value bet. In short deck these blocking effects are amplified by the high value of flushes/pairs.

Example: Short-deck flop K♠9♠4♠ (three spades), you hold A♦A♣ (no spade A). You block no flushes — the opponent can have A♠X♠ nut flush or a smaller flush. Your AA's bluff-catching value drops; lean fold. Conversely, if you hold A♠ (no flush made), you block all A♠X♠ nut-flush combos and the opponent's "strongest hand" is falsified — your bluff or call success rises.

Example 2 (preflop blocking): Short deck, you (BB) face an SB open and consider a 3Bet bluff. The difference between A♦5♦ and 7♦6♦: A5s's A blocks the opponent's AA and AK (fewer top hands, lower 4Bet frequency), and after a 4Bet A5s folds cleanly; 76s blocks no strong hands and runs into QQ+ more often when 4Bet. Short-deck pair density is high, so the A blocker is more valuable.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck blockers are a marginal tool, not a master key. Holding A♠ raises bluff success but doesn't guarantee it; using it to overturn base range analysis is abuse. Blockers carry more weight in short deck (high flush/pair value) but remain the "icing after the base range is right".

Short-deck blocker quick memory: on a three-suited board holding A♠ → blocks the nut flush, bonus for bluffing/calling; holding a pair → blocks the opponent's pairs. Off-the-table drill: set up random three-suited boards and count "opponent nut-flush combos" with and without your A♠, until you can judge in 10 seconds in play.
t5sd-gto-short: Short-deck poker (ignoring rake) approximates a multiway non-zero-sum game, but heads-up short deck is still a two-player zero-sum game where the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee applies. The core difference from standard hold'em GTO is range and made-hand structure: higher pair density, bigger flush value, and common draws lead to higher equilibrium betting frequencies, higher bluff density, and clearer polarization.

Short-deck GTO is a "bulletproof vest": it guarantees you're not exploited but doesn't promise maximum profit. Against a leaky opponent, targeted exploitation earns more — at the cost of opening your own leaks. Short-deck pros switch between "wearing the vest" and "switching to the knife".

Short-deck value:bluff ratio and MDF (formulas unchanged, inputs adjusted):

Value:bluff ratio = b/(1+2b) (b = bet/pot ratio)
Full pot: 1/3 bluffs (2:1 value)
Half pot: 1/4 bluffs (3:1)

MDF = 1/(1+b): half pot defend 67%, full pot 50%

Short-deck adjustment points:
1. Higher made-hand value (flushes/straights) → value bets can use bigger sizes
2. Draws more common → bluff density can be a bit higher (semi-bluff with strong draws)
3. High pair density → defense ranges contain more pairs, supporting higher MDF

Concept from: Short Deck Poker GTO frequencies and 6+ structure

Short-deck GTO practice: because flushes/straights are highly valuable and draws common, short-deck betting ranges are more polarized (strong made hands + semi-bluff draws) and bet sizes can be larger (big bets extract made-hand value). But frequency balance remains core — value:bluff ratios and defensive MDF must be sound, or the opponent counters you.

Example: Short-deck river full-pot bet, equilibrium value:bluff ratio 2:1. You mix a flush (value) with a missed straight draw (bluff). If you only bet flushes (0% bluffs), the opponent folds everything to your full-pot bets and exploits you; if you bluff more than half, he calls everything and exploits you. The equilibrium ratio leaves the opponent torn.

Example 2 (minimum necessary deviation): You observe a short-deck opponent calls big river bets only 25% (equilibrium ~50%). Based on this you can raise your river overbet bluff frequency overall — but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 40%". That's "using GTO as the baseline and making disciplined deviations from observable biases".

Counterintuitive point: short-deck GTO isn't "playing tight" but "keeping everything at ratios the opponent can't counter". Short-deck GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbet shoves, and semi-bluffs — equilibrium frequencies just look more "aggressive" because made-hand value is high and draws are common.

Short-deck GTO learning path: first use a solver to understand the equilibrium "shape" (why play this way), then use node locking to study "harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate live. The baseline gives you invincibility; deviations give you profit.
t5sd-bluff: Short-Deck Bluffing: Higher Reward, Higher Risk

Short-deck bluffing has higher profit potential: because made hands (flushes/straights) are valuable and pots are usually big, a successful pot steal pays well; and opponents may fold more often given high draw density. But risk is higher too — calling ranges are wide and draws get there often, so your bluff is more likely to be "accidentally called into". The key to short-deck bluffing is semi-bluffing with strong draws to reduce risk.
Short-deck bluffing rule: prefer semi-bluffs with strong draws (flush/straight draws) over pure air. A semi-bluff has improvement room even when called, converting bluff risk into an investment.
The Math of Semi-Bluffs and Bluff Frequency

Short-deck semi-bluff EV (flop, strong draw):

EV(bluff) = f×P − (1−f)×(1−E_win)×Bet + (1−f)×E_win×(P+Bet)
(f = opponent fold rate, E_win = equity when called)

Versus pure-air bluff (E_win ≈ 0):
Pure air: EV = f×P − (1−f)×Bet
Semi-bluff: higher EV because of the E_win improvement room

Example: pot 8, bet 4, opponent folds 50%, your straight-draw equity when called is 35%:
EV(bluff) = 0.5×8 − 0.5×(0.65)×4 + 0.5×0.35×12 = 4 − 1.3 + 2.1 = 4.8

Semi-bluff EV 4.8 is clearly above pure air's EV = 0.5×8 − 0.5×4 = 2. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker semi-bluffs and the 6+ game)

Short-deck bluff-frequency practice: because flush/straight draws are common and made-hand value is high, short-deck bluffing ranges should be semi-bluff-heavy. Pure-air bluffs are risky in short deck (wide calling ranges, easily accidentally called into). Also optimize with blockers — holding A♠ blocking the opponent's nut flush raises bluff success.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♥9♥ on a K♥8♦3♣ flop. You have a flush draw (6 outs) + A high. The opponent bets and you raise as a semi-bluff: if he folds you win the pot directly; if he calls you have flush/overcard improvement room. Short-deck flush value is enormous, so this semi-bluff's EV far exceeds pure air.

Example 2 (blocker bluff): Short-deck flop K♠9♠4♠ (three spades), you hold A♠5♦ (lone A♠, no flush). You block every A♠X♠ nut-flush combo — the opponent's "strongest hand" is falsified. Raising to represent a flush now has a significantly higher success rate. A blocker turns the same "air" into a differently-strength bluff.

Counterintuitive point: pure-air bluffing in short deck is high-risk behavior. Because opponent draw density is high and calling ranges wide, your air bluff easily gets "accidentally called" or even outdrawn by a draw. Short-deck bluffs should be semi-bluff-heavy — convert risk into investment with strong draws.

Short-deck bluffing quick memory: prefer semi-bluffs (flush/straight draws), EV 2-3× pure air; holding an A blocking the nuts adds to bluffs; raise bluff frequency against high fold rates. Avoid mindless pure-air bluffing in short deck.
t6sd-sizing: In standard hold'em, 1/3-pot, half-pot, and 2/3-pot sizes are widely used. In short deck some "traditional sizes" fail or need adjustment: because draw density is high and made-hand value is large, half-pot/small bets may not protect your made hands (opponents draw too cheaply), while big bets/overbets are more effective when made-hand value is high.

Short-deck sizing rule: with high draw density, small bets can't protect made hands; with high made-hand value (flushes/straights), big bets/overbets extract more. Use big sizes for protection on wet boards; small thin-value bets are fine on dry boards.

Short-deck value:bluff ratio for bet sizes (formulas unchanged):
Bluff share f = b/(1+2b)
1/3 pot → 20%; half pot → 25%; full pot → 33%; 2× pot → 40%

Short-deck adjustments:
1. Wet boards (many draws) → big sizes (2/3 pot+) to protect made hands and charge draws
2. Dry boards → small sizes (1/3 pot) for thin value
3. High made-hand value (flushes/straights) → overbets can extract more

The essence of "traditional small bets failing": small bets give draws too cheap a price, and short-deck draws get there easily — you must protect with big sizes. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker bet sizing and 6+ protection)

Short-deck sizing practice: because pots are usually bigger and draw density high, sizing trends larger overall — use 2/3 pot or even full pot to protect made hands and charge draws. But also account for stack depth (SPR): deep stacks build pots with big sizes, shallow stacks are more direct. In short deck, "small thin-value bets" are often an error on wet boards.

Example: Short deck, you hold K♠K♦ on a 9♦8♣3♥ flop (wet, 98 connected). Your overpair is easily outdrawn by straights/two pair on a wet board, and opponent draw density is high. Use a 2/3+ pot big bet (pot 6, bet 4+) to protect — charge the opponent's straight/flush draws rather than giving a cheap price. A half-pot small bet isn't enough to protect an overpair on a wet short-deck board.

Example 2 (dry-board small bet): Short-deck flop K♠7♦2♣ (dry), you hold A♠K♣. The opponent rarely hits this board; use a 1/3-pot small thin-value bet — weak hands in a wide range pay and junk folds, so small works. Small bets still work on dry boards; only wet boards need big sizes.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck "small thin-value bets" aren't always right. On wet boards (high draw density), a small bet gives draws too cheap a price — effectively letting the opponent chase for free. Short-deck draws get there easily, so you must protect with big sizes. Small bets are only right on dry boards.

Short-deck sizing quick memory: wet boards → 2/3+ pot big bets to protect made hands; dry boards → 1/3-pot small thin-value bets; high made-hand value (flushes/straights) → overbets to extract. First judge board wetness, then choose the size.
t6sd-barrel: Barreling is more frequent in short deck than standard hold'em because made-hand value is high and strong made hands (flushes/straights) need multiple streets to extract. Short-deck pros fire three barrels on strong hands like flushes/straights/two pair, building the pot with big sizes every street to extract full value. But when the board changes hands (turn/river completes the opponent's draws), adjust frequency.

Short-deck consecutive value-barrel rule: fire three barrels with strong made hands (flushes/straights/two pair) to extract value; but lower frequency when the turn/river changes hands (completes the opponent's draws). Value betting is more frequent but not mindless.

Short-deck consecutive value-bet pot geometry (starting pot P):
Three barrels (2/3 pot each street):
Flop 2/3P → turn 2/3×new pot → river 2/3×new pot

With P=6:
Flop bet 4, pot 14
Turn bet 9.3, pot 32.6
River bet 21.7, pot 75.9

Deep-stacked, strong made hands need big sizes so the pot grows geometrically and the shove lands on the river.

Board-change adjustment:
If the turn/river completes the opponent's draw (e.g. a straight/flush card), lower firing frequency and switch to pot control. (Concept from: Short Deck Poker multi-street value betting)

Short-deck barreling practice: because flush/straight made-hand value is high and draw density is large, short-deck value betting is more frequent — but the key is "barrel strong hands", not "barrel mindlessly". Dry boards allow three barrels (the opponent rarely hits), while wet boards that complete the opponent's draws (a flush/straight card on the turn) call for reducing frequency.

Example: Short deck, you hold A♠K♠ and flop top pair of Aces on a K♠7♦2♣ flop (dry). You bet 1/3 pot, he calls. Turn 5♥ (blank), you continue with a half-pot bet (top-pair value). River 9♣ (blank), you bet 2/3 pot for value. Three streets of consecutive value betting because the board stays dry and the opponent rarely hits.

Example 2 (board change): Short deck, you hold 7♠8♠ on a 9♦6♣3♥ flop (open-ended straight draw), you semi-bluff bet and he calls. Turn 5♠ — completes your straight (5-6-7-8-9)! Now you make a straight and continue betting for value. But if the turn were 5♦ (the opponent can also have 5-6 or 4-7), you must assess whether he also made a straight and adjust when the board changes hands.

Counterintuitive point: short-deck consecutive value betting is more frequent, but "the board changing hands" matters more than your hand strength. When the turn/river completes the opponent's draw (a flush/straight card), even if you're still ahead, lower frequency — because the combos in his range that beat you have multiplied.

Short-deck barreling three questions: (1) whose draw does this board improve? (2) how many streets does my made hand need to extract? (3) can the pot geometry support an all-in? After three questions: barrel strong hands, pot-control when the board changes hands.
t7sd-mistakes: Most short-deck players come from standard hold'em carrying full-ring mental inertia. These "cognitive biases" are an exploitable gold mine: calculating short-deck equity with the full-ring outs table, underrating flush value (thinking full house > flush), overrating AK, set-mining too loosely, and slow-playing wet boards. Recognizing these error patterns is the prerequisite for short-deck exploitation.

The core of short-deck exploitation: identify the opponent's "standard hold'em inertia". Players who don't recalculate outs on 36 cards, underrate flush value, or set-mine too loosely are exploitable targets.
Characterizing Common Errors and Exploiting Them

The four most common short-deck player errors: (1) wrong outs — using the full-ring outs table, treating a flush draw as 9 outs (actually 5 in short deck), overestimating equity; (2) underrating flushes — thinking full house > flush, using standard hold'em rankings, misjudging strength; (3) overrating AK — thinking AK is a slight coin-flip favorite when it actually trails pairs; (4) set-mining too loosely — using the full-ring threshold when short-deck trips are less valuable. Identify and exploit each.

Example: You notice the opponent chases draws with the full-ring outs table (flush draw as 9 outs). His actual equity is overestimated, so he chases too loosely. Exploit: your value bets can be bigger and your calls tighter — his chases are expensive and rarely get there. After recognizing this cognitive bias, you can extract targeted value.

Example 2 (underrating flushes): The opponent uses standard hold'em rankings and thinks full house > flush. When you make a flush and he makes a full house, he mistakenly thinks the full house is bigger and keeps calling your big bets. Exploit: your value bets on flush boards (which beat full houses) can be more aggressive because he misjudges strength.

Example 3 (overrating AK): The opponent thinks AK is a slight preflop coin-flip favorite and shoves AK frequently. Exploit: call his shove with pocket pairs, because short-deck pairs > AK (43%-45%), so you're slightly ahead. Recognizing his AK overrating turns your pair calls +EV.

Counterintuitive point: "the opponent using full-ring intuition" is the most exploitable leak in short deck. Their outs are wrong, their hand rankings are wrong, and their starting-hand values are overestimated — these biases make your value bets more valuable and your calls more profitable. Identifying biases matters more than memorizing more GTO.

Short-deck exploitation quick memory: watch four signals in opponents — do they chase with short-deck outs, misjudge strength on flush boards, shove AK too often, or set-mine too loosely? Each signal maps to an exploitation direction.
t7sd-adjustment: From NLHE to Short Deck: A Mindset Shift

The biggest obstacle moving from standard hold'em (NLHE) to short deck is mental inertia. The key short-deck mindset shifts: (1) rankings — flush > full house, trips > straight; (2) starting hands — pairs > AK; (3) chasing — recalculate outs on 36 cards; (4) variance — higher, demanding more conservative bankroll. Complete these shifts before you can decide with a short-deck mindset instead of a full-ring one.

Short-deck mindset rule: before every decision ask "is this short deck or full ring" — were the outs recalculated? Is the ranking right? Is AK overrated? Is the variance buffer enough? All five correct — that's short-deck thinking.

The core short-deck strategic adjustments: (1) ranges — pairs and suited hands rise, offsuit high cards fall; (2) betting — big sizes on wet boards for protection, small bets on dry; (3) chasing — recalculate outs on 36 cards, flush chases are high-value; (4) bankroll — more conservative (≥150 buy-ins). These adjustments make short-deck strategy fundamentally different from standard hold'em.

Example (mindset shift): In standard hold'em you're used to "AK is a strong hand to shove". After switching to short deck, facing an all-in you must realize AK is about 43%-45% against a pocket pair (trailing). If pot odds only need 40%, call; if 45%, fold. Use short-deck-corrected equity rather than full-ring intuition.

Example 2 (chase shift): In standard hold'em a flush draw has 9 outs and you're used to chasing. In short deck a flush has 5 outs (15% single-street) — seemingly not worth it — but making a flush is the nuts (beats full houses) with excellent implied odds. So chasing a short-deck flush isn't "few outs, fold" but "few outs yet high made value, look at implied odds". A typical mindset shift.

Counterintuitive point: the short-deck mindset shift isn't "memorizing new rules" but "re-evaluating every hand". The same hand and board can produce completely opposite decisions between short deck and full ring — using full-ring memory auto-makes errors. The mark of a short-deck pro is "always reminding yourself you're in short deck".

Short-deck mindset-shift five questions (every hand): (1) is the ranking right? (2) are the outs on 36 cards? (3) is AK overrated? (4) big sizes on wet boards? (5) enough variance bankroll? All five correct — the short-deck mindset is built.
t8sd-variance: Short-Deck Variance: The Test of Mental Resilience

Short-deck variance is significantly higher than standard hold'em (flop rates/draws/pot sizes), making mental resilience a short-deck player's core asset. Losing multiple 45%-55% all-ins in a row is mathematical normalcy in short deck. The key to handling variance isn't "holding back tears" but "treating variance as an uncontrollable external variable and controlling only decision quality".

Short-deck variance rule: variance is uncontrollable weather; decision quality is controllable ability. Treat losing streaks as weather, not a verdict, to keep your strategy undistorted through variance.

Short-deck variance budget (mental resilience framework):

Single all-in standard deviation σ = √(p(1−p)) × pot size
Short-deck all-in equity p often lands in 45%-55%, so σ is relatively high

N-hand cumulative variance = σ×√N, expectation = N×marginal edge×pot size

Example: p=50%, pot 100:
σ = √(0.5×0.5)×100 = 50
50-hand cumulative variance = 50×√50 ≈ 354, expectation 0

Conclusion: even at EV neutrality, short deck can swing ±350 chips over 50 hands — the variance budget is the mathematical basis of psychological tolerance. (Concept from: The Mathematics of Poker variance framework + short-deck high variance)

Short-deck resilience practice: preset a variance budget (pause after losing 40-50BB), use a decision log instead of a win/loss log, and accept that "short-deck variance is structural". Resilience isn't "enduring bigger losses" but "maintaining the same decision quality while both wins and losses are violent".

Example: Short deck, you shove 8 hands in a row at 50% equity (draws vs made hands colliding), and losing all 8 is 0.5^8 ≈ 0.4%; short deck has frequent all-ins per hour, so a session may contain one. Your mind knows "EV neutral" but emotions want "to get even". The right move: recognize the revenge impulse → pause → restart with "what is this hand's EV".

Example 2 (executing the variance budget): Short deck, you've lost 45BB in a session (near the 50BB budget). Even if the table is still good, execute "pause at 50BB" — because continuing may make your worst adjustments during the most violent variance. Stop and restart, don't chase and re-buy.

Counterintuitive point: the hardest part of handling short-deck variance is "letting your guard down after winning". After winning a few hands, players often relax, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. Short-deck discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose.

Short-deck variance-handling triad: (1) preset a variance budget (pause after losing 40-50BB); (2) use a decision log instead of a win/loss log; (3) stand up every 100 hands to break losing-streak inertia. These three keep variance from steering your strategy.
t8sd-tilt: Short-Deck Tilt: The Emotional Trap of High Variance

Short deck is a tilt hotspot: high variance, high flop rates, big pots, and violent win-loss alternation. Tilt comes from three triggers: result dependence, dashed expectations, and revenge psychology. In short deck, with large variance and common losing streaks, tilt triggers more easily. Tilt distorts your range (opening too loose, calling too wide, chasing too aggressively), systematically deviating from baseline.

Short-deck tilt-defense triad: self-awareness (set an emotional red light), preset discipline (stop-loss point), and process attribution (only ask EV). Build the defense off the table so it's ready when tilt hits.

Tilt's horror is that it distorts your range: you open looser, call wider, and chase harder — all deviating from equilibrium. Three defenses: (1) self-awareness — set an "emotional red light" (N consecutive hands wanting revenge/raise to get even) and force a pause; (2) pre-commitment — set the stop-loss off the table and leave at the line; (3) process attribution — review only whether decision EV was correct, never change play because of results.

Example: Short deck, you lose 6 consecutive 50% all-ins (0.5^6 ≈ 1.6%, encountered several times an hour in short deck). Your mind knows "I played right" but emotions want "to get even". If you size up to chase losses, that's a tilt loop. The right move: recognize the revenge impulse → pause 10 minutes → restart with "what is this hand's EV".

Example 2 (process vs result): Short deck, you shove AK vs 55 (short-deck AK vs 55 ≈ 43%-45%) and 55 wins. You lost the result, but the process: with proper pot odds, calling was +EV — you played right. Short-deck pros review only process: "was this decision EV-correct?" Tilters review only results: "I lost to junk again."

Counterintuitive point: the most dangerous tilt in short deck isn't "impulse when losing" but "letting your guard down after winning". After winning a few hands, players relax, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. Short-deck discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose.

Short-deck tilt-control triad: (1) emotional red light — pause after N consecutive hands wanting revenge; (2) preset stop-loss — leave after losing 40-50BB; (3) process attribution — review only EV. Build all three off the table so they're ready when tilt hits.
t9sd-integration: From Fragments to a System: The Short-Deck Decision Loop

Each chapter of T1-T8 is a building block of the short-deck system: T1 probability (36-card combos/outs), T2 odds (ante structure/implied odds), T3 starting hands (pairs>AK/flushes), T4 ranges, T5 GTO, T6 betting, T7 opponents, T8 psychology. The short-deck master doesn't "memorize each chapter" but connects them into a decision loop — facing any situation, run automatically through "range → math → betting → opponent → psychology".

Short-deck decision loop: first ask "does my range dominate this board" (T4), then compute "EV and odds" (T2), then "what size" (T6), then "what short-deck inertia does the opponent have to exploit" (T7), finally "am I emotionally stable" (T8). All five questions, none optional.

Short-deck theory deforms along two parameters: stack depth and game type. Deep stacks (100BB+): wider ranges, more polarized betting, more aggressive draw chasing (good implied odds). Short stacks (under 20BB): more frequent preflop all-ins, adjusted set-mining thresholds, smaller positional value. Cash: unlimited re-buy, manageable variance, measured in bb/100. Tournaments: finite chips, ICM pressure, strategy shifts by stage (see l6sd-tourney).

Example: Short deck, deep stack 100BB, you hold 7♠8♠ facing a BTN open. Decision loop: range — 78s is the speculative tier in short deck (can make flushes/straights); math — call price vs implied odds (high made value); betting — chase actively but pot-control wet boards; opponent — does he have short-deck inertia (overrating AK / underrating flushes); psychology — don't tilt when outdrawn. One decision, all five questions passed.

Example 2 (short stack): Short deck, 20BB deep, you hold A♠Q♠. Range — AQ is secondary value in short deck; math — EV of shove vs min-raise; betting — just shove with a short stack; opponent — read the fold rate; psychology — accept variance. Stack depth changes how the same hand plays — short stacks are more direct.

Counterintuitive point: a short-deck master's "cleverness" isn't perfect decisions but "system stability". Occasional mistakes are inevitable, but a stable decision loop plus strict emotional discipline keep the long-term expectation curve climbing. Chasing "every-hand perfection" instead causes overthinking and tilt.

Building your short-deck system in four steps: learn (T1-T8 theory) → drill (solver/hand examples) → play (execute the loop live) → review (hand-by-hand review + notes). Four-step loop, and your short-deck level climbs steadily with every session.
t9sd-case-study: The core value of studying professional short-deck players (like top Triton Series performers) is understanding their decision framework rather than imitating a specific move. Top short-deck players share: short-deck thinking (outs recalculated, correct rankings), frequency balance (not leaking ranges), range polarization (value pairs + semi-bluff draws), and emotional stability (maintaining quality under high variance).

The dividing line between pros and amateurs isn't luck but "decision framework". Pros rely on systems (short-deck thinking + frequency balance + discipline); amateurs rely on full-ring intuition. Studying pros means learning systems, not copying cards.
Deconstructing the Pro Short-Deck Decision Framework

Top short-deck players' frameworks usually have four layers: (1) preflop ranges — pairs and suited hands first, AK next, adjusted by opponent; (2) postflop ranges — bet/check by board ownership (whose range/nut advantage); (3) bet sizing — big sizes on wet boards for protection, small bets on dry; (4) psychology — maintaining decision quality under high variance. Each layer has clear inputs and outputs, not improvisation.

Example (preflop ranges): A pro short-deck player facing a BB who 3Bets too much narrows his opening range, reducing the marginal hands that only fold after a 3Bet; against an over-folder, he raises the open frequency toward 100%. This is a computable "micro-adjust range by opponent tendency" decision, not feel.

Example 2 (postflop range allocation): A pro short-deck player uses 2/3+ pot big bets to protect overpairs on wet boards (9♦8♣3♥) because short-deck draw density is high and small bets give draws too cheap a price; on dry boards (K♠7♦2♣) he bets small for thin value. Short-deck's signature "big sizing on wet boards" is the dividing line between pros and amateurs.

Example 3 (emotional discipline): Top short-deck players still decide with the same framework after losing 10 consecutive 45%-55% all-ins — they treat variance as an uncontrollable variable and control only decision quality. This is T8's "process vs result" separation manifested at the professional level.

Counterintuitive point: the value of studying pro short-deck players isn't "how great they are" but "how replicable their system is". An amateur drilling the pro framework for a month often improves faster than "ten years of full-ring feel" — because systems are trainable and feel isn't replicable.

Pro short-deck hand-study process: (1) record all actions of a hand; (2) deconstruct layer by layer with the decision loop (range/math/betting/opponent/psychology); (3) compare with your own handling to find gaps; (4) distill one reusable principle. Every 10 hands studied makes your short-deck framework more complete.
t1hu-probability: From Full Ring to Heads-Up: Everything Changes

Heads-Up (HU) has only two players: each hand you and the opponent alternate as SB and BB. The structural differences deeply reshape the probability framework: the SB forces 0.5 (which also acts as an ante, and the SB is the button), the BB forces 1; preflop the SB acts first and the BB acts last, so the SB's raise can't "steal" blinds; postflop the BB acts first, and the SB (button) acts last with positional advantage. As a result, the playable starting-hand share jumps from about 15%-20% in full ring to 50%+ — because you only have to beat one opponent.
A hand's value is decided by "how many people you must beat". In heads-up you face one person instead of eight — this single fact reshuffles nearly every hand's win rate.

Probability the opponent has at least one Ace (you hold two non-Ace cards):
Remaining deck 50 cards: 4 Aces, 46 non-Aces
Total opponent combos: C(50,2) = 50×49÷2 = 1225
Both opponent cards non-Ace: C(46,2) = 46×45÷2 = 1035
At least one Ace = 1 − 1035÷1225 ≈ 15.5%

The comparison that truly shows the heads-up difference is "the density of strong hands in the opponent's range". When you hold AA, only 2 Aces remain in 50 cards, so a HU opponent has AA just 1/1225 ≈ 0.08%; in full ring at least one of 8 opponents has AA about 8/1225 ≈ 0.65% — in heads-up your strongest hand's dominance is rarely offset by a "crash". More crucially: in heads-up you're ahead of 50%+ of the opponent's range, whereas full ring you're ahead of at most 3-4 people — the "density" difference is what truly drives decisions. (Concepts from: The Theory of Poker, David Sklansky Ch.1 hand value and number of opponents; Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.1 heads-up range narrowing)

What does 15.5% mean? In heads-up, about once every 6-7 hands the opponent has at least one Ace — but your hand is also often ahead, because his range is wide and most of the time his Ace is a bare Ace rather than a pair dominating you. What truly demands caution isn't "he has an Ace" but "what kicker is the Ace paired with". In full ring "someone has an Ace" almost equals "someone has a stronger hand", but in heads-up that's far from true.

Example: 100BB deep heads-up, you (SB) hold A♠K♥ and the opponent (BB) has a near-random range. Preflop all-in, AKo vs random is about 65.4%; if you just raise to 3BB and he calls, A-high remains a strong showdown hand postflop. Compare full ring: UTG's AKo facing 8 opponents all-in drops to about 30% — the same hand is crushing in heads-up and marginal in full ring. That's the practical meaning of the "reshuffle".

Heads-up preflop all-in equity anchors vs random cards:
AA ≈ 85%｜KK ≈ 82%｜QQ ≈ 80%
AKo ≈ 65%｜AQs ≈ 66%｜KQs ≈ 62%
22 ≈ 50%｜T9s ≈ 52%｜72o ≈ 35%
In a nine-handed all-in the worst hand falls below 15%, but in heads-up the worst hand still keeps about 35% — no two cards are dead in heads-up. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.1 heads-up starting-hand rankings)

Example 2: You hold A♠A♥. In heads-up the opponent has AA with probability 1/1225 ≈ 0.08% (after your two Aces only 2 remain in 50 cards); in full ring at least one of 8 opponents has AA about 8/1225 ≈ 0.65%. Meanwhile AA vs random is about 85%, but AA in a nine-handed all-in vs 8 people is only about 31% — in heads-up your strongest hand's dominance is both less often offset by a crash and less diluted by multiway pots.

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up, "bad hands" are far less bad than imagined. 72o still has about 35% equity vs random — no raise by the opponent can "represent" a hand much stronger than yours. Carrying the full-ring mindset of "wait for good hands" bleeds money slowly in heads-up.

Build three-tier anchors: big pairs/high cards 65%-85%, small/medium pairs about 50%, garbage about 35%. When facing a preflop all-in, first estimate the spot with these tiers, then talk pot odds — the anchors are your table-side mental math dictionary.
t1hu-outs: Outs in Heads-Up: First Answer "Who's Ahead"

The definition of outs is unchanged — unknown cards that let your hand overtake the opponent. But heads-up changes the standard of "clean outs": the opponent's range is wide, often only one pair or even just high cards, so your overcard outs are rarely reverse-dominated; the full-ring multiway risk of "one of my outs gives another opponent a flush" almost disappears in heads-up, and the discount can relax from 70-80% to about 90%.
Outs are always relative to a range. In heads-up first judge "am I ahead or behind now", then decide whose outs to count — getting this order wrong is the biggest math mistake of heads-up beginners.
The Reversed View: Count the Opponent's Outs

Classic scenario: you're ahead with high cards, the opponent has two smaller high-card draw cards, giving him 6 outs (3+3). Exact two-street derivation (flop, 45 unknown cards):
P(hit on turn) = 6÷45 ≈ 13.3%
P(miss turn, hit river) = (39÷45)×(6÷44) ≈ 11.9%
P(at least one hit) ≈ 25.2% (the 2/4 rule estimates 24%, about 1 point off)
Your leading equity ≈ 1 − 25.2% ≈ 74.8% (reverse redraws adjust slightly; magnitude unchanged). (Concepts from: The Mathematics of Poker, Bill Chen / Jeremie Ankenman Ch.5-6 outs and probability trees; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.4 heads-up draw confrontations)

Example: HU blinds 0.5/1, preflop SB completes to 1 and BB checks, pot 2. Flop 9♠7♦2♣, you (BB) hold K♠Q♠ and the opponent (SB) holds J♣T♦. You're ahead with K-high; he has only 6 outs (3 Js + 3 Ts) and overtakes about 25.2% over two streets, giving you about 67% total equity (you still have K/Q redraws after he hits). He bets 1 (half pot). Decision: if you just call 1, he only pays one more bet on the turn to see the river — buying about 25% overtake chance at low cost, a bad starting point; the correct play is to raise to about 3: if he folds you win the 3-pot directly (2+1), and if he calls he's overpaying for his 25% chance. In heads-up, "protecting when ahead" appears far more often than in full ring.

Exact equity of a 15-out combo draw (flop → two cards to river):
15 outs = flush 9 + overcards 6
P(both miss) = (32÷47)×(31÷46) ≈ 45.9%
P(at least one hit) = 1 − 45.9% ≈ 54.1%
The 2/4 rule gives 60%, overestimating by about 6 points — for outs ≥ 13 use the corrected formula Outs×4 − (Outs−8) = 53%, or just memorize 54%.

Example 2: HU blinds 0.5/1, you (BB) hold A♥K♥, call the opponent's (SB) 3Bet, pot 8. Flop 9♥7♥2♣, he (about 5♠5♦) bets 5. You have flush 9 outs + overcards 6 outs = 15 outs, about 54.1% equity, but currently only A-high and behind. Decision: raising or shoving is +EV — if he folds you win 13 directly (pot 8 + bet 5), and if called you still have 54%; his pair is actually the one drawing to two pair/trips. In a full-ring multiway pot this combo draw's equity would dilute below 50%, but in heads-up you can be comfortably aggressive. (Concept from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.6 semi-bluffs and combo draws)

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up, draws aren't "passive waiting" but offensive weapons. A 15-out combo draw is a coin-flip favorite even when currently behind — whoever is closer to the nuts owns the initiative.

Table mantra: first ask "who's ahead", then count outs. Ahead → count the opponent's outs and make them pay; behind → count your own outs and compute pot odds. Repeat this flow on every heads-up hand — speed decides win rate.
t1hu-variance: Heads-Up Variance: Faster, Denser, More Violent

In heads-up you're in a blind (SB or BB) every hand — about 4.5× the blind frequency of a nine-handed table; the SB only needs to complete 0.5 to see a flop, so nearly every hand sees one; online HU can reach 200-300 hands/hour, 2-3× full ring. The same equity edge is "compressed" into a shorter time in heads-up — variance isn't a flaw of HU but the mathematical necessity of high-frequency confrontation.
A heads-up downswing isn't an anomaly but an inevitability: the number of decisions, all-ins, and blind pressure per hour all double, and so does the density of luck's influence.
Variance Math: The Stacking of High-Frequency All-Ins

Standard deviation of a single all-in (Bernoulli model: win +100, lose −100 chips, p = 60%):
σ = √(p×(1−p)) × 100 = √(0.6×0.4) × 100 ≈ 49 chips
N-hand cumulative: σ_total = σ×√N
50 hands: σ ≈ 49×√50 ≈ 347; expectation = 50×(0.6−0.4)×100 = 1000
Loss probability: 1000÷347 ≈ 2.9σ → about 0.2%
Conclusion: even a positive-expectation 1000 chips can end up a loss — 60%-equity all-ins happen daily in heads-up, which is the mathematical root of "winners also experience long drawdowns". (Concepts from: The Mathematics of Poker, Bill Chen / Jeremie Ankenman Ch.3 variance and standard deviation; The Mental Game of Poker, Jared Tendler Ch.4 variance tolerance and emotion)

The intuition of the √N rule: variance grows with the square root of the sample while expectation grows linearly. Doubling the sample only shrinks variance's relative impact to 1/√2 ≈ 70%, and you need 4× the sample to halve it. Heads-up's high-frequency play means you accumulate samples faster — but also experience the full variance cycle faster. This is the mathematical root of "winners also experience long drawdowns".

Example: 55% equity is a common heads-up preflop all-in spot (e.g. small pair vs two overcards ≈ 55:45). Losing 5 in a row = 0.45⁵ ≈ 1.8%, appearing about 3-4 times per hour of 200+ hands; losing 8 in a row ≈ 0.17%, about once every 3 hours. In other words: "losing a big streak" in a HU session isn't bad luck but steadily present background noise — treat it like weather, not a verdict.

Heads-up vs full-ring variance parameters (typical bb/100 magnitudes):
Full ring: winner 5bb/100, standard deviation 80-100
Heads-up: winner 5-15bb/100, standard deviation 120-180
Heads-up's "variance/expectation" ratio is higher: the same 5bb edge needs 2-4× the sample to converge reliably — that's why HU players doubt their own skill more easily than full-ring players. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.10 bankroll management and variance)

Example 2 (bankroll simulation): Suppose your HU win rate is 55%, buy-in 100 chips, standard deviation 150 per 100 hands. With only 20 buy-ins (the full-ring standard), there's about a 5% chance of a 20-buy-in (2000-chip) downswing — HU's high-frequency variance can realize such a downswing within weeks; with 50 buy-ins, the same variance consumes only about 40% of the bankroll. Conclusion: HU demands a higher bankroll bar — Moshman suggests at least 50 buy-ins, executed strictly by "move down/rebuild" rules rather than "one more game to get even".

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up, "losing many hands" almost never proves "playing badly". The hourly sample is packed with 55%-60%-equity all-ins; losing 8-10 in a row is mathematical normalcy. Review with a decision log (recording the reasoning of each key decision) instead of a win/loss log, or you'll make your worst strategic adjustments during the most violent variance.

HU session-management triad: (1) preset a variance budget — in a 100BB-deep game pause and review after losing 40-50BB, a stop-and-restart not a chase; (2) stand up every 100 hands to break losing-streak inertia; (3) review only EV, never results — Tendler's "process vs result" separation is a survival skill for HU psychology.
t2hu-odds: Heads-up blind structure differs fundamentally from full ring: the SB posts 0.5BB (which also acts as an ante), the BB posts 1BB, and the preflop pot is only 1.5BB — negligible relative to a 100BB effective stack. The key point: the SB's 0.5 is "dead money", and any not-yet-invested player (here only the BB) can see the flop for free — because the SB already posted part, he only completes 0.5 to make the full 1.5BB. This makes the preflop "contest frequency" in heads-up far higher than full ring: you don't need to wait for a raise to see favorable odds — limping gets you into the flop at a required equity of about 25%. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 preflop odds structure; Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.3 blind games)
Pot odds are just numbers, not emotions. In heads-up the SB's dead money means every limped pot is an automatic +EV opportunity as long as your hand beats the required equity.
Deriving the Call Price After an SB Limp

Preflop SB-limp scenario: SB has posted 0.5, BB has posted 1, pot 1.5BB. For the SB to complete to 1 (finish the blind) and see the flop, he must invest 0.5 more.

Required-equity formula:
Required equity = call ÷ (current pot + opponent bet + call)

Application:
• Current pot = 1.5BB (includes the SB's 0.5, but that's already dead money)
• Opponent bet = 0 (no one raised)
• Call = 0.5BB (the SB's completion)
• Required equity = 0.5 ÷ (1.5 + 0 + 0.5) = 0.5 ÷ 2.0 = 25%

Verification: let equity be E. EV(call) = E×1.5 − (1−E)×0.5. At break-even: E×1.5 = (1−E)×0.5 → 1.5E = 0.5 − 0.5E → 2E = 0.5 → E = 25%. (Concept from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.3 pot-odds formula, Dan Harrington / Bill Robertie)

Example: HU blinds 0.5/1, you hold Q♠J♠. Preflop SB limps (completes 0.5), you (BB) check. Flop T♦8♣3♥, you have an open-ended straight draw. Turn A♠, pot 2.5BB, BB bets 1.25BB (half pot). You call 1.25; required equity = 1.25 ÷ (2.5+1.25+1.25) = 1.25÷5 = 25%. QJ on T83A still has K+9 = 8 outs ≈ 17% (river only); plus 2 top-pair outs (one Q and one J remain) = 10 outs ≈ 21.7%. Below 25% on one street — fold or check-raise. This example shows: even with cheap pot odds (25%), if your hand equity doesn't cover it, fold. Compute odds and equity separately rather than judging vaguely.

Example 2: SB holds J♠T♠ and limps to see the flop (odds 25%). Flop J♣7♦2♠, top pair. BB bets 1BB (pot 2BB). Required equity to call = 1 ÷ (2+1+1) = 25%. Your top pair is far above 25% (wide range, you may be ahead) → easy call. Compare the same spot in full ring: 5-way pot of 5BB, bet 2.5BB (half pot), required equity still 25% (formula is size-independent) — but your actual equity is diluted by multiple opponents, possibly falling from 60% to 40%, while HU vs one opponent stays 60%. That's the essence of "odds dilution": the pot's price is unchanged, but equity must be recalibrated by player count.

Call odds comparison facing a raise (open to 3BB):

Heads-up scenario (BB defense):
• SB opens to 3BB (total 3), BB has posted 1, pot = 4BB
• BB must call 2BB (3−1)
• Required equity = 2 ÷ (4+2) = 33.3%

Full-ring scenario (BTN calls UTG's 3BB open):
• UTG opens 3BB; SB/CO fold; BTN faces a pot of 4.5BB (UTG's 3 + SB 0.5 + BB 1)
• BTN must call 3BB
• Required equity = 3 ÷ (4.5+3) = 40%

Conclusion: for the same open size, the BB's call is cheaper (33.3% < 40%). Reason: the SB's 0.5 dead money lowers the call cost, and in HU the opponent's range is wide (usually >60%) so your equity is higher. Facing a full-ring UTG range (about 15%) your equity is lower, the required equity is higher, and marginal hands fold directly. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop odds calculation)

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up, "small cards" aren't junk. 9-high can still win postflop in heads-up — because the opponent's calling range is extremely wide (30%-50% of starting hands), 9-high's showdown value far exceeds full ring. At the same 25% pot odds, 9-high may be ahead 40%+ of the time in heads-up vs only 15%-20% in full ring.
Quick anchors: half-pot bet needs 25% required equity, 1/3 pot 20%, 2/3 pot 28.6%, full pot 33.3%. Limp to see flop 25%, call a 3BB open 33.3%. Memorize these — faster than counting at the table.
t2hu-ev: The EV Framework: Fold / Call / Raise Branches

Every poker decision decomposes into three branches: fold, call, raise. Each branch has an independent EV formula, and the optimal strategy is to choose the branch with the highest EV. Heads-up EV calculation differs in: extremely wide ranges (60%+), high dead-money share (SB's 0.5), and clear positional advantage (BB has postflop information every hand). These factors affect branch EV magnitudes but don't change EV logic itself. (Concept from: The Theory of Poker, David Sklansky Ch.6 expectation-value basics)

The call EV formula:
EV(call) = P(win) × (Pot + CallOpponent) − P(lose) × CallHero

Derivation:
Assume pot = P, opponent bet = B, your call = B.
• If you win: net profit = P + B (win the pot + opponent's bet)
• If you lose: net loss = B (your call)
• Win rate = E, loss rate = 1 − E

Therefore: EV(call) = E×(P+B) − (1−E)×B
            = E(P+B) − B + EB
            = E(P+2B) − B

Break-even: EV(call) = 0 → E(P+2B) = B → E = B ÷ (P+2B), exactly the required-equity formula.

Example: P=4BB, B=2BB, E=30% → EV = 0.3×6 − 0.7×2 = 1.8 − 1.4 = +0.4BB
Positive — calling is correct. (Concept from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.3)

The fold EV is always 0 and serves as the baseline. The bet EV has two parts:
EV(bet) = fold rate × current pot + (1−fold rate) × [win rate × new pot − loss rate × bet]

Simplified model (pure bluff: must lose at showdown):
EV(bluff) = f×P − (1−f)×Bet
Break-even fold rate f*: set EV=0 → f×P = (1−f)×Bet → f(P+Bet) = Bet → f* = Bet ÷ (P+Bet)

Example: P=6BB, Bet=3BB → f* = 3 ÷ 9 = 33.3%. As long as you estimate the opponent folds > 33.3%, the pure bluff is +EV. (Concept from: The Mathematics of Poker, Bill Chen / Jeremie Ankenman Ch.5 expectation-value calculation)

Example: Flop pot 4BB, you (BB) hold a 9-out flush draw and the opponent (SB) bets 2BB. One card to the turn: hit probability = 9/47 ≈ 19.1% (exact single-street). EV(call) = 0.191×6 − 0.809×2 = 1.146 − 1.618 = −0.47BB. Purely mathematically, calling is −EV. But factoring implied odds (win X more after hitting), break-even X = 0.47/0.191 ≈ 2.5BB. If you can average 2.5BB more when you hit, the call turns +EV. That's why draws can chase against opponents with good implied odds — deep stacks willing to pay. (Concept from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.2 expectation-value calculation)

Example 2 (limp vs raise EV): SB holds Q♠J♠, 100BB deep. Option A (limp): BB raises 30% (you fold −0.3BB or call −0.1), BB checks 70% (postflop EV +0.5BB). EV(limp) = 0.7×0.5 − 0.3×0.2 = 0.35 − 0.06 = +0.29BB. Option B (raise to 2.5BB): BB folds 60% (+1.5BB), BB calls 30% (you're OOP, −0.4BB), BB 3Bets 10% (−2.5BB fold, losing the entire raise). EV(raise) = 0.6×1.5 + 0.3×(−0.4) + 0.1×(−2.5) = 0.9 − 0.12 − 0.25 = +0.53BB. Conclusion: raise > limp (0.53 > 0.29), because of the steal EV from SB's dead money (60% fold wins 1.5BB directly) plus the range advantage of raising. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

Quantifying positional value:
Research estimates heads-up positional advantage at about 0.5-1BB/hand. Reasoning:
• BB acts last postflop every hand (information advantage); SB acts first (no position)
• Positional value comes from: a) information (see SB's action before deciding) b) pot control (cheap realization) c) free cards (check to the aggressor)

Quantitative model: the positional gap shows up in per-hand expectation differences. E.g. the same 98s averages +0.75BB/hand in the BB and −0.25BB in the SB, a 1BB difference. Over 100 hands that's about 100BB, but given equity variance itself (±15bb/100), position contributes about 25%-50% of total profit. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position and equity)

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up, "raise" is often permanently superior to "call" even when calling is +EV. Because EV picks the maximum, not just the positive — 0.53BB (raise) > 0.29BB (limp). Remember: your job is to maximize EV, not to find a "no-loss" option.
Review template: for each key decision write three EV estimates: Fold EV = 0; Call EV = E×(P+B) − (1−E)×B; Raise EV = f×P + (1−f)×[...]. Even rough estimates — three lines beat one.
t2hu-risk: Pricing the Risk of the Positional Disadvantage

The key heads-up rule: the SB acts last preflop (preflop position) and the BB acts last preflop too; but postflop the SB acts first (no position) and the BB acts last (position). So the SB is the postflop positional disadvantage (OOP) and the BB is in position (IP). The risk of the disadvantage: information asymmetry (you don't know what BB will do), being forced to make the first decision, and difficulty realizing equity (easily raised out). The value of the advantage: you decide after seeing the opponent's action, realize equity more cheaply, and control pot size. The positional disadvantage requires strategic compensation — that's this chapter's core. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position theory)

Check-raise vs check-call EV comparison:

Setup: pot = 6BB, SB (OOP) bets 3BB, BB (IP) may check-call or check-raise.

Option A (check-call): BB calls 3BB
• If win: profit = pot + opponent bet + your call = 6+3 = 9BB (excluding your 3BB cost; net 6BB)
• If lose: loss = 3BB (the call)
• Win rate = W
• EV(CC) = W×9 − (1−W)×3 = 9W − 3 + 3W = 12W − 3

Option B (check-raise to 9BB): BB raises to 9BB (6BB more than calling)
• If SB folds (probability f): BB wins 6+3 = 9BB
• If SB calls (1−f): BB invests 9BB total; final pot = 6+3+9+6 = 24BB (SB calls 6)
• BB net profit = W×24 − 9
• EV(CR) = f×9 + (1−f)×(24W − 9)

Comparison: CR's advantage is the f×9 leverage term (fold takes the pot immediately); the cost is the 6BB extra exposure when called.
Parameter test: W=35%, f=60% → EV(CC)=12×0.35−3=4.2−3=+1.2BB
                        EV(CR)=0.6×9+0.4×(24×0.35−9)=5.4+0.4×(8.4−9)=5.4−0.24=+5.16BB
When fold rate is high, CR >> CC. (Concept from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.6 semi-bluffs and combo draws)

Example 1: Blinds 0.5/1, effective 100BB. You (BB) hold 7♠6♠; SB opens 2.5BB and you call. Pot 5BB. Flop 8♣5♦2♠ (double-gutshot draw). SB c-bets 2.5BB (half pot).

Option A (call): EV(CC) ≈ double-gutshot 8 outs × 1/47 ≈ 17% × (5+2.5) − 83% × 2.5 ≈ 1.275 − 2.075 = −0.8BB (single-street simplified)

Option B (check-raise to 8BB):
• SB fold rate 55% (HU SB c-bet ranges are wide; fold rate vs a raise is high)
• When called, BB equity 32% (double-gutshot + backdoor flush)
• EV(CR) = 0.55×7.5 + 0.45×(15.5×0.32 − 8) = 4.125 + 0.45×(4.96 − 8) = 4.125 − 1.398 = +2.73BB

Comparison: CR (+2.73) > call (−0.8). Conclusion: the BB uses the fold-rate lever to turn a draw into an immediate profit tool via check-raise. Standard operation for the positional-advantage side. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.4 draw-conflict strategy)

Example 2 (implied-odds shift): In heads-up the opponent's range is wide (60%+ starting hands), which affects implied odds counterintuitively. Full-ring set mining: you call the CO's 3BB open with 55, effective 150BB, SPR≈50. When you hit a set (12%), the opponent's 15% range more often has a strong hand to pay you. But in heads-up he opens 60% (almost anything); when you hit a set he may have air (won't pay) or only a weak pair (you extract 3-5BB). Research suggests raising the HU set-mining threshold to 20-25× the call (higher than full ring's 15-20×) because the wide range means low payment density. (Concept from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

SPR (Stack-to-Pot Ratio) and risk exposure:
SPR = effective stack ÷ pot

Reading:
• SPR < 4: low SPR, top pair rises in value. The flop basically commits all chips; the positional disadvantage matters less (small pot).
• SPR 4-12: medium risk, weigh position vs hand strength. The OOP side tends toward check-call or small bets, avoiding being squeezed by raises.
• SPR > 12: high risk, deep stacks amplify the positional disadvantage. The OOP side must play top pair tighter, and the positional-advantage player can exploit (e.g. float the turn).

Example: 100BB deep, SB raises 2.5BB, BB calls. Pot 5BB, SPR = 97.5/5 ≈ 19.5. Flop K♥9♦3♣, SB (OOP) holds K♠Q♦. No position + high SPR → top pair is risky, easily crushed by better Kx (AK/QK). Correct strategy: small bet or check-back, avoid building a big pot.
Compare short stacks: 15BB deep, same spot, SPR = 12.5/5 = 2.5. Then top pair gets it in directly; the positional disadvantage is neutralized by "low SPR" — you don't worry about later-street control. (Concept from: Harrington on Hold'em Vol.1 Ch.4 SPR theory)

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up the positional-advantage side (BB) often uses check-call rather than check-raise. With position you don't need to risk a raise to compensate — check-call lets the opponent keep bluffing or value betting while you retain the fold option. Position is a low-risk high-reward tool.

Decision flow: 1) call SPR: <4 get it in, 4-12 medium risk, >12 pot control; 2) call position: OOP favors raise to compensate, IP favors check-call for control; 3) assess hand strength: nut draws favor raise, medium hands favor call. These three steps become muscle memory.
t3hu-sb-strategy: The HU SB: The Only Player Who Acts Last Preflop

In full ring the SB is the worst seat: second-to-last preflop, permanently OOP postflop, forced to post a blind with almost no postflop advantage. The HU SB is completely different — you face a single opponent in the BB, act last preflop forever, and your posted 0.5 also acts as an ante: whether or not you eventually participate, that 0.5 has entered the pot as dead money. These two structural facts make the HU SB the position with the most preflop initiative but the most postflop passivity: preflop you decide last after seeing the BB's action; postflop you speak first. Understanding this dual identity is the starting point of all strategies in this chapter. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy; Easy Game, Andrew Seidman Ch.4 position)

The SB's 0.5 in heads-up is a "forced ante": it isn't an avoidable sunk cost but part of the prize pool you and the BB contest. You act last preflop — the treatment the full-ring SB dreams of — at the price of speaking first postflop (the position reversal, detailed in chapter 3).
Opening Size: Min-Raise Is the Main Weapon

The math of an SB min-raise to 2BB (SB already posted 0.5, extra risk 1.5BB; BB posted 1, can fold or complete 1):

Pure blind-steal model: SB extra risk 1.5BB, target prize 1BB (BB's blind)
EV(raise) = f×1 − (1−f)×1.5 (f = BB fold rate)
Break-even: f×1 = (1−f)×1.5 → f = 1.5÷2.5 = 60%
So if the BB folds more than 60%, the SB's min-raise with any two cards is automatically profitable;
equivalently, the BB's minimum defense frequency MDF = 1 − 60% = 40%.

Opening sizes compared (SB extra risk → break-even fold rate):
min-raise 2BB: 1.5BB → 1.5÷2.5 = 60%
2.5BB: 2BB → 2÷3 ≈ 66.7%
3BB: 2.5BB → 2.5÷3.5 ≈ 71.4%

Conclusion: the smaller the size, the lower the automatic-profit bar; in heads-up the BB actually defends 60%-70%+, so the min-raise's pure blind-steal part is near break-even — the real profit is postflop. (Concepts from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.3 blind games; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

Why min-raise dominates HU opening? Three points: (1) low steal bar — 2BB needs only 60% fold rate, while the real HU BB fold rate vs min-raise is only about 30%-40%, so pure blind-stealing barely profits; the open's value is postflop, and the smaller the size the easier postflop pot control; (2) big sizes in heads-up are "self-punishment" — the BB's calling range narrows with size, so spending 3BB only buys a stronger, in-position calling range, and playing a big pot OOP postflop costs far more than in full ring; (3) frequency and balance — min-raise lets you open about 80% of hands, and only a wide enough range covers various flops. The full-ring wisdom "steal blinds with bigger sizes" must be reversed in heads-up: sizing serves postflop, not the steal.

The HU SB limp is an exception to full-ring dogma. In full ring the SB almost never limps, because after a limp, facing a multiway raise loses position, enters passively, and gives up fold equity; but in heads-up three reasons make limping a GTO-reasonable option: (1) odds — completing 0.5 to see a 1.5 pot needs only 25% required equity, and any hand against the BB's wide range is close to or above that line; (2) structure — the BB acts last preflop, so after a limp he can only check or raise (isolate), and you're OOP postflop either way — limping no longer "loses position" extra; (3) range protection — mixing AA/KK into the limp range stops the BB from mindlessly isolating limps. Solvers show the HU SB limps about 20%-30% of the time (adjusting by stack depth and opponent), with min-raise the rest. (Concepts from: Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.3 preflop play and limp mixing; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

Example: HU 100BB deep, you (SB) hold A♠5♠. First tier the hand: strong made hands (JJ+, AK) go into the raise pile for both value and steal; speculative hands (small pairs, suited connectors, A5s-like) mix between the limp and raise piles; junk (K8o, Q6o) folds. A5s's home depends on the BB's 3Bet frequency: at a 15% BB 3Bet, A5s gets 3Bet about 15% of the time and usually must fold — the min-raise EV erodes about 0.15×1.5 ≈ 0.23BB, making the limp pile cheaper; below an 8% 3Bet, A5s's blocker value (fewer AA/AK for the opponent) and postflop nut-draw potential make min-raise the better choice. The same hand's home is decided by the opponent's 3Bet frequency — the first practical taste of "ranges move with the opponent".

Example 2: You (SB) hold 7♥6♥, 100BB deep. Against a calling station (almost never folds postflop): min-raise steal EV = 0.35×1 − 0.65×1.5 ≈ −0.63BB (pure-steal basis), while after a limp 76s has about 43% equity vs the BB's random range, and deep-stacked your made straights/flushes get paid in full — limping into the flop (or even folding marginal hands) is clearly better than raising. Different opponent: BB is a nit (folds about 70%), min-raise steal EV = 0.7×1 − 0.3×1.5 = +0.25BB, and 76s is worth raising too. The same 76s: limp against a station, raise against a nit — the HU SB's sizes and actions aren't fixed but respond directly to the BB's defense frequency.

Counterintuitive point: "limping is weak and always wrong" is full-ring dogma; transplanting it into heads-up bleeds EV continuously. The HU SB limp has GTO backing: dead-money odds of 25%, acting last preflop, and range protection combined. The real error isn't limping itself but "a limp range with no strong hands" — that's what gets mindlessly isolated.

SB opening three-pile quick memory: raise pile (JJ+, AK, A5s-type blockers), limp pile (small/medium pairs, suited connectors, weak suited Ax), fold pile (junk below K8o). Every 50 hands check: does your limp pile have enough strong hands mixed in? Is the BB's 3Bet driving you out of the raise pile? Both answers decide the next round's frequency adjustments.
t3hu-bb-defense: BB: The Most Profitable Seat in Heads-Up

The full-ring BB is a long-term losing seat: acting last preflop is the only comfort, and being permanently OOP postflop makes 85%-92% equity realization the norm. The HU BB is completely different — acting last preflop AND acting last postflop: the SB speaks first, you speak last. Two "act-last" effects stacked make the BB the best-positioned, widest-ranging, and most profitable seat in heads-up. The essence of the position reversal: every hand in heads-up gives one side the double bonus of "preflop information advantage + postflop positional advantage", and the BB is that side. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position and equity; Easy Game, Andrew Seidman Ch.4 position)

BB's defense floor vs an SB 3BB open (MDF):

Perspective 1 (dead-money): SB's total 3BB is the risk, both blinds 1.5BB the prize
SB automatic-profit fold rate f* = 3 ÷ (1.5+3) = 3 ÷ 4.5 ≈ 66.7%
BB minimum defense frequency MDF = 1 − 66.7% ≈ 33.3%

Perspective 2 (raise amount): SB's raise amount 2.5BB, pre-bet pot 1.5BB
MDF = 1 − 2.5 ÷ (1.5+2.5) = 1 − 2.5 ÷ 4 = 37.5%

Both perspectives give the same conclusion: BB's defense floor is about 33%-38% — below this the SB auto-profits opening any two cards. (Concepts from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.3 blind games and MDF; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop odds calculation)

But MDF is only the floor that "stops auto-profit", not the optimal defense frequency. Solvers show the HU BB actually defends about 60%-70% against an SB open (calls ~35%-50% + 3Bets ~15%-25%), far above the 33%-38% floor, for three reasons: (1) postflop position — the BB is IP with equity realization over 100%, so the call EV exceeds the zero assumed by the MDF model; (2) dead money — the SB's 0.5 makes calls cheap: vs a min-raise, calling 1BB contests the SB's invested 2BB (BB view), required equity = 1 ÷ (2+1) ≈ 33.3%; note the call-odds denominator only counts the opponent's dead money, not your own blind — consistent with t2hu's EV(call) = E×(P+B) − (1−E)×B formula (P is the opponent's invested part); (3) the SB's range is wide and weak — the HU SB opens about 80% of hands, so the BB's weak hands naturally have decent equity against a wide range. MDF answers "how little must I defend"; position and dead money answer "how much more can I defend" — the HU BB's 60%+ is the sum of the two.

The HU BB's "60%+ defense" is defense with position: you act last preflop and last postflop, so calling with marginal hands costs far less than in full ring. Transplanting the full-ring intuition "BB must play tight" into heads-up is throwing away positional advantage.
Call vs 3Bet: The Two Legs of Defense

Against an SB open, the BB's defense range splits into two piles. The call pile: small/medium pairs (22-TT), suited connectors (65s+), weak suited Aces (A2s-A9s), weak suited Kings (K6s-K9s) — these realize equity through position and implied odds, winning without showdown. The 3Bet pile has two layers: value (JJ+, AK — clearly ahead of the SB's wide range, and also compress the SB's steal frequency) and bluff (blocker-bearing combos like A5s, A4s, K8s — blocking AA/KK/AK, making the SB harder to 4Bet). Facing a 3Bet the SB either 4Bets or folds, so the bluff layer must pick hands that "can fold cleanly to a 4Bet". The Gap Concept corrected for the HU BB: full ring requires stronger hands to call a raise (the gap), but the HU BB has already posted 1BB dead money and has postflop position, so he can push well past the gap — this is the source of the 60%+ BB defense vs the 25%-50% full-ring BB defense. (Concepts from: The Theory of Poker, David Sklansky Ch.2-3 Gap Concept; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

Example: HU 100BB deep, SB min-raises to 2BB, you (BB) hold K♠7♠. K7s is a typical marginal hand in solver BB calling ranges: calling 1BB contests the SB's invested 2BB (BB view), required equity = 1 ÷ (2+1) ≈ 33.3%; K7s vs the SB's ~80% open range wins about 48% — about 15 points of surplus. Postflop you're IP: a K flop lets you bet thin value, flush/straight draws chase cheaply, and a complete miss can fold. Folding gives up 48% equity at 33% odds — the most typical HU BB error: importing the full-ring memory "K7s is a bad hand". Facing a full-ring UTG open K7s is indeed a fold, but vs the HU SB's 80% range it's a +EV call.

Example 2 (isolate): SB limps (completes 0.5), you (BB) hold A♠8♠, 100BB deep, and the SB folds to a raise about 55%. Isolate-raise to 4BB: EV ≈ 0.55×1.5 (win dead money on a fold) + 0.45×(+0.5) (IP positional advantage about +0.5BB when called) ≈ +1.05BB; while checking is only about +0.7BB (small pot, letting the SB realize a weak range for free). Isolating earns about 0.8BB more than checking. But note: isolating isn't blind-stealing — the SB's limp already exposed a weak range, and your raise is "punishing the weak range + seizing initiative"; when called, A8s's showdown value leaves you comfortable postflop. The higher the opponent's limp-fold frequency, the higher your isolate frequency should be.

Counterintuitive point: BB defending 60%+ isn't "calling station". A real station has no 3Bet pile and no isolating raises — while the HU BB's 60% consists of calls, 3Bet value, and 3Bet bluffs, each moving with the SB's tendencies. Defense width and defense passivity are two different things.

BB defense three-step quick check: (1) call the pot odds — calling line ≈33% vs a 2BB open, 33% vs 3BB; (2) split piles — in-position call pile, strong-made 3Bet value, blocker-bluff 3Bet; (3) watch the SB — raise 3Bet frequency vs an over-folder, raise isolate frequency vs a big limper, narrow the call pile vs a frequent 3Better. After three steps, 60% defense is structured choice rather than "reluctant to fold".
t3hu-position-reversal: Position Reversal: The Unique Identity Swap in Heads-Up

Full-ring position is "assigned": the BTN acts last every hand, the SB/BB are OOP every hand, and positional attributes never change. Heads-up position "reverses": the SB acts last preflop (has preflop position) and first postflop (no postflop position); the BB is the opposite — second preflop, last postflop. Every hand, the one who got the preflop advantage pays it back postflop, and the one passive preflop collects rent postflop. This reversal is heads-up's most overlooked structural fact: full-ring players new to HU often play postflop with the full-ring mentality "I'm the aggressor, I have initiative", and get repeatedly harvested by the BB's positional advantage. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position theory; Easy Game, Andrew Seidman Ch.4 position)

The cruel face of the reversal: the SB's last action preflop can't buy postflop position. Preflop you're the aggressor; postflop you're OOP — "initiative" belongs to you only until the flop; once the flop comes, every BB decision lags yours by one step.

Street-by-street positional-value model (limp pot starting 2BB, half-pot bet + call each street):

Pot sequence: flop 2BB → turn 4BB → river 8BB
Per-street bet: flop 1BB → turn 2BB → river 4BB

Assume position gives a "5% decision advantage per street" (information + pot control folded in):
Flop contribution: 1BB × 5% = 0.05BB
Turn contribution: 2BB × 5% = 0.10BB
River contribution: 4BB × 5% = 0.20BB
Total positional value ≈ 0.35BB/hand, with the river at 0.20 ÷ 0.35 ≈ 57%

Conclusion: more than half of positional value is realized on the river — "river position matters most" isn't a slogan but the mathematical necessity of geometric pot growth. Note: T2's 0.5-1BB/hand positional value estimates the total including preflop positional advantage; this section's 0.35BB quantifies only the postflop part under conservative assumptions, a component of the former. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position and equity; Harrington on Hold'em, Dan Harrington Vol.1 Ch.5 position and equity)

Why is river positional value greatest? Three mechanisms: (1) biggest pot — the same 5% decision advantage operates on an 8BB pot, 4× the chip magnitude of the flop; (2) narrowest range, most complete information — after two rounds of flop/turn filtering both ranges have narrowed greatly, and the last actor makes the final ruling on the most precise read; (3) irreversible decision — the river is the last street: IP can "bet, fold to a raise", while OOP suffers the dilemma of "checked and stolen from, or bet and raised". The full-ring BTN enjoys these three too, but the HU BB is the BTN every hand — the quantitative explanation for the HU BB's high profitability.

Example: HU 100BB deep, SB min-raises to 2BB with A♠Q♠, BB calls, pot 4BB. Flop K♥8♦3♣. The first frame of the reversal: you were the preflop aggressor but now act first OOP. BB bets 2BB (half pot, pot to 6BB); you call, pot 8BB, you've invested 2BB, required equity 25%. Your AQ equity: Kx density in the BB's calling range about 30%; without a K, AQ has about 27% via 6 overcard outs plus a backdoor flush; with a K only about 6% — weighted ≈ 0.7×27% + 0.3×6% ≈ 21%, below the 25% call line, so the standard answer is check-fold. The same A♠Q♠ from the BB's view (IP): you can bet half pot to take the pot or check for a free turn; AQ goes from "a fold at the call-line edge" to "a vehicle of initiative". The reversal makes the same hand worth nearly a full pot difference between the two seats.

OOP compensates for the reversal with three tools: (1) check as the default — the OOP default is handing the decision to IP, hiding hand strength with the "checking range", and if BB checks you see a free card; (2) check-raise (x/r) — about 10%-15% of OOP decisions choose x/r, with a range of nuts/very strong hands + suitable bluffs (strong draws, blockers), whose purpose is suppressing IP's betting frequency and protecting the check-call range from exploitation; (3) donk bet — OOP leads out, rare in solvers (about 2%-5% of board structures), because the donk range is naturally strong, can't balance when raised, and gives up the x/r lever; exceptions occur on specific boards where OOP's range dominates (e.g. after an SB limp on 6♠5♦4♣ with high two-pair/straight density), where donking to protect equity is actually optimal. Remember: donk is the exception, not the norm — full-ring beginners love to donk to "protect their hand", and in heads-up it's a free advertisement of range imbalance. (Concepts from: Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.4 postflop play and OOP structure; Harrington on Hold'em, Dan Harrington Vol.1 Ch.5 position and equity)

Example 2 (river positional value): HU blinds 0.5/1, preflop SB min-raises 2BB, BB calls, pot 4BB. Flop Q♠8♦3♣, BB bets 2BB, SB calls, pot 8BB. Turn 2♥, BB bets 4BB, SB calls, pot 16BB. River 9♠, both hold K♠Q♠ (top pair Q + K kicker). Scenario A — you're in the BB (IP): SB checks, you bet about 5BB (1/3 pot) for thin value, and can safely fold to a raise (88/33/99 in the SB's range all raise reasonably), netting about 5BB; Scenario B — you're in the SB (OOP): you check, BB bets 8BB, and your top pair degrades into a "call to catch bluffs or fold" choice; if you lead 8BB, top pair Q is hard to fold when raised in a 100BB-deep game. Same hand, same betting line — IP realizes 5BB of thin value while OOP can only respond passively. The river's 57% positional-value share becomes real money here.

Counterintuitive point: the preflop aggressor often must cede initiative postflop. The SB's continuation-bet frequency is far below the full-ring BTN — because an OOP c-bet is extremely expensive against IP floats and raises, and the SB's range gets "diluted" postflop by the BB's wide defense range. The right use of initiative is as "narrative rights", not "the right to bet": an OOP check isn't weakness but kicking the ball to IP and deciding whether to accept.

OOP decision-flow four questions: how big is the pot (does SPR call for pot control)? How often will IP bet after my check (decides check-call vs x/r)? Do I have nuts in my range (decides x/r frequency)? Does my range dominate this board (decides whether to donk)? After four questions, the reversed position goes from passive suffering to structured game.
t4hu-range-width: Why Heads-Up Ranges Are So Wide

Range width is the share of starting hands a position is willing to play. Full ring: UTG ~15%, BTN ~40%; heads-up: the SB opens about 80% and the BB defends about 60%+. Two structural facts stack up: first, you only have to beat one opponent, and any two cards keep about 35% equity against a random range (an anchor established in T1); second, the position reversal makes the BB act last postflop and the SB's 0.5 dead money makes calls extremely cheap. Range width isn't a style choice — it's the mathematical necessity of heads-up's rule structure.

In heads-up "wide" isn't an error but the default. The full-ring dogma "wait for good hands preflop" bleeds money slowly in heads-up — because every fold hands the opponent 0.5-1BB of dead money. Range width is heads-up's first discipline.
SB Opening Width: Where the ~80% Comes From

The SB opening range contains all hands with "at least 40% equity vs the BB's random range", plus marginal hands realized by postflop positional advantage:

Openable hands (about 80%):
Strong hands (JJ+/AK/AQ) + suited connectors + suited Ax + any pair + most suited hands and some offsuit high cards

Folds (about 20%):
Complete junk (72o, 83o, etc.) and offsuit weak hands with poor blocker value

The SB completes 0.5 to see a 1.5BB pot (25% required equity), and any hand against the BB's wide defense range is near or above that line; even when 3Bet, the SB's fold loses only the 1.5BB raise — low-frequency high-risk 3Bet encounters are covered by the high-frequency profit of a wide range. (Concept from: Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.3 heads-up range narrowing and widening)

The BB's ~60%+ defense math is just as clear: vs an SB min-raise to 2BB, the BB calls 1BB to contest the SB's 2BB, required equity = 1÷(2+1) ≈ 33.3%; and the BB is the postflop positional-advantage side (IP) with equity realization over 100% — at the same 33% pot odds the HU BB's call is more favorable than full ring. That's why the HU BB can defend above the MDF floor (about 33%-38%) and still profit.

Example: HU 100BB deep, you (SB) hold K♦6♦. By full-ring standards this is a clear fold, but in heads-up: against the BB's ~60% defense range K6s has about 46%-48% preflop equity, plus postflop pot-control ability from the position reversal — K6s is a standard member of the solver's SB opening range. If you fold because "K6s isn't good enough", you're letting the opponent win blinds with junk for free.

Example 2 (ranges move with the opponent): The same J♠8♠ — against a BB who 3Bets at a high 25%, after a 3Bet J8s usually only folds and the min-raise steal EV erodes, so consider narrowing the open; against a passive BB 3Betting only 8%, J8s's postflop flush/straight potential realizes fully and it's worth opening. Range width is never a fixed number but a direct response to the opponent's aggression frequency.

Example 3 (the key to postflop realization): You (BB) call the SB's min-raise with 6♠5♠. Flop K♠8♦4♣, SB bets 1/3 pot; your 65s has only a gutshot (2 sevens) + backdoor flush, about 20% equity, below the 25% call line — standard fold. But on a 7♠6♦4♣ flop you have a pair with a straight draw, equity jumping to about 55%, warranting a call or even a check-raise. Wide ranges matter not as "call anything" but as "giving you enough hands to win on the right boards".

Counterintuitive point: a wide range isn't loose play. HU pros enter with 80% but quickly give up about half postflop — they "participate a lot, invest little", extracting value via postflop position and board fit. The real error is "wide range but reluctant to fold on every street" — that's a calling station.

HU range quick reference: SB opens about 80% (top 15% strong + mid suited connectors/Ax + bottom junk mixed), BB defends about 60% (call pile ~35%-45% + 3Bet pile ~15%-25%). Every 50 hands check: is your fold rate being targeted by the opponent's steal profit? Is your 3Bet frequency too low, letting the SB open forever? Both answers decide the next round's width.
t4hu-polarization: Polarized vs Linear: Two Betting-Range Philosophies

A polarized range contains only strong hands and weak hands, giving the middle to checking; a linear range enters betting continuously from strong to weak. In heads-up, postflop betting ranges are generally polarized: because the opponent's range is wide and his calling frequency high, you need nuts to extract value and junk to apply pressure, while middle hands (medium pairs, weak top pairs) are more easily raised and suit check-control.
