HU betting is a "two-world" game: the betting range consists of nut value + bluffs (including semi-bluffs), with middle hands given to checking. This leaves the opponent torn — calling wins bluffs, folding loses value, and neither end is easy to handle.
The Math of the Value:Bluff Ratio

Equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a river full-pot bet (pot P, bet P, opponent has a bluff catcher):

Opponent call EV = f×2P − (1−f)×P (f = bluff share)
Break-even: set = 0 → 2fP = (1−f)P → 3f = 1 → f = 1/3

So value:bluff = 2:1: about 2/3 value and 1/3 bluffs in a full-pot range.

Half pot (0.5P): opponent call EV = f×1.5P − (1−f)×0.5P = 0 → f = 0.25, value:bluff = 3:1. (Concept from: Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.2-3 polarized betting and frequencies)

Turn and flop polarization differ slightly: because later streets remain, bluff share can be higher — some bluffs (draws) may later complete into value or keep bluffing. In heads-up the opponent's range is wide and his calling frequency high, so the flop can aggressively polarize-bet the whole range; but by the turn and river the pot is bigger and the opponent's range narrower, so polarized sizing and frequency should adjust accordingly.

Example: HU 100BB deep, SB min-raises, BB calls, flop K♠9♦4♣. SB holds A♦A♣ (overpair, value) and A♦5♦ (air + backdoor flush, bluff). SB bets half pot 1BB (pot 2BB), value:bluff about 2:1 — AA bets value and A5s represents a flush draw for pressure. If the SB checked A5s, his betting range would be only AA, and the opponent would quickly identify it and fold every marginal hand — the polarization structure breaks.

Example 2 (correct handling of middle hands): On the same board the SB holds K♦Q♦ (top pair weak kicker). KQ shouldn't be in the HU betting range: it can't beat AK/AA but loses to any bigger K kicker; betting and being raised leaves it torn. The correct play is checking for pot control and bluff-catching. The value of a polarized range is precisely "sparing middle hands like KQ from awkward decisions".

Example 3 (draw converts to bluff): Flop 8♠6♣2♦, SB bets with 7♦5♦ (open-ended straight draw), BB calls. Turn A♠, 75s misses the straight. Now 75s converts from a "draw" to a "pure bluff": the A is a great bluff card (blocks the opponent's AA and compresses his top-pair range), so the SB double-barrels representing an A, and if BB folds the SB takes the pot directly. A draw converting to a bluff is the dynamic core of the HU polarized range.

Counterintuitive point: middle hands (medium pairs, weak top pairs) aren't "valueless" but "most valuable when checked". Forcing them into the betting range hands the opponent a chance to raise and extract from you. Polarization isn't "bet everything strong and weak" but "bet value + pressure with the extremes and check the middle".

Building a betting range in three steps: (1) list nut value hands (overpairs, two pair, straights, etc.); (2) list bluff hands (strong draws first, converting to pure bluffs when they miss the turn); (3) put all middle hands into the checking range. Your betting range is then naturally polarized, with no deliberate balancing needed.
t4hu-blocking: Blockers: Your Hole Cards Are Range Information

A blocker is a card you hold that reduces the count of specific opponent combos. Holding A♠ zeroes the opponent's A♠X♠ nut-flush combos; holding a K drops his KK from 6 to 3 combos. In full ring, blockers are an advanced technique; in heads-up, where both ranges are wide and decisions are dense, blockers become a standard tool on every hand — your two cards are both a filter for the opponent's range and a regulator of your own attacking and defending frequencies.

Blockers don't change hand strength; they change probability distributions. The same "air hand" bluffs more successfully holding A♠ than 2♠ — because you block the opponent's strongest calling hand (the nut flush).

First: blocking bluffs — if your cards are strong hands in the opponent's range, your bluff's credibility rises because the nuts he "claims" are falsified. Second: value unblocking — if your cards don't block the opponent's bluff catchers, your value bets get paid more easily (e.g. not holding A♠ means he's more likely to have a flush and call you). Third: preflop combo math — choosing blocker-bearing bluffs for the 3Bet range (e.g. A5s blocking AA/AK) while keeping clean folds to a 4Bet.

Example: Three-spade board K♠9♠4♠, you hold A♦A♣ (no spade A, can't make the nut flush). The opponent shoves. Your blocker situation: you block no flushes, so he may have the A♠X♠ nut flush or a smaller flush. AA without A♠ is the typical "unblocking value" case — his calling range skews strong and your bluff-catching value drops; lean fold.

Example 2 (bluff blocking): Same K♠9♠4♠ board, you hold A♠5♦ (lone A♠, no flush). You block every A♠X♠ nut-flush combo — the opponent's "strongest hand" is half-falsified. Your raise-bluff (representing a flush) now succeeds significantly more often, because his bluff-catching range contains far fewer strong hands. A blocker turns the same "air" into a differently-strength bluff.

Example 3 (preflop 3Bet selection): In heads-up you (BB) face an SB open and consider a 3Bet bluff. The difference between A♦5♦ and 7♦6♦: A5s blocks parts of AA and AK (fewer top-tier hands in his range, lower 4Bet probability) and can fold cleanly to a 4Bet; 76s blocks no strong hands and runs into QQ+ more often when 4Bet. So A5s is the better 3Bet-bluff card. Blockers turn "bluff combos" from a vague count into precise selection.

Quantitative blocker effect (you hold A♦A♣ on a three-spade board):

Opponent's nut-flush A♠X♠ combos:
No blocker: A♠ with any of the remaining 12 spades = 12
You hold A♦ (doesn't block spades): still about 12
You hold A♠ (blocking): A♠ is in your hand, nut-flush combos = 0

Comparison: holding A♠ cuts the opponent's "strongest calling hand" from 12 combos to 0 — the mathematical source of bluff success. (Concept from: The Mathematics of Poker, Bill Chen / Jeremie Ankenman Ch.10 blockers and combo counting)

Counterintuitive point: blockers are a marginal effect, not a master key. Holding A♠ raises bluff success but doesn't guarantee it; using it to overturn base range analysis is abuse. Blockers' value in heads-up is the "marginal EV of edge spots" — icing when the base range is right, and unable to save you when it's wrong.

Off-table drill: set up random three-suited boards and count the difference in "opponent nut-flush combos" with and without your A♠. Once fluent, you need only 10 seconds in play: does my hand block the opponent's value or his bluffs? Blocking value → bluff more; not blocking → call cautiously.
t5hu-gto-he: Heads-up poker (ignoring rake) is a textbook two-player zero-sum game: one side's profit is exactly the other's loss. John Nash proved such games have equilibrium strategy profiles — when both sides play their equilibrium, neither can improve by deviating unilaterally. This means heads-up has a set of "unexploitable" strategies (GTO): no matter how the opponent plays, your long-term expectation is never below the game value. This is a theoretical advantage unique to heads-up; multiway equilibrium guarantees weaken under coalition effects.

GTO's positioning is a "bulletproof vest" not a "weapon": it guarantees you're not exploited but doesn't promise maximum profit. Against a leaky opponent, targeted exploitation earns more — at the cost of opening your own leaks. HU pros switch between "wearing the vest" and "switching to the knife".

The minimax theorem (von Neumann 1928):
there exists a game value v such that max_a min_b U₁(a,b) = min_b max_a U₁(a,b) = v

Meaning: an equilibrium strategy guarantees your expectation ≥ v and the opponent can't push it lower unilaterally.

Rock-paper-scissors equilibrium: randomize each 1/3. If the opponent always throws rock, the equilibrium still breaks even (expectation 0), but the exploitative "always paper" wins every round; however, once you always throw paper you become exploitable too (he switches to scissors). Poker is exactly isomorphic. (Concept from: The Mathematics of Poker, Bill Chen / Jeremie Ankenman Ch.2 basic game theory)

The difference between HU GTO and full-ring GTO: heads-up ranges are extremely wide (SB opens 80%, BB defends 60%+), so the equilibrium means very high betting frequency and bluff density; in full-ring equilibrium most players can only play tight. Solvers output lots of "aggressive bets" and "polarized ranges" in heads-up — GTO isn't "playing tight" but "keeping everything at ratios the opponent can't counter".

Example: In a HU SB vs BB solver, the SB opens about 80%, the BB defends about 60%+, the OOP SB checks at high frequency postflop, and the IP BB bets at high frequency. These frequencies look "loose", but they're all part of equilibrium — any deviation by one side (e.g. the SB opening only 50%) lets the other side exploit it by widening defense or raising steal frequency.

Example 2 (minimum necessary deviation): You observe a HU opponent who calls big river bets only 25% (equilibrium ~50%). Based on this you can raise your river overbet-bluff frequency overall — but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 40%". That's "using GTO as the baseline and making directed, disciplined deviations from observable biases", not blind escalation.

Example 3 (HU GTO's aggressiveness): In solvers, the HU BB facing an SB open check-raises on many boards — pressuring with a polarized range of draws and strong hands. This stems from IP positional advantage and a wide range. If you only call against an aggressive BB and never raise, your defense frequency is high but harmless — the opponent can keep raising his C-Bet frequency to exploit you.

Counterintuitive point: "GTO is playing tight" is the biggest misreading. HU GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbet shoves, and thin value — it just keeps all of it at ratios the opponent can't counter. When studying solvers, don't memorize frequencies — ask three whys: why this sizing on this board? Why is this hand in the betting range? Why did the frequency change on the turn?

HU learning path: first use a solver to understand the equilibrium "shape" (why play this way), then use node locking to study "harvest schemes for common opponent leaks", finally validate live. The baseline gives you invincibility; deviations give you profit — exploitation without GTO is running naked, and GTO without deviation is self-shackling.
t5hu-frequency: An equilibrium strategy isn't "this hand always plays this way" but "this hand allocates actions at some frequency at a specific node". In heads-up, with wide ranges and dense decisions, frequency balance is critical: if your C-Bet frequency is constant and your 3Bet range predictable, observant opponents will node-lock your patterns and counter you. Mixed Strategy and the Indifference Principle together form the mathematical foundation of frequency balance.

Indifference Principle: in equilibrium a hand is mixed only when all its actions have exactly equal EV. The purpose of mixing isn't "confusion" but making the opponent's marginal hands (like bluff catchers) exactly indifferent between calling and folding — nothing for him to counter.

MDF (Minimum Defense Frequency) = 1 − fold rate = 1/(1+b) (b = bet/pot)

Example: half pot b=0.5 → defend 67%; full pot b=1 → defend 50%; 2× pot b=2 → defend 33%

Alpha (bluff break-even fold rate) = b/(1+b) = 1 − MDF

HU half-pot bet: the opponent must defend 67%, and your pure bluff needs him to fold ≥33% to break even. (Concept from: The Mathematics of Poker, Bill Chen / Jeremie Ankenman Ch.5-6 bet-fold subgame)

In heads-up, defense isn't only calling: raises also count toward defense frequency. Against high-frequency bluffers, substitute some calls with raises to both defend and collect value; against tight-passive value bettors, over-folding (below MDF) is the exploitation. First compute the total, then allocate — the HU BB's 60%+ defense consists of calls, 3Bet value, and 3Bet bluffs, each moving with the SB's tendencies.

Example: HU flop pot 2BB, SB (OOP) bets half pot 1BB with a strong+bluff mixed range. You're the BB (IP) and need to continue with about 67%. Rank the continuing hands by strength + improvement potential: top pairs and good draws first, pure junk into the folding 33%. If you only defend 40%, the SB's every bluff profits 0.60×2 − 0.40×1 = 0.8BB on average — you're feeding the opponent automatic profit.

Example 2 (mixed execution): On the river you hold a bluff catcher facing a full-pot bet; in equilibrium the opponent bluffs 1/3 and your required equity is exactly 33% — call and fold have equal EV. Solvers may output "call 50% / fold 50%". Practical meaning: the single-decision cost of getting these wrong is about zero, so don't agonize; the real EV differences live in range construction on earlier streets.

Example 3 (frequency exploitation in HU): You observe a HU opponent who folds to C-Bets 60% on the flop (equilibrium ~45%). This is a clear MDF leak — your flop C-Bet frequency and bluff density can be raised overall because he over-folds. But cap it at "I still don't lose if he tightens to 50%", keeping correction room. Frequency balance isn't only defense — it's also a microscope for identifying and harvesting opponent imbalance.

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up, "should I mix" isn't a philosophical question but a mathematical one. Both sides of a mixed node have equal EV, so a single wrong choice costs ≈0; pure-strategy nodes (with a unique clearly-best action) contribute most of the EV. Investing effort in high-EV-difference decisions beats obsessing over the precise execution of a 50% mix.

Memorize the three frequency anchors: defend 67% vs half-pot, 50% vs full-pot, 33% vs 2× pot; bluff 25% on a half-pot bet, 33% on full-pot. In review, track your actual fold rate against big turn/river bets — most players fold far above equilibrium, which is why the opponent's big bets always seem to "just happen" to make you fold.
t6hu-sizing-optimal: Sizing: The First Knob of Betting Engineering

Bet sizing is one of the most important postflop decisions in heads-up. It simultaneously conveys three signals: hand strength (big value vs bluff), range structure (polarized vs linear), and pot-control intent (small keeps the opponent, big contests the pot). The core logic of HU sizing is "small bets control, big bets polarize" — similar to full ring but more extreme: because the opponent's range is wide and decisions dense, both the pot-control value of small bets and the polarization value of overbets are amplified.

Sizing doesn't decide whether you "have value" but "how you realize value". A straight-flush nuts can overbet-shove to drain the opponent, while top pair weak kicker can only thin-value bet 1/3 pot — choosing the wrong size means choosing the wrong realization method.
How the Value:Bluff Ratio Changes With Size

Bet-size value:bluff ratio (pot P, bet bP):

Bluff share f = b/(1+2b)

Examples:
1/3 pot b≈0.33 → f = 0.33/1.66 ≈ 20% (value:bluff = 4:1)
Half pot b=0.5 → f = 0.25 (3:1)
Full pot b=1 → f = 1/3 (2:1)
2× pot b=2 → f = 0.4 (3:2)

Conclusion: the bigger the size, the more bluffs it can carry — the mathematical root of "big bet = polarization". (Concept from: Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.2-3 GTO betting structure)

Practical HU sizing preferences: dry high boards use high-frequency 1/3-pot small bets (the opponent's wide range rarely hits; a small bet makes him fold or prices marginal hands); wet connected boards use 2/3+ pot bets or overbets (protect equity, polarize). And the HU flop usually leans small (1/3 pot) — because the pot is small, the opponent wide, and your range-advantage large, so a small bet already realizes thin value and steals pots.

Example: HU flop K♠7♦2♣ (dry), SB min-raises, BB calls, pot 2BB. SB holds A♠K♣ (top pair top kicker). The board is dry and the BB's range rarely has a K, so the SB bets small at 1/3 pot (about 0.7BB): the top-pair K's thin value gets weak hands in the wide range to pay, while not giving the BB's junk a free card. With a full-pot bet the BB only continues with stronger Ks or sets, wasting the K's thin value.

Example 2 (SPR-planned all-in): HU 100BB deep, preflop SB raises 2.5BB, BB calls, pot 5BB, SPR = 97.5/5 ≈ 19.5. Flop 9♠8♥4♣, SB holds 6♠5♠ (straight draw). At high SPR the SB bets big (about 2/3 pot, 3.3BB) to build the pot — paving the way for a turn/river all-in: pot 11.6BB → turn bet 7.7BB → pot 27BB → river shove the remaining 86BB, chips go in naturally. With a 1/3-pot flop bet the pot grows too slowly and the deep stack can't complete an all-in on the river.

Example 3 (small-bet pot control): Same 9♠8♥4♣ board, the SB holds J♣T♣ (top pair + straight draw, but easily outdrawn). Medium strength doesn't seek to play for all the chips; the SB bets small at 1/3 pot to control pot size, avoiding getting raised by the BB's strong hands into a big pot. A small bet is both "making weak hands pay" and "controlling risk exposure".

Counterintuitive point: in heads-up a small bet isn't "weakness" but "precision" — high-frequency 1/3-pot small bets on dry boards are GTO normal because they maximize the thin-value/steal ratio. The full-ring intuition "bets must be big to threaten" becomes wastefulness against wide HU ranges.

Sizing quick check: (1) call SPR — low SPR plays for stacks, high SPR needs multi-street planning; (2) read the board — dry high boards small bets at high frequency, wet low boards big bets for protection; (3) grade the hand — nuts overbet, top pair small, draws medium. Three steps and your sizing has structure, not feel.
t6hu-barrel: Multi-Street Betting: One Decision, Three Streets to Reel In

HU postflop isn't just "bet or not on this street" but "how this hand gets reeled in across three streets". After a flop bet, whether the turn/river keep barreling or check depends on: your hand-strength tier, how the opponent's range narrows each street, and how the pot grows geometrically each street. A well-designed betting line lets strong hands extract the whole way and bluffs reel in at the right moment.

The golden rule of multi-street betting: value hands can fire three barrels, semi-bluffs close on the turn, pure bluffs close on the river. But re-evaluate every street — when the turn/river completes the opponent's draw (the board changes hands), your firing frequency must drop accordingly.
The Mathematical Structure of the Triple Barrel

HU flop betting-line pot geometry (starting pot P):

Triple-barrel plan (2/3 pot each street):
flop 2/3P → turn 2/3 × new pot → river 2/3 × new pot

With P=5BB:
flop bet 3.3BB, pot → 11.6BB
turn bet 7.7BB, pot → 27BB
river bet 18BB, pot → 63BB

To shove 97.5BB on the river, the pot must grow geometrically at about 2/3 pot from the flop — a 1/3-pot small bet can't do it. (Concept from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.9 street-by-street pot management and sizing)

But a triple barrel isn't mindless betting every street. The three-street firing combination depends on board evolution: dry high boards (like K♠7♦2♣→5♥→9♣) where the opponent's range rarely hits allow high-frequency triple barrels representing strength; wet connected boards (like 9♠8♥4♣→7♦→6♣) easily complete straights/flushes, so beware the turn/river board change and cut firing frequency sharply.

Example: HU flop K♠7♦2♣, SB bets 1/3 pot with A♠A♣, BB calls (pot 8BB). Turn 5♥ blank, AA still ahead, SB bets half pot 4BB, BB calls (pot 16BB). River 9♣ blank, SB bets 2/3 pot about 10.7BB for value. AA fires all three streets — because the board stays dry, AA's lead holds completely and value is maximized.

Example 2 (board change): Same SB with A♠A♣ bets the 9♠8♥4♣ flop, BB calls. Turn 7♦ — completes QT, T6, and 65 straights. AA's lead weakens: the BB's wide defense range contains plenty of straight combos. The SB should lower turn betting frequency (mixing checks) because continuing only gets called or raised by stronger hands. AA goes from "three streets of value" to "two streets of value + one street of control".

Example 3 (semi-bluff closes on the turn): Flop 8♠6♣2♦, SB bets 1/3 pot with 7♦5♦ (open-ended straight), BB calls. Turn A♠ (blocker + board dries). 75s missed the straight. The turn continues with a half-pot bet representing an A — if BB folds, the SB closes on the turn with a "near-nut draw". This is the standard semi-bluff path: bet a draw on the flop, convert to a pure bluff on a favorable turn and take the pot.

Counterintuitive point: the turn/river "board change" matters more than your hand strength. AA is three streets of value on a dry board and two on a wet board — not because AA got weaker, but because the combos in the opponent's range that beat it multiplied. Firing frequency must follow "how the opponent's range is improved by new cards", not your own hand.

Betting-line planning three questions: (1) whose draw does this board improve? (2) how many more streets can the pot sustain? (SPR and the all-in plan) (3) after a call, what's left in the opponent's range? After three questions, your triple barrel goes from "habit" to "plan".
t7hu-patterns: Heads-Up Is the Battlefield of Reading People

Heads-up faces one opponent, so reading people is amplified enormously — you don't juggle multiple table images, just this one player. HU player tendencies usually classify into a few types: Calling Station (almost never folds postflop), nit/tight-passive (very narrow range, folds too much), Maniac (aggressive and loose), TAG (balanced but predictable). After identifying the type, your exploitation strategy has direction.

Reading people isn't guessing hands — it's estimating ranges. "Calls too much" means his range skews wide and weak; "folds too much" means his range is very narrow and stealable. Inferring ranges from frequencies is the core of pattern recognition.
From Frequency to Range: Four Key Dimensions

Watch four frequencies of a HU opponent: (1) preflop open rate — how wide he plays; (2) fold rate vs C-Bets — whether he over-folds; (3) 3Bet rate — his aggression; (4) showdown tendency — calling station or controlled. Cross these four frequencies and you get a fairly complete portrait. Sample at least 50-100 hands; single-hand impressions don't count.

Example: A HU opponent opens 85% preflop (wide) but folds to C-Bets 60% (over-folds). Portrait: wide open + many folds = "wide range + weak defense". Exploitation direction: postflop as IP you should C-Bet at high frequency to steal, because his fold rate is high; and his wide open means your BB defense can also widen. Harvest two leaks at once.

Example 2 (calling station): The opponent almost never folds postflop (fold rate <25%) but opens moderately. Portrait: calling station. Exploitation: don't use pure bluffs (he doesn't fold); switch to value-bet thin value — top pair weak kicker can also bet for money because he calls with worse. Meanwhile reduce bluff frequency, converting bluffs to semi-bluffs or checks.

Example 3 (nit): The opponent opens only 30% and folds too much to raises. Portrait: nit. Exploitation: raise steal and raise frequency (his fold rate is automatic profit); but beware his occasional strong-hand re-raise — when a nit enters a pot he's usually strong.

Counterintuitive point: don't reclassify an opponent because he "once" showed the nuts. Heads-up is high-frequency; a single all-in win/loss is noise; only 50-100 hand frequency statistics form an exploitable signal. Concluding from a single-hand impression is exploitation's biggest enemy.

Build an opponent notebook: every 20 hands record the four frequencies (open rate / fold rate / 3Bet rate / showdown tendency). Among HU pros, "note-taking while playing" is the discipline that turns short-term impressions into long-term advantage.
t7hu-exploit: Exploitation Isn't Abandoning GTO — It's Calibrating It

Exploitative strategy profits from the opponent's deviations from equilibrium. But HU pros don't "abandon" GTO; they "calibrate" it: using equilibrium frequencies as the baseline and making minimum necessary deviations against the opponent's clear deviations. The key discipline — every deviation opens your own leaks, so the magnitude must be controlled and you must return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

The right posture of exploitation: aim the direction at the opponent's leak (Maximally Exploitative), keep the magnitude minimal (Minimally Exploitative). The goal of deviating is "earn enough before he corrects", not "turn yourself into a leak too".
Node Locking: Turning Exploitation Into Calculation

Node locking is an advanced solver feature: lock the opponent's strategy at a node to the real tendency you observed (e.g. "this opponent never bluffs the river" or "folds to C-Bets 60%"), then re-solve your optimal response. The output is the maximally exploitative strategy against that leak. This turns exploitation from "feel" into "calculation".

Raising steals against an over-folding opponent (SB min-raise to 2BB, BB fold rate f):

EV(steal) = f×1.5 − (1−f)×1.5

Equilibrium fold rate about 40% (f=0.4) → EV = 0.4×1.5 − 0.6×1.5 = −0.3BB (unprofitable, needs postflop recovery)

If the opponent folds 60% (f=0.6) → EV = 0.6×1.5 − 0.4×1.5 = +0.3BB (pure steal already profits)

Conclusion: for every 10% the opponent's fold rate rises, your steal frequency should rise too — but capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 50%". (Concept from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.13 exploitative betting and frequencies)

Example: After locking "BB folds to turn double-barrel 55% (equilibrium ~45%)" and re-solving, the solver immediately pushes your turn bluff frequency higher, even adding weak hands that originally checked into the betting range. It precisely shows "how much you should deviate for every 1% the opponent deviates" to harvest. Node locking turns exploitation from intuition into calculation.

Example 2 (value vs the calling station): The opponent calls too loosely postflop (station). After locking this tendency, your value-bet sizes can increase and thin-value hands (top pair weak kicker) all enter the betting range — because the station calls with weak hands, your wide value range gets overpaid.

Example 3 (when to return to baseline): After you raise steal frequency, the opponent starts 3Betting frequently in response — he's discovered your deviation. Now you must return to the GTO baseline (narrow the steal range, reduce pure bluffs), or your newly opened leaks get harvested in reverse. Exploitation is a dynamic game: deviate → get detected → return to baseline, looping.

Counterintuitive point: the biggest risk of exploitation isn't "exploiting too little" but "over-exploiting and becoming the leak yourself". While harvesting the opponent's leaks, HU pros always keep one hand on the GTO baseline wheel — the moment the opponent adjusts, they snap back.

Exploitation execution in five steps: (1) HUD-collect enough samples to confirm the leak; (2) lock the node in a solver for the optimal response; (3) compare to baseline and mark the pushed-up frequencies and sizes; (4) execute live; (5) re-check the sample every 500 hands. A "lock" without data support is exploitation on paper.
t8hu-pressure: Heads-Up: The Ultimate Test of Emotion

Heads-up is the most emotionally stressful poker format: you're in a blind every hand, 200+ hands/hour, compressed variance, no teammates to share it, and the opponent watches you the whole time. Losing 8-10 all-ins in a row is mathematical normalcy (T1's 55%-60% all-in equity means a 0.45^8 ≈ 0.17% streak appears often). In this environment, emotion management matters as much as strategy itself — one tilting decision can erase hours of +EV.
A HU downswing isn't an anomaly but an inevitability. Treating consecutive losses as "weather" rather than "a verdict" prevents your worst strategic adjustments during the most violent variance.
The Mechanisms and Defenses of Tilt

Tilt stems from three triggers: result dependence (happy when winning, hurt when losing), dashed expectations ("I should have won"), and revenge psychology ("I must win it back next hand"). Tilt's horror is that it distorts your range — you open looser, call wider, chase harder, all deviating from baseline. Three defenses: (1) self-awareness — set an "emotional red light" (N consecutive hands wanting revenge or raising to get even) and force a pause; (2) pre-commitment — set the stop-loss off the table and leave at the line; (3) process attribution — review only whether decision EV was correct, never change play because of results.

Example: You lose 6 consecutive 60%-equity all-ins in HU (0.4^6 ≈ 0.4%, rare but encountered several times an hour). Your mind knows "I played right" but emotions want "to get even". If you keep sizing up to chase losses, that's a classic tilt loop. The right move: recognize the revenge impulse → pause 10 minutes → restart with "what is this hand's EV" rather than "I must win it back".

Example 2 (process vs result): You shove AK vs 55 and 55 wins. Result: you lost. Process: AK vs 55 is about 43% equity; the shove's EV depends on pot odds — with proper odds it's +EV and you played right. HU pros review only process: "was this decision EV-correct?" Tilters review only results: "I lost to junk again." The long-term difference between the two is astronomical.

HU variance budget (Tendler's psychological framework):

Single all-in standard deviation σ = √(p(1−p)) × pot (Bernoulli approximation)
N-hand cumulative variance = σ×√N; expectation = N×marginal edge×pot

Example: p=60%, pot 100, edge 20:
expectation(50 hands) = 50×0.2×100 = 1000
variance(50 hands) = 49×√50 ≈ 347

Conclusion: even with positive expectation, "winners experience long drawdowns" in heads-up is normal — the mathematical root of psychological pressure and why you need a preset variance budget. (Concept from: The Mental Game of Poker, Jared Tendler Ch.4 variance tolerance and emotion)

Counterintuitive point: the most dangerous tilt isn't "impulse when losing" but "letting your guard down after winning". After winning a few hands, players often relax, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. HU discipline must be consistent throughout, win or lose.

HU session-management triad: (1) preset a variance budget — pause and review after losing 40-50BB, a stop-and-restart not a chase; (2) stand up every 100 hands to break losing-streak inertia; (3) review only EV, never results.
t8hu-reads: Reads fall into two types: live physical reads (Physical Tells — betting gestures, body, eyes) and online frequency reads (Frequency Reads — betting rhythm, timing, size). In heads-up reads are highly valuable, but the traps are many: physical tells get counterplayed (the opponent acts), frequency tells have insufficient samples. The most reliable is combining "observation" with "action narrative" — does the opponent's action sequence tell a self-consistent story?

The best read is "action consistency": an opponent who checks the flop and turn then suddenly overbet-shoves the river has the narrative "I have the nuts". If this narrative contradicts his frequency statistics, that's a read signal.

You read the opponent, and the opponent reads you. Counter-reading (Balanced Play) requires your actions not to leak range information: don't bet fast because "this hand is strong" or hesitate because "I'm bluffing". In heads-up the opponent watches your every rhythm; unconscious "bet fast with strong, bet slow with weak" is a classic leak. Pro counter-reading deliberately keeps action rhythm consistent, or masks with mixed frequencies.

Example: Online HU, the opponent thought 20 seconds before calling your turn bet. Frequency read: long think = a hard decision, possibly a marginal hand (station trait) or a draw. But with insufficient samples it could be acting. The right approach is cross-verification: his tendency to call big bets, his river showdown choices — judge comprehensively rather than relying on one rhythm alone.

Example 2 (counter-reading): You hold AA and watch your rhythm when betting the flop. If you bet instantly because "I have a strong hand" and hesitate because "I'm bluffing", the opponent will quickly crack you. Counter-reading drill: set the same think time for all your bets, or deliberately break rhythm at key moments (hesitate with strong, be decisive with bluffs).

Example 3 (narrative consistency): The opponent bets the flop, bets the turn, checks the river. Narrative: strength on flop/turn, giving up on the river. If he checks the river but the sizes are odd (big on the flop, small on the river), combined with his frequencies it may be "thin value" rather than "giving up". Reads must combine "action sequences" with "frequency statistics" — a single action doesn't count.

Counterintuitive point: the enemy of reads isn't "reading wrong" but "overconfidence". HU pros admit "this read is only 60% sure" and bet accordingly, rather than "I know what he has". Converting reads into probabilities rather than certainties is the sustainable strategy.

Read discipline: (1) only conclude from statistically significant frequencies (50+ hand samples); (2) cross-verify action narrative with frequency; (3) admit read uncertainty and fold it into equity and pot-odds calculations. After these three, reads go from mysticism to math.
t9hu-mastery: From Fragments to a System: The HU Decision Loop

Each chapter of T1-T8 is a building block: T1 probability basics, T2 odds and EV, T3 position and starting hands, T4 ranges, T5 GTO, T6 betting, T7 exploitation, T8 psychology. The HU master doesn't "memorize each chapter" but connects them into a decision loop — facing any situation, automatically running through "range → math → betting → exploitation → psychology". This loop makes you at the table no longer "I memorized the formula for this decision" but "I see every dimension of this spot".

HU decision loop: first ask "what are both ranges" (T4), then compute "my EV and odds" (T2), then "what size to bet" (T6), then "what deviation can I exploit" (T7), finally "am I emotionally stable" (T8). All five questions, none optional.

HU theory isn't monolithic; it deforms along two parameters: stack depth and game type. Deep stacks (100BB+): wider ranges, more polarized betting, greater postflop positional value, and high SPR needs multi-street planning. Short stacks (under 20BB): more frequent preflop all-ins, smaller positional value, more direct betting. Cash: unlimited re-buy, manageable variance, measured in bb/100. Tournaments: chips are a resource, ICM pressure, blinds rise over time, and strategy shifts dynamically by stage (see l6hu-tourney).

Example: Deep stack 100BB, HU SB holds A♠5♠. Decision loop: range — A5s is in the SB opening range (within ~80%); math — min-raise 2BB, pure steal needs 60% fold rate; betting — deep stacks lean small bets for control + postflop play; exploitation — if the BB folds a lot, raise open frequency; psychology — keep rhythm consistent, don't leak. One decision, all five questions passed.

Example 2 (short stack): HU 15BB deep, SB holds K♠Q♠. Range — KQs has about 60% equity vs the BB's wide range; math — shove 15BB or min-raise then shove; KQs is clearly ahead of the calling range; betting — short stacks skip multi-street; shove directly or small-raise to induce; exploitation — if the BB over-folds, just push; psychology — accept variance. Short-stack strategy is more direct than deep — stack depth makes the same hand play completely differently.

Example 3 (review methodology): After a HU session, review hand by hand with the "decision loop" — was my range judgment right? Was the EV right? Was the size right? Was the opponent-tendency read right? Did emotion influence me? Five questions turn every hand into training. Tendler emphasizes "process vs result": review only process (decision quality), never results (wins/losses).

Counterintuitive point: the HU master's "cleverness" isn't perfect decisions but "system stability". Occasional decision errors are inevitable, but a stable decision loop plus strict emotional discipline keeps the long-term expectation curve climbing. Chasing "every-hand perfection" instead causes overthinking and tilt.

Building your personal system in four steps: learn (T1-T8 theory) → drill (solver verification) → play (execute the loop live) → review (hand-by-hand review + notes). Four-step loop, and your HU level climbs steadily with every session.
t9hu-pro-study: The core value of studying professional HU players (like seasoned HU players in the Moshman system or top solver-era grinders) isn't imitating a move but understanding their decision framework. Top players' common traits are highly consistent: frequency balance (not leaking ranges), range consistency (self-consistent action narratives), emotional stability (unaffected by results), and disciplined execution (strictly following preset strategy).

The dividing line between pros and amateurs isn't "luck" or "talent" but "decision framework" — amateurs rely on feel, pros rely on systems. Studying pros means learning their systems, not copying their cards.

Top HU players' decision frameworks usually have four layers: (1) preflop range construction — starting from the GTO baseline, micro-adjusted by opponent tendencies; (2) postflop range allocation — bet/check by board ownership (whose range/nut advantage); (3) bet-sizing discipline — sizes chosen by SPR and hand-strength tier; (4) exploitation switching — switching to maximal exploitation when the opponent deviates and returning to baseline when he adjusts. Every layer has clear inputs and outputs, not improvisation.

Example (preflop range micro-adjustment): A pro facing a BB who folds too much deliberately raises SB opening frequency toward 100% and lowers the raise size (mostly min-raises), because a wide range plus small sizes maximizes steal EV. This isn't "feeling like stealing" but a computable decision "supported by the opponent's fold-rate statistics".

Example 2 (postflop range allocation): On a dry high board A♠8♦3♣ a pro C-Bets the entire betting range at high frequency and small size — because the raiser's range advantage is clear (lots of Ax) and the caller rarely hits an A. On a wet 7♠6♥4♣ board he cuts C-Bet frequency sharply — because the caller's range contains more straights/draws. Range advantage decides betting frequency — a reusable methodology.

Example 3 (emotional discipline): Top players still decide with the same framework after losing 10 consecutive 60% all-ins — because they treat "variance" as an uncontrollable external variable and control only "decision quality". This is T8's "process vs result" separation manifested at the professional level.

Counterintuitive point: the value of studying pros isn't "how great they are" but "how replicable their systems are". An amateur drilling the pro framework for a month often improves faster than "ten years of memorized feel" — because systems are trainable and feel isn't replicable.

Pro hand-study process: (1) record all actions of a hand; (2) deconstruct layer by layer with the decision loop (range/math/betting/exploitation/psychology); (3) compare with your own handling to find gaps; (4) distill one reusable principle into your notes. Every 10 hands studied makes your decision framework more complete.

t1-combinatorics-q1.question: What is the total number of starting-hand combinations in Texas Hold'em?
t1-combinatorics-q1.explanation: C(52,2) = 52×51÷2 = 1326. 169 is the class count after grouping by equivalence, not the combo count.

t1-combinatorics-q2.question: How many combos does a specific offsuit hand (e.g. AKo) have?
t1-combinatorics-q2.explanation: AK has 4×4=16 total combos, of which 4 are suited; offsuit = 16−4 = 12.

t1-combinatorics-q3.question: The claim "I got AA last hand, so my chance of AA this hand drops":
options: True — good hands come in turns
False — every hand is an independent event
t1-combinatorics-q3.explanation: After re-shuffling, every hand is independent; the probability is always 6/1326 ≈ 0.45%. Thinking "good hands come in turns" is the classic gambler's fallacy.

t1-combinatorics-q4.question: An opponent's range is {AA, KK, AKs}. How many total combos?
t1-combinatorics-q4.explanation: AA and KK each have 6 (pocket pair C(4,2)=6), AKs has 4: 6+6+4 = 16.

t1-combinatorics-q5.question: Why divide by 2 when computing C(52,2)?
options: Each card can only be used once
Combinations don't distinguish internal order — A♠K♥ and K♥A♠ are the same hand
Hole cards must be one red one black
t1-combinatorics-q5.explanation: Picking the 1st of 52 then the 2nd of 51 gives ordered pairs (52×51). But starting hands have no order — each hand is counted 2! = 2 times, hence divide by 2. That's the mathematical meaning of "combinations are unordered".

t1-outs-q1.question: With an open-ended straight draw on the flop, the hit rate for one card (turn) is about:
t1-outs-q1.explanation: OESD has 8 Outs; one card ≈ 8×2% = 16% (exact 8/47 ≈ 17%). 32% is the two-card (flop to river) estimate.

t1-outs-q2.question: How many Outs does a flush draw have?
t1-outs-q2.explanation: Each suit has 13 cards; your hand and the flop show 4, leaving 13−4 = 9.

t1-outs-q3.question: When should Outs be discounted?
options: When your out also completes a bigger hand for the opponent
When the pot is already big
When the opponent has a deeper stack
t1-outs-q3.explanation: The core of discounted Outs: if an out completes your straight while also giving the opponent a flush, it isn't a clean Out. Position and stack depth don't affect Outs themselves.

t1-outs-q4.question: In the Rule of 2 and 4, when does "×4" apply?
options: Deciding on the flop whether to see one card (turn)
Facing an all-in on the flop — seeing both turn and river at once
Computing bluff frequency on the river
t1-outs-q4.explanation: ×4 estimates the total two-card hit rate, only valid for a flop all-in (no more bets needed to see both cards). If more bets follow, evaluate street by street with ×2.

t1-outs-q5.question: You have 15 Outs and shove on the flop. The ×4 rule (60%) overestimates the exact value (~54%) by about:
t1-outs-q5.explanation: Exact = 1 − (32/47)×(31/46) ≈ 54.1%; ×4 gives 60%, an overestimate of ~6 points. For Outs ≥ 13 use the correction Outs×4 − (Outs−8).

t1-variance-q1.question: You shove as an 80% favorite and lose the hand. This means:
options: Your decision was wrong — you should have folded
The decision was correct; losing is normal variance
The opponent reads better than you
You should lower bet sizes to avoid risk
t1-variance-q1.explanation: 80% equity means losing once per five on average. Decision quality is determined by EV, unrelated to a single result — the core of the long-term view.

t1-variance-q2.question: For skill to reliably overcome luck in cash games, the typical sample size needed is about:
t1-variance-q2.explanation: With typical win rates and standard deviations, results within 10,000 hands are still heavily luck-driven; usually 50,000-100,000+ hands are needed to reliably reflect true skill.

t1-variance-q3.question: Expanding the sample 100x, luck's relative impact on results:
t1-variance-q3.explanation: Fluctuation's relative impact is inversely proportional to the square root of the sample: √100 = 10, so it shrinks to 1/10. That's the math behind "the long run filters out luck".

t1-variance-q4.question: After understanding variance, the correct review standard is:
options: Track how much you won each day
Check whether each key decision's EV is positive
Keep winning lines, change losing lines
t1-variance-q4.explanation: Result = EV + fluctuation. Reviewing by wins/losses treats noise as signal (keeping won-but-wrong lines, discarding lost-but-right lines); only the EV standard filters variance.

t1-variance-q5.question: The standard deviation of bet results +200, −150, +300, −100, +50 is about:
t1-variance-q5.explanation: First the mean μ=60, then squared deviations sum to 147000, σ²=147000/5=29400, σ=√29400≈171. The mean 60 is the expected value; the standard deviation 171 far exceeds it, showing single results swing violently — the meaning of variance.

t2-ev-q1.question: Pot is 100, opponent shoves 50, you have 30% equity after calling. The call's EV is:
t2-ev-q1.explanation: EV = 0.30×(100+50) − 0.70×50 = 45 − 35 = +10. Below 50% equity can still be a +EV call because the pot offers odds.

t2-ev-q2.question: You make a pure-bluff 2/3-pot bet (loses at showdown every time). What minimum fold rate does the opponent need for break-even?

t2-ev-q3.question: A semi-bluff's (e.g. betting a draw) EV comes from:
options: Whether the opponent sees through you
t2-ev-q3.explanation: A semi-bluff can win both ways: the opponent folds and you take the pot, or he calls and your draw hits at showdown. That's the math behind it being better than a pure bluff.

t2-ev-q4.question: "Once a decision is made, its EV is fixed" means:
options: Later community cards no longer affect this decision's quality
t2-ev-q4.explanation: EV is determined at the decision moment by the information then available; cards dealt after are just variance on display and can't retroactively prove the decision right or wrong.

t2-ev-q5.question: You've already put 80 in the pot and face a turn all-in of 120. The correct attitude when deciding whether to call:
options: The 80 invested should count as cost — not calling wastes it
Only look forward: compare call EV with fold EV (=0); invested money is irrelevant
At least call, otherwise your earlier investment is wasted
t2-ev-q5.explanation: Invested chips are sunk cost, irrelevant to the current decision. Correctly compute whether "call EV" exceeds "fold EV (always 0)"; options A/C are sunk-cost fallacies, and D ignores that pot odds may make calling +EV.

t2-pot-odds-q1.question: Pot is 100, opponent bets 50. The minimum equity you need to call is:

t2-pot-odds-q2.question: Facing a pot-size bet, the required equity to call is about:
t2-pot-odds-q2.explanation: Full-pot bet: you call P, total pot 3P, required equity = P÷3P = 33.3%.

t2-pot-odds-q3.question: Why is required equity always below 50% when facing a bet?
options: Because the opponent might be bluffing
Because there's already "dead money" in the pot — you win more than you pay
Because you can improve on later streets
t2-pot-odds-q3.explanation: Calling wins "pot + opponent bet + your call" while you only pay the call amount. The chips already in the pot subsidize your price.

t2-pot-odds-q4.question: An opponent keeps small-betting 1/4 pot while you only continue with strong hands. This leak is:
options: Folding too much to small bets — any two cards he bets profit
You should raise back every time
You should shove to punish small bets
t2-pot-odds-q4.explanation: A 1/4-pot bet only needs 16.7% equity to call. If you fold all medium hands, his small bets become automatically profitable with any two cards.

t2-pot-odds-q5.question: Facing a 1/3-pot bet, the minimum equity you need to call is about:
t2-pot-odds-q5.explanation: Required equity = (1/3) ÷ (1+1/3+1/3) = 1/5 = 20%. Option A's 16.7% is for a 1/4-pot bet and D's 33% for a full-pot bet — this size-to-equity table is the foundation of postflop calling.

t2-implied-odds-q1.question: Compared to pot odds, what does implied odds additionally consider?
options: Future chips you can win from the opponent after hitting your draw
t2-implied-odds-q1.explanation: Implied odds = pot odds + expected future-street winnings; it makes calling some draws profitable even when current odds are insufficient.

t2-implied-odds-q2.question: Which situation has the best implied odds?
options: Effective stacks 200bb, opponent is a calling station, you hold a pocket pair
t2-implied-odds-q2.explanation: Three factors: deep stacks + a willing-to-pay opponent + a disguised made hand (a set). When the opponent is all-in, implied odds are zero.

t2-implied-odds-q3.question: Set mining (digging a set with a small pair) generally requires effective stacks of at least how many times the call?
t2-implied-odds-q3.explanation: Set probability is ~1/7.5, and you can't always fully collect the opponent's stack after hitting, so the empirical standard is 15-20x (leaving ample margin over the theoretical 7.5x).

t2-implied-odds-q4.question: The risk described by reverse implied odds is:
options: Losing the call amount when the draw misses
Still being behind after hitting, and losing a bigger pot
Winning too little when the opponent folds
The pot being too small to participate in
t2-implied-odds-q4.explanation: Classic reverse implied odds: a non-nut flush hitting into a bigger flush, a weak-kicker top pair into a strong kicker — win small pots when ahead, lose big pots when behind.

t2-implied-odds-q5.question: Pot 150, opponent bets 75, your flush-draw hit probability is 18% (required 25%). After calling, hitting lets you win X more on average. What minimum X makes the call break even?
t2-implied-odds-q5.explanation: EV = 0.18×(150+75+X) − 0.82×75 = 0, solving 0.18×(225+X) = 61.5 → X ≈ 117. On a hit you currently win 225; you need ~120 more in future winnings to break even; above that it's +EV. Options A/B make the call lose long-term, and D overestimates the implied odds needed.

t3-position-value-q1.question: Which seat has the highest long-term win rate at the table?
t3-position-value-q1.explanation: BTN is the only seat always last to act postflop, maximizing information and pot-control advantage — the highest win rate in all tracking-database statistics.

t3-position-value-q2.question: "Equity Realization" describes:
options: The share of raw equity actually converted into win rate
t3-position-value-q2.explanation: With the same raw equity, in position realizes a higher share (even over-realizing), while OOP is forced to give up part of the equity under unfavorable conditions.

t3-position-value-q3.question: Why can BTN's opening range be far wider than UTG's?
options: Fewer opponents behind and position postflop — marginal hands have higher EV
t3-position-value-q3.explanation: Range width is set by EV: BTN only needs to get through two blinds and always has position postflop, turning many marginal hands from -EV to +EV.

t3-position-value-q4.question: Which of the following is NOT a source of positional advantage?
options: The ability to take free cards
t3-position-value-q4.explanation: Dealing is random; position doesn't change the cards you get, only how much value the same cards can realize.

t3-position-value-q5.question: Holding Q♥J♥, calling an open on the BTN vs calling in the SB. Which statement is correct?
options: Both have identical EV because the hand is the same
The SB call has lower equity realization — OOP and pressured postflop, prone to forfeiting equity
On the BTN you can take free cards without paying anything
The SB's blind discount actually raises realization
t3-position-value-q5.explanation: Position determines equity realization: IP QJs can control the pot and chase, still partially realizing under pressure; OOP QJs is often forced to fold, discounting R. Option A ignores position, the biggest realization variable; C makes free cards sound unconditional; D's "blind discount" is unrelated to postflop realization.

t3-starting-hands-q1.question: The core of the Gap Concept is:
options: Adjacent positions have a fixed 5% range gap
Calling an open requires stronger hands than opening yourself
The smaller the gap between connectors, the better
Preflop and postflop strategies must differ
t3-starting-hands-q1.explanation: The raiser has shown strength and you've lost the Fold Equity winning path, so your calling bar must exceed your opening bar.

t3-starting-hands-q2.question: Why is raising recommended over limping when first into the pot?
options: Raising keeps Fold Equity and initiative; limping only has the made-hand winning path
Raising lets you see more community cards
t3-starting-hands-q2.explanation: Raising can win the blinds outright, builds initiative, and avoids multiway equity dilution; limping gives up these structural advantages.

t3-starting-hands-q3.question: After a UTG open, you hold A9o in the CO. The theoretically best action is usually:
t3-starting-hands-q3.explanation: A9o is severely dominated by AQ/AK/Ax with big kickers in UTG's strong range — hitting an A can even lose big (reverse implied odds). Standard play is fold.

t3-starting-hands-q4.question: What environment do small pocket pairs (like 44) prefer for entering?
options: Shallow stacks, heads-up, high preflop investment
Deep stacks, cheap entry, collecting after flopping a set
Only seeing the flop free in the BB
t3-starting-hands-q4.explanation: Small pairs are speculative: the outcome hinges almost entirely on the ~12% set probability, needing deep stacks for implied odds and cheap entry to control cost.

t3-starting-hands-q5.question: In the spot "UTG opens, you're in the CO", which hand usually belongs to the 3Bet range's "value 3Bet"?
t3-starting-hands-q5.explanation: Against an open, AK/QQ+ are value 3Bets (ahead of the opponent's calling range and folding his dominated hands); 55, 76s are speculative calls (deep-stack implied odds), A9s marginal. The preflop value/speculative tiering is exactly Gap logic in action.

t3-fundamental-theorem-q1.question: The Fundamental Theorem states your profit comes from:
options: Opponents playing differently from "how they'd play seeing your cards"
Only playing the strongest starting hands
t3-fundamental-theorem-q1.explanation: Poker's profit is fundamentally opponent decision errors. Card strength equalizes long-term; poor decision quality is the profit source.

t3-fundamental-theorem-q2.question: Limping preflop with AA lets the opponent see a free flop. From the theorem's view, the problem is:
options: You fixed the error the opponent should have made (paying to enter)
No problem — slowplay is an advanced skill
t3-fundamental-theorem-q2.explanation: The opponent's weak hand should have paid to enter (erred); your limp lets him realize equity free, returning profit to the opponent.

t3-fundamental-theorem-q3.question: Opponent errors can only take two directions:
options: Betting too big or too small
Calling too much or folding too much
Playing too fast or too slow
Playing too tight or sitting in the wrong seat
t3-fundamental-theorem-q3.explanation: Facing a bet there are only call/fold directions — impossible to "call too much" and "fold too much" simultaneously. Identifying the direction finds the exploitation entry.

t3-fundamental-theorem-q4.question: The "initiative" gained by the last preflop raiser means:
options: You must bet every postflop street
You can bet first representing the strongest range, forcing opponents to decide first
You can see opponents' hole cards
t3-fundamental-theorem-q4.explanation: Initiative is narrative right: the raiser's range "should" contain the strongest hands, so postflop continuation bets carry built-in credibility. It doesn't mean you must bet.

t3-fundamental-theorem-q5.question: River, you hold unpaired A♠K♠, the opponent checks, and you bluff-shove into a 100 pot. By the theorem, the correct understanding is:
options: If the opponent could see your cards and correctly call any pair, your bluff is still long-term profitable
The opponent's fold itself is the profit source — he's making a "fold too much" error
This decision has no EV because there's no showdown yet
Bluff success depends on your image, unrelated to the theorem
t3-fundamental-theorem-q5.explanation: Theorem view: if he could see your cards he'd call your high-card bluff with a pair — he can't, and folds, making a "fold too much" error you profit from. That's the source of bluff value. Option A is reversed (correct play kills the bluff); C ignores that bluffs have a clear EV structure; D substitutes image for the theorem's mechanism.

t4-range-thinking-q1.question: The core claim of range thinking is:
options: Guess the exact hand the opponent holds
Treat the opponent as a set of hand combos that keeps updating with each action
Only care about your own hand strength
Memorize every hand the opponent shows down
t4-range-thinking-q1.explanation: A single hand is unknowable, but a range can be continuously inferred and updated through position and action sequences — this is the computable method of hand reading.

t4-range-thinking-q2.question: "Actions are filters" means:
options: Every action narrows the opponent's range
t4-range-thinking-q2.explanation: At every decision point the opponent continues with part of his range and folds the rest. Doing set operations along the action sequence narrows the range further. Checks filter too (removing most strong value).

t4-range-thinking-q3.question: After three streets of strong betting, your top pair with a weak kicker faces an all-in on the river. The correct decision framework is:
options: Evaluate whether the bluff share of his shoving range meets the required equity
Call because you've invested too much
t4-range-thinking-q3.explanation: Your hand is now a bluff catcher: it only beats bluffs and loses to all value. Decision = bluff share of his range vs the equity required by pot odds.

t4-range-thinking-q4.question: Under the "range vs range" view, the right question when evaluating a bet is:
options: Can my hand win if I bet?
How does my range allocate actions at this node, and which part does this hand belong to?
How big should I bet to make him fold?
t4-range-thinking-q4.explanation: A single hand's action only has meaning inside the whole range's allocation — the mindset prerequisite for moving from exploitation to equilibrium thinking.

t4-range-thinking-q5.question: After the opponent 3Bets you preflop, the most accurate statement about "how his range changed" is:
options: The action filters the range down to strong hands plus balancing bluffs, and your continuing range narrows accordingly
A 3Bet means he must have AA
His range actually widens after a 3Bet
t4-range-thinking-q5.explanation: A 3Bet is a strong filter: the range narrows to a polarized strong-hand set, and your opening range must contract to the part entitled to continue — "actions are filters" applied preflop.

t4-combinatorics-q1.question: With one K on board, how many combos of KK can the opponent hold?
t4-combinatorics-q1.explanation: Three Ks remain: C(3,2) = 3. Every related card on the board trims combo counts — you must count while looking at the board.

t4-combinatorics-q2.question: The mechanism of a blocker is:
options: A card you hold reduces the count of specific opponent combos
It prevents the opponent from raising
It hides your range from the opponent
t4-combinatorics-q2.explanation: Each card you hold removes every opponent combo containing that card — your hole cards thus become information about his range.

t4-combinatorics-q3.question: A three-spade board, you hold a lone A♠ (no flush). What does this mean for bluffing?
options: Nothing — you don't have a flush
You block the opponent's nut-flush combos, raising bluff success
The opponent definitely has no flush
t4-combinatorics-q3.explanation: Holding A♠ zeroes out his A♠X♠ nut-flush combos, trimming his strongest call/raise-back hands and boosting your bluff's fold equity. Note it trims ratios, not "definitely no flush".

t4-combinatorics-q4.question: The opponent's shoving range is 11 value combos and 6 bluff combos, facing a full-pot all-in (needs 25%). Your bluff catcher should:
t4-combinatorics-q4.explanation: Bluff ratio = 6/17 ≈ 35%, above the 25% required by pot odds, so calling profits long-term. The numbers answer directly; no feel needed.

t4-combinatorics-q5.question: You hold AK and read the opponent's range as {AA, KK, QQ, AK}. After your AK, the share of that range where you're truly ahead is about:
t4-combinatorics-q5.explanation: After blocking, the range total drops from 34 to 21, of which QQ (you're ahead) has 6 combos = 6/21 ≈ 29%. Without a blocker it's 18% — blocking shifts the share upward, a key input to preflop all-in EV.

t4-range-advantage-q1.question: The difference between range advantage and nut advantage is:
options: Two names for the same concept
The former means higher overall average equity; the latter means more of the strongest combos
The former only looks preflop, the latter only at the river
The former belongs to the raiser, the latter to the caller
t4-range-advantage-q1.explanation: Range advantage is an average concept (overall equity); nut advantage is a distribution-top concept (density of strongest combos). They can diverge and carry different strategic meanings.

t4-range-advantage-q2.question: On a dry A♠K♦7♣ high board, the typical UTG-opener strategy vs BB is:
options: Frequently small C-Bet the whole range
Check everything to control the pot
t4-range-advantage-q2.explanation: UTG holds both range and nut advantage on this board and BB has almost no counter combos — betting small across the full range is standard.

t4-range-advantage-q3.question: On a low connected 6♥5♥4♠ board, the nut advantage usually belongs to:
options: The BB defender (who keeps small connectors and small pairs)
t4-range-advantage-q3.explanation: Hands like 87s, 53s, and 22-66 that hit this board live almost only in BB's defense range; UTG's strong range (big cards and pairs) mostly misses.

t4-range-advantage-q4.question: What condition grants a player the license to use overbet sizes?
t4-range-advantage-q4.explanation: Oversized sizing needs "I have more nuts than you" as support: the opponent's best hands are merely targets of my range and he can't effectively fight back.

t4-range-advantage-q5.question: Low connected 8♥7♥5♠ flop, BTN opener vs BB. The most accurate judgment is:
options: BTN has absolute range advantage and should bet the whole range
BB holds more nut combos; BTN should lower betting frequency and BB earns check-raise space
t4-range-advantage-q5.explanation: On low connected boards the nuts (straights, sets, two pairs) concentrate in BB's defense range, while BTN has many big cards that rarely hit — the classic "caller owns the nuts, raiser contracts" structure, and why the overbet license goes to the nut-advantage side.

t5-game-theory-q1.question: The definition of a Nash equilibrium is:
options: The strategy profile that maximizes everyone's payoff
A strategy profile where no single player benefits from deviating unilaterally
A strategy with over 50% win rate
t5-game-theory-q1.explanation: Equilibrium doesn't promise maximum payoff — only that "unilateral deviation is unprofitable", which is exactly where being unexploitable comes from.

t5-game-theory-q2.question: Against a leaky weak opponent, the equilibrium (GTO) strategy:
options: Doesn't lose, but earns less than targeted exploitation
Is identical to the exploitative strategy
t5-game-theory-q2.explanation: Equilibrium guarantees expectation no lower than the game value (a floor) but doesn't actively exploit opponent errors; exploitation extracts more — at the cost of opening your own leaks.

t5-game-theory-q3.question: An equilibrium strategy must include randomized (mixed) components because:
options: It makes the game more exciting
Deterministic strategies get observed and countered; mixing makes every opponent guess unprofitable
t5-game-theory-q3.explanation: A strategy that always takes the same action in the same spot can be deciphered. Mixing makes the opponent's expectation identical no matter which side he bets on — nothing to attack.

t5-game-theory-q4.question: The "unexploitable" guarantee of Nash equilibrium strictly applies to:
options: Pots of any size in player count
t5-game-theory-q4.explanation: In games with three or more players the equilibrium floor can fail (coalition dynamics can harm one side). Heads-up and "two players left preflop" are the strict applicability domain.

t5-game-theory-q5.question: In the toy game, mixing "write 1 / write 2" at 50/50 achieves:
options: The same expectation for the opponent on either guess, locking your payoff to the game value
t5-game-theory-q5.explanation: Once mixing makes all opponent choices equal in expectation, he can no longer push your payoff down — the minimax-locked game value. Poker solver mixing frequencies work the same way.

t5-gto-concept-q1.question: The equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a full-pot river bet is about:
t5-gto-concept-q1.explanation: Bluff share = b/(1+2b) = 1/3, i.e. 2/3 value and 1/3 bluffs, value:bluff = 2:1. It exactly equals the opponent's required call equity of 33%.

t5-gto-concept-q2.question: Why does a larger bet size allow the equilibrium strategy to carry more bluffs?
options: The opponent's required call equity rises, so the indifferent bluff share rises with it
Big bets can afford to lose
That's wrong — bluffs should be small
t5-gto-concept-q2.explanation: b/(1+2b) rises monotonically with b: the bigger the sizing, the worse the opponent's calling price, so your range can carry higher bluff density while keeping him indifferent.

t5-gto-concept-q3.question: The exploitable flaw in "you only bet the nuts big and never bluff" is:
options: The opponent can fold everything to your big bets
The opponent can call everything to your big bets
The opponent will re-raise you every time
t5-gto-concept-q3.explanation: A betting range with no bluffs means the opponent loses nothing by folding everything except the nuts — your value bets never get called and your strong hands' EV shrinks drastically.

t5-gto-concept-q4.question: The mature relationship between GTO and exploitation in practice is:
options: Pick one, it's a style choice
Use GTO as the baseline, deviate with direction based on observable opponent biases
GTO at low stakes, exploitation at high stakes
t5-gto-concept-q4.explanation: The baseline provides an unexploitable floor and the cognition of the "correct shape"; exploitation turns opponent errors into extra profit on top — they're foundation and floors of a building.

t5-gto-concept-q5.question: The equilibrium bluff share of a half-pot bet (formula f = b/(1+2b)) is:
t5-gto-concept-q5.explanation: b=0.5 → f = 0.5/2 = 25%, value:bluff = 3:1. It exactly equals the opponent's required call equity, making both sides indifferent.

t5-mdf-alpha-q1.question: Facing a half-pot bet, MDF is about:
t5-mdf-alpha-q1.explanation: MDF = 1/(1+0.5) = 2/3 ≈ 67%. You need to continue with roughly your strongest two-thirds, or any opponent bluff becomes profitable.

t5-mdf-alpha-q2.question: Alpha (α) represents:
options: The minimum frequency of value bets
The minimum fold rate a pure bluff needs to break even
The minimum equity needed to call
t5-mdf-alpha-q2.explanation: α = b/(1+b), the bluff's break-even fold rate, complementary to MDF (α = 1−MDF).

t5-mdf-alpha-q3.question: You only defend 30% against full-pot bets (MDF should be 50%). The opponent's correct exploitation is:
options: Raise bluff frequency with any two cards
t5-mdf-alpha-q3.explanation: A 70% fold rate far exceeds the 50% a full-pot bluff needs to break even — the opponent's bets with any two cards are automatically profitable, so he should bluff aggressively more.

t5-mdf-alpha-q4.question: When is folding well below MDF actually correct?
options: When you read the opponent as almost never bluffing
When the pot is especially big
t5-mdf-alpha-q4.explanation: MDF is the floor against balanced opponents. When his betting range is heavily value-skewed, over-folding is exactly maximizing exploitation — with information, exploitation beats equilibrium.

t5-mdf-alpha-q5.question: Pot 100, opponent bets 200 (2x pot). MDF is about:
t5-mdf-alpha-q5.explanation: MDF = 1/(1+2) = 1/3 ≈ 33%. Bigger bets shrink defense responsibility; but the overbet range's equilibrium bluff share rises to 40%, so judge by "value:bluff" matching rather than mechanically applying the defense floor.

t5-mixed-strategy-q1.question: In equilibrium, a hand is mixed across multiple actions only if:
options: The hand is too hard to decide
All actions have exactly equal EV
It was chosen randomly to confuse the opponent
t5-mixed-strategy-q1.explanation: Indifference principle: when EV differs, a rational strategy always picks the higher one. Mixing only occurs on critical hands with equal EV, and its frequencies maintain the opponent's indifference.

t5-mixed-strategy-q2.question: Against an equilibrium opponent's full-pot bet, your bluff catcher's call and fold EV are:
t5-mixed-strategy-q2.explanation: The equilibrium bluff share makes your equity exactly equal the required equity — the two actions are indifferent. That's how equilibrium "leaves the opponent torn".

t5-mixed-strategy-q3.question: The purpose of node locking is:
options: Lock your own strategy to prevent misclicks
Fix the opponent's strategy to the observed real tendency and solve the maximally exploitative response
t5-mixed-strategy-q3.explanation: Node locking feeds "how the opponent actually plays" into the solver and outputs the optimal harvest scheme for that deviation — the bridge from equilibrium tools to exploitation.

t5-mixed-strategy-q4.question: For live players, the most pragmatic attitude toward mixed-strategy nodes is:
options: Recognize that either side loses almost nothing, and invest effort in high-EV-difference decisions
Avoid all spots where mixing appears
t5-mixed-strategy-q4.explanation: Both sides of a mixed node have equal EV, so a single "wrong choice" costs ≈0; what actually separates results is pure-strategy nodes and range construction on earlier streets.

t5-mixed-strategy-q5.question: The most critical execution discipline in node locking is:
options: Set the locked frequency as high as possible
The locked opponent tendency must come from real observation over a sufficient sample, and be re-checked periodically
A lock lasts forever once set
Locks can only be used on preflop ranges
t5-mixed-strategy-q5.explanation: Locking imaginary leaks into the solver produces "exploitation on paper"; real biases need HUD sample support and re-verification as the opponent adjusts — that's the line between node locking and self-deception.

t6-bet-purpose-q1.question: The first-principles question for judging whether a bet is reasonable is:
options: Can I get worse hands to call or better hands to fold
Is the opponent afraid of me
t6-bet-purpose-q1.explanation: Value and bluff are the only two fundamental purposes of betting. A bet that achieves neither (like a medium-strength probe bet) loses on both ends.

t6-bet-purpose-q2.question: The strict standard for a value bet is:
options: More than half of the opponent's calling range is worse than me
I hold top pair or better
t6-bet-purpose-q2.explanation: To profit on the calls a bet collects, most of the calling range must be worse than you. "I might be ahead" while all calls are stronger is digging your own hole.

t6-bet-purpose-q3.question: Why should strong hands also check at some frequency?
options: To show respect to the opponent
To protect the checking range, preventing "check = weak" from being attacked at full force
Checking strong hands is an error
t6-bet-purpose-q3.explanation: If the checking range is only weak hands, the opponent can auto-pressure whenever you check. Mixing in strong hands gives your checking line teeth — the core of range protection.

t6-bet-purpose-q4.question: The structural reason a semi-bluff beats a pure bluff is:
options: It has an extra "draw hits" winning path
It doesn't need to consider fold equity
t6-bet-purpose-q4.explanation: A semi-bluff = fold equity + improvement equity: the opponent folding wins immediately, and calling still leaves your draw's chance to outdraw (see the T2 betting EV breakdown).

t6-bet-purpose-q5.question: You make a half-pot value bet and have 30% win rate when called. Long-term this bet:
options: Profits, because break-even only needs w > 25%
Depends on whether the opponent notices
t6-bet-purpose-q5.explanation: From w > B/(P+2B), half-pot break-even is only 25%; w=30% already profits — the math behind long-term thin-value profit. "Must exceed half" is conservative intuition.

t6-sizing-theory-q1.question: A polarized range consists of:
options: A continuous distribution from strong to weak
Strong value and bluffs, with the middle missing
t6-sizing-theory-q1.explanation: Polarized = the two-pole structure of nuts or air. It naturally matches big sizing: value doesn't fear calls and bluffs need pressure.

t6-sizing-theory-q2.question: On a dry high board with clear range advantage, the standard C-Bet scheme is:
options: Only bet strong hands with big sizing
Small bets (about 1/4-1/3 pot) with the whole range
t6-sizing-theory-q2.explanation: Linear range + small bets: collect rent at minimum cost from the opponent's entire continuing range, making his marginal hands torn, while protecting your own medium hands.

t6-sizing-theory-q3.question: The problem with mixing medium hands (like a weak top pair) into an overbet range is:
options: Worse hands get scared off and only better hands call — loss on both ends
The opponent will see through it
No problem — big bets protect hand strength
t6-sizing-theory-q3.explanation: A big bet filters the calling range to strength far above medium hands — in this sizing it collects no value and can't fold out stronger hands (back to the betting-purpose sentence completion).

t6-sizing-theory-q4.question: The core purpose of a blocking bet is:
options: The OOP player uses a small lead to set the price, avoiding facing the opponent's big bet
Preventing the opponent from seeing cards
t6-sizing-theory-q4.explanation: A blocking bet lets OOP medium hands see showdown / collect thin value at a self-chosen low price; equilibrium requires mixing in strong hands to prevent raise exploitation.

t6-sizing-theory-q5.question: The most fundamental reason polarized ranges naturally fit big (overbet) sizings is:
options: Big bets are scarier and the opponent folds more easily
Value doesn't fear calls, bluffs need maximum fold pressure, and b/(1+2b) gives big bets more bluff capacity
Big bets can represent more hand types
Big bets make future bluffs more credible
t6-sizing-theory-q5.explanation: Polarized = nuts or air, and both ends benefit from big bets; the formula also shows bigger sizings carry higher bluff density — the mathematical root of the polarization-sizing match.

t6-geometric-q1.question: The definition of SPR is:
t6-geometric-q1.explanation: SPR = effective stack / flop pot, measuring relative pot depth and deciding which hand strengths are worth fighting for all the chips.

t6-geometric-q2.question: The hand type most favored by low-SPR (≤3) pots is:
options: Single-pair strong hands like top pair good kicker and overpairs
t6-geometric-q2.explanation: In shallow pots, a single pair can commit all chips without giving the opponent implied odds; speculative hands lose their deep-stack realization room. That's why 3Bet pots favor AA/KK.

t6-geometric-q3.question: The meaning of geometric sizing is:
options: Bet the same amount every street
Use the same pot percentage each street so the river shove lands exactly
Only bet big on the river
t6-geometric-q3.explanation: Growing the pot geometrically spreads pressure evenly across three streets and maximizes value, avoiding the abrupt "small then huge" shove that scares off the opponent's calling range.

t6-geometric-q4.question: "The turn is the watershed" refers to:
options: The turn pot is the largest
The flop betting range is wide; the range that keeps firing on the turn clearly narrows and strengthens
t6-geometric-q4.explanation: The flop contains many one-shot semi-bluffs; a second barrel needs real equity or a plan behind it. This natural frequency decay also means an opponent checking the turn often exposes his range's ceiling.

t6-geometric-q5.question: Pot 100, effective stack 400 (SPR=4). The three-street geometric sizing is about:
t6-geometric-q5.explanation: x = ((1+2×4)^(1/3) − 1)/2 = (9^(1/3) − 1)/2 ≈ (2.08−1)/2 ≈ 54%. Matches the heuristic anchor "SPR≈4 → about 55% pot each street".

t7-stats-q1.question: A very large VPIP-PFR gap (like 40/8) usually means:
options: A loose-passive player who limps into pots a lot
A tight player who only plays big pairs
t7-stats-q1.explanation: The gap = limp frequency. Entering a lot but raising little is the fingerprint of loose-passive; professionals' two values are usually close (like 24/20).

t7-stats-q2.question: AF (Aggression Factor) is calculated as:
t7-stats-q2.explanation: AF = (Bet+Raise)/Call, measuring the ratio of postflop active to passive actions. <1.5 passive, >4 high-pressure.

t7-stats-q3.question: Against an opponent with WTSD as high as 38%, the correct response is:
options: Stop bluffing, and make value bets bigger and wider
t7-stats-q3.explanation: A player who calls everything to showdown: bluffing is pure money-burning, while thin value on every street gets paid — maximal exploitation toward "lots of value, zero bluffs".

t7-stats-q4.question: The correct understanding of sample size for metrics is:
options: Ten hands can define a player
VPIP/PFR are basically reliable within dozens of hands; AF/WTSD need hundreds
All metrics need tens of thousands of hands
t7-stats-q4.explanation: High-frequency events (preflop decisions) converge fast; low-frequency events (showdowns) converge slowly. Under-sampled metrics are only unverified hypotheses.

t7-stats-q5.question: An opponent's first 35 hands show VPIP 38%, PFR 34%, with about 12 hands in a row of QQ+/AK. The safest judgment is:
options: Confirm he's a loose-aggressive LAG and adjust immediately
Sample too small — 38/34 may be inflated by card luck; keep observing at least 100 hands
He's cheating; normal people can't keep getting big hands
His position selection is very strong
t7-stats-q5.explanation: 35 hands plus a run of big cards inflates VPIP/PFR short-term. Even high-frequency metrics need around 100 hands to stabilize; short-term data is hypothesis, not conclusion. Option A is the classic "small sample as conclusion" error; C/D over-explain random phenomena.

t7-player-types-q1.question: The two axes of the four-quadrant classification are:
t7-player-types-q1.explanation: Entry width (tight/loose) × action style (aggressive/passive) generates TAG/LAG/NIT/calling station, each with its own leak list.

t7-player-types-q2.question: The standard plan against a NIT (rock) is:
options: Steal his blinds frequently preflop and retreat decisively when he fights back
Bluff him with big bets often
t7-player-types-q2.explanation: NITs fold at extremely high rates — blind stealing is steady profit; and when he enters or fights back his range is very strong, so fold marginal hands without a fight.

t7-player-types-q3.question: Against a LAG's constant pressure, the correct adjustment is:
options: Fight every bet with a wider range
Tighten entry range, but use strong hands so he builds the pot for you
t7-player-types-q3.explanation: Against LAGs: raise the entry bar (range solidity), but refuse to be pushed around once in — his high bluff frequency automatically pays for your strong hands.

t7-player-types-q4.question: The most common trigger of "type drift" is:
options: Tilt after losing a big pot
t7-player-types-q4.explanation: Emotional swings push players across quadrants (NIT to LAG, TAG to calling station). Recognizing drift windows and switching responses instantly is the daily work of advanced exploitation.

t7-player-types-q5.question: A TAG at your table, after losing a big pot, starts 3Bet-bluffing frequently and stealing blinds with marginal hands. The correct response is:
