options: Keep playing his initial TAG portrait; he's just doing it occasionally
Recognize the type drift and counter his widened range with medium-strong 3Bets/calls
Target him with the whole table, raising every bet he makes
Leave the table to avoid risk
t7-player-types-q5.explanation: The common "LAG-ification" drift after a big loss lasts a while. Recognizing the drift and adjusting immediately (tighter counter standards, strong hands to absorb pressure) is correct; option A misses the harvest window with the old portrait, C is an emotional overreaction (backfires), and D gives up high-profit windows.

t7-hand-reading-q1.question: The correct order of the four-step hand-reading process is:
options: Watch tells → guess the hand → verify → act
Starting range → street filtering → board crossover → combo counting
t7-hand-reading-q1.explanation: Set the starting point from position/preflop actions, filter through the action sequence, re-estimate strength on the board, count combos on key decisions — a trainable pipeline.

t7-hand-reading-q2.question: "Checking is also information" means:
options: A check also eliminates "hands he'd usually bet", cutting the range ceiling
A check is always a trap
t7-hand-reading-q2.explanation: Logically consistent players bet their strong hands most of the time; his check therefore removes most strong value — often the attack window for thin value and bluffs.

t7-hand-reading-q3.question: The correct way to use physical tells is:
options: Only as a tie-breaker when range analysis is near balanced, never overturning math
t7-hand-reading-q3.explanation: Tells have noise and can be faked; ranges and combo counts are hard information. The correct position of tells is an auxiliary weight on marginal decisions.

t7-hand-reading-q4.question: A validated behavioral baseline is:
options: Strong hands relaxed and natural, bluffs stiff and controlled
Strong and weak hands behave identically
Blink rate is proportional to hand strength
t7-hand-reading-q4.explanation: Caro's classic observation: those holding strength are psychologically safe, hence relaxed and talkative; bluffers fear exposure and hold their breath, going rigid. This is among the few tells stable across populations.

t7-hand-reading-q5.question: 3Bet pot, board K♠8♦5♣2♥3♥, opponent shoves. You count 14 value combos and 5 bluff combos, facing a 0.75-pot bet (needs 30%). The correct decision is:
options: Call — top pair is strong enough
Fold — bluff share about 26% is below the required 30%
t7-hand-reading-q5.explanation: Bluff share = 5/19 ≈ 26% < 30% (required equity); calling loses long-term. Combo counting gives the precise answer; option A judges by hand strength and D by feel, both skipping the quantitative range-vs-pot-odds comparison.

t7-exploit-q1.question: The opponent folds too much to big bets. The correct exploitation direction is:
t7-exploit-q1.explanation: A fold rate above Alpha means bluffs are automatically profitable (T5) — pressing on the fold leak is the most direct exploitation mapping.

t7-exploit-q2.question: Exploitation intensity should be inversely proportional to:
options: The opponent's observation and adaptation ability
t7-exploit-q2.explanation: Non-adapting opponents allow maximal exploitation; strong opponents who fight back deserve only small deviations while keeping the ability to return — because your deviation opens your own leaks too.

t7-exploit-q3.question: The complete exploitation loop is:
options: Execute the same deviation forever once a leak is found
Observe and profile → directed deviation → monitor adaptation → retreat or counter
t7-exploit-q3.explanation: Exploitation is an arms race: the opponent adapts and your deviation must evolve. A static exploitation strategy eventually gets counter-harvested.

t7-exploit-q4.question: Against a completely unknown opponent, the optimal default strategy is:
options: Default to exploiting the average leaks of the player pool at this stake (population tendencies)
t7-exploit-q4.explanation: Population tendencies are the statistically best prior (e.g. low-stakes river pools under-bluff); individual profiles then gradually override the default.

t7-exploit-q5.question: You bet 100% when the BB checks, and get check-raised by the BB for two straight orbits (encounter rate from 12% to 30%). The correct adjustment is:
options: Lower your automatic betting frequency in that spot and add a checking range (including strong traps)
Keep auto-betting; he can't raise forever
Never enter pots in that position again
Bet bigger to scare him off
t7-exploit-q5.explanation: A rising check-raise encounter rate is the signal that YOU are being counter-exploited. Fixing your own betting frequency and restoring equilibrium makes his check-raises fail; option B is the classic death of static exploitation (the arms race doesn't end itself), C sacrifices the whole position pointlessly, and D's "scaring" treats symptoms.

t8-tilt-q1.question: Tendler's core claim about Tilt is:
options: Tilt is innate personality and can't change
Most players produce most of their losses during a minority of Tilt time
Tilt increases aggression so it's beneficial
t8-tilt-q1.explanation: 80% of losses come from 20% of Tilt time — the cost of emotional leaks is highly concentrated, so psychological training has a very high ROI.

t8-tilt-q2.question: The shared cognitive fuse of almost all Tilt types is:
t8-tilt-q2.explanation: Those who truly internalize "correct decisions also lose in streaks" see Bad Beats as noise; mistaking fluctuation for targeted injustice lights the fire every time.

t8-tilt-q3.question: After AA gets outdrawn, you raise K4o from UTG the next hand. This is most likely:
options: A Tilt symptom: the goal drifted from +EV decisions to "win it back now"
t8-tilt-q3.explanation: The decision basis shifting from math to emotion (revenge/can't-lose) is the hallmark of Tilt. Recognizing this kind of behavioral drift is exactly what the precursor checklist does.

t8-tilt-q4.question: The standard intervention after spotting a Tilt precursor is:
options: Physical interruption (leave the table / breathe), and end the session if you haven't hit the calm line
Move to another table and continue
Raise stakes to find your form
t8-tilt-q4.explanation: In an emotionally activated state you can't restore decision quality by willpower; physical interruption is the only reliable tool. The plan must be written in advance; on the spot you only execute.

t8-tilt-q5.question: A player, after a Bad Beat, starts playing any two suited cards and frequently raising to "teach the opponent a lesson". This is:
options: Bad-luck Tilt; only better luck can fix it
Injustice/Revenge Tilt combined: the goal drifts from +EV to retribution
Despair Tilt; he should keep playing
t8-tilt-q5.explanation: Attributing losses to "the game is unfair" (injustice) while locking onto a revenge target (revenge) is a typical combination. The key signal is the decision basis shifting from EV to emotion — start the precursor plan then.

t8-session-q1.question: The core goal of session management is:
options: Play as many hands as possible in A/B state and compress C-Game time
t8-session-q1.explanation: Decision quality is a consumable resource. One hour of C-Game loss often exceeds several hours of A-Game profit; managing state is managing profit.

t8-session-q2.question: The true function of a stop-loss line (like stopping after losing 2-3 buy-ins) is:
options: Forcing an exit before Tilt and decision-quality collapse (a state stop-loss)
t8-session-q2.explanation: Every hand is independent; a stop-loss doesn't change EV. It manages you — after consecutive losses the C-Game probability spikes, so the stop-loss is a preset breakwater.

t8-session-q3.question: The correct basis for deciding whether to keep playing or leave is:
options: Table quality and your own state
Whether half the time has passed
t8-session-q3.explanation: Extend when fish are present and state is good (even if you're winning a lot); leave when state drops a tier (even if you're winning). Profit/loss is variance on display, not a stay/leave basis.

t8-session-q4.question: Structured review should prioritize:
options: The 2-3 hardest decisions (win or lose) plus moments your state dropped a tier
t8-session-q4.explanation: Reviewing by pot size gets dragged by variance; reviewing by decision difficulty targets your own knowledge boundaries, and adding the psychological review completes the loop.

t8-session-q5.question: You're up 3 buy-ins, but all the fish at the table have left and only tight-aggressive regulars remain. You should:
options: Keep playing; leaving while winning is a waste
Move to a softer table or finish — the table-quality change altered EV
t8-session-q5.explanation: Stay/leave only depends on "table quality × your state": a lower table quality = negative EV for you; continuing is grinding your luck against tougher games, unrelated to whether you're winning.

t8-bankroll-psych-q1.question: Besides preventing bankruptcy, the equally critical second function of bankroll management is:
options: Making single win/loss "not hurt", so you can execute correct high-variance decisions
t8-bankroll-psych-q1.explanation: When stakes are within psychological tolerance, loss aversion doesn't distort decisions. Under Scared Money your technique can't function normally.

t8-bankroll-psych-q2.question: The typical behavioral signature of Scared Money is:
options: Systematically abandoning thin edges: not calling what you should call, not bluffing what you should bluff
t8-bankroll-psych-q2.explanation: Loss aversion makes correct "might lose" decisions get avoided — the accumulated abandonment of thin edges is enough to turn a winner into a loser.

t8-bankroll-psych-q3.question: A healthy "take a shot" is:
options: Keep playing higher stakes while it feels good
Set an explicit budget (like 3 buy-ins), drop back immediately when gone, no re-buy
t8-bankroll-psych-q3.explanation: Budgeted attempts keep the variance of moving up inside your bankroll structure; "re-buy after losing" is the bankroll version of can't-lose Tilt.

t8-bankroll-psych-q4.question: The root reason many players refuse to move down after a drawdown is:
options: Moving down psychologically feels like admitting defeat, and ego blocks the correct decision
t8-bankroll-psych-q4.explanation: Moving down is a purely correct financial move; all resistance comes from self-image. Writing it as a mechanical rule and executing unconditionally is the only solution.

t8-bankroll-psych-q5.question: The correct understanding of Kelly's criterion and poker bankroll management is:
options: Kelly provides the mathematical ceiling; in practice use half-Kelly or more conservative, and psychological tolerance provides the floor
Kelly only applies off the table
t8-bankroll-psych-q5.explanation: Full Kelly assumes no psychological wear and precisely known edges; most players' real edges can't support it. Half-Kelly or more conservative balances growth and variance, while psychological tolerance (e.g. distorting after losing N buy-ins) sets the actual floor.

t8-mindset-q1.question: The definition of "resulting" is:
options: Inferring decision quality from a single result
Ignoring results and only watching process
t8-mindset-q1.explanation: In a variance-dominated game, a single result is almost unrelated to decision quality; judging decisions by results systematically contaminates the learning curve.

t8-mindset-q2.question: "I've already put 200 in the pot; folding wastes it" commits:
options: The sunk-cost fallacy: invested chips aren't yours; only current odds matter
No error — with that much invested you should call
t8-mindset-q2.explanation: The chips you've put in the pot are no longer yours. A call decision depends only on the current call amount vs equity and pot odds (T2).

t8-mindset-q3.question: After correctly bluff-catching and running into the nuts, the probability-thinking review conclusion is:
options: Check whether the frequency judgment was justified; if yes, the decision was correct and just landed in the low-probability branch
t8-mindset-q3.explanation: Decouple decision from result: with a 40% bluff frequency the call is correct, and losing 60% of the time is part of the expectation.

t8-mindset-q4.question: In variance-dominated poker, you should set goals as:
options: Controllable process goals (review count, state management, learning progress)
t8-mindset-q4.explanation: Result goals are contaminated by variance and uncontrollable; chasing them necessarily triggers emotional swings. Process goals are fully controllable, and results are their long-term byproduct.

t8-mindset-q5.question: After the showdown you write "I knew he had AA; I shouldn't have called". This most likely reflects:
options: Hindsight bias: using the showdown result to rewrite the information state at decision time
t8-mindset-q5.explanation: At the decision moment you didn't know he had AA, otherwise the call's EV would be negative. Hindsight distorts review — the correct practice is recording the judgment before deciding and comparing after showdown to verify true precision.

t9-mop-q1.question: MOP's core methodology is:
options: Statistical analysis of massive real hands
Constructing precisely solvable toy games and distilling general structural rules
t9-mop-q1.explanation: Real poker is too complex to solve directly; the precise solutions of simplified games reveal structures (bluff ratios, MDF, indifference) that still hold in real hands.

t9-mop-q2.question: In the AKQ game, K (the medium hand) 's equilibrium strategy is:
options: Never bet — only call as a bluff catcher at the right frequency
t9-mop-q2.explanation: K loses both ways if it bets (A always calls, Q always folds); its only value is catching Q's bluffs. This is the theoretical prototype of "medium strength should be passive".

t9-mop-q3.question: "The weak think about single hands, the strong think about ranges" reflects the stratification of:
options: The tactical layer (this hand) and the strategic layer (whole range construction)
t9-mop-q3.explanation: A single hand's optimal action can only be determined inside range-construction rules — solvers output range-level strategy, not single-hand answers.

t9-mop-q4.question: Per MOP's risk-aversion theory, a technically superior side should:
options: Moderately avoid small +EV spots with high variance, preserving room to realize the technical edge
t9-mop-q4.explanation: The superior side's edge produces EV every hour, so bearing huge variance for tiny immediate EV isn't worth it; the weaker side's logic is reversed and should actively raise variance.

t9-mop-q5.question: In the AKQ game, K (the medium hand) facing a 1-pot bet calls at an equilibrium frequency of:
t9-mop-q5.explanation: c = B/(P+B): when the bet equals the pot (B=P), c = P/(P+P) = 1/2. Call and bluff frequencies share the formula and mirror each other — the toy-model prototype of MDF.

t9-icm-q1.question: The core problem ICM solves is:
options: Converting tournament chip counts into true prize expectation ($EV)
t9-icm-q1.explanation: The prize ladder makes chip utility nonlinear; ICM computes each-place probabilities by chip share and weights the prizes to get chips' true monetary value.

t9-icm-q2.question: A "+cEV but −$EV" situation means:
options: Chip expectation rises but prize expectation falls — survival itself has value in tournaments
t9-icm-q2.explanation: Decreasing chip marginal value plus losing all expectation on bust makes chip-slightly-positive gambles negative in prize terms. Tournaments run on $EV.

t9-icm-q3.question: Under bubble ICM pressure, the typical behavior by stack size is:
options: Medium stacks tightest, big stacks most aggressive, small stacks near normal
t9-icm-q3.explanation: Medium stacks lose the most prize expectation so are the most suppressed; big stacks bully through this; small stacks have little remaining expectation and the least constraint.

t9-icm-q4.question: The correct understanding of ICM's model boundaries is:
options: ICM is perfect and must be strictly followed
It ignores position, skill edge, and blinds rising — technically superior players may deviate moderately from its conservative solutions
ICM only applies to cash games
ICM can't be used at final tables
t9-icm-q4.explanation: ICM assumes equal skill and immediate settlement. With a clear technical edge, future value supports leaning beyond survival/conservative choices. The model is a map, not the territory.

t9-icm-q5.question: 3-player SNG (prize 50/30/20), chips A=5000/B=3000/C=2000. A's $EV is about:
t9-icm-q5.explanation: P(A 1st)=0.5, 2nd≈0.339, 3rd≈0.161; $EV = 0.5×50+0.339×30+0.161×20 ≈ 38.4. Note it's well below the 50 his chip share implies — the visible face of decreasing chip marginal value.

t9-multiway-q1.question: The pattern of starting-hand value changes in multiway pots is:
options: Hands that can make the nuts appreciate; easily dominated hands crash
t9-multiway-q1.explanation: Equity dilution raises the made-hand threshold: suited connectors/pocket pairs (nut potential) relatively appreciate, while weak Ax/KJo (often second place) crash.

t9-multiway-q2.question: Bluff frequency in multiway pots should:
options: Rise, because the pot is bigger
Drop sharply, because everyone must fold and success drops with player count
t9-multiway-q2.explanation: Bluff success ≈ the product of each opponent's fold rate, decaying exponentially with player count; and more players means more chance someone has hit the board.

t9-multiway-q3.question: The correct understanding of GTO in multiway pots is:
options: The unexploitable guarantee fails; fundamentals and opponent reads weigh more
Multiway pots have no theory at all
t9-multiway-q3.explanation: The Nash floor only holds for two-player zero-sum games; multiway dynamics can hurt even "equilibrium" players. Tight, value-oriented play and position are more reliable anchors.

t9-multiway-q4.question: The problem with slow-playing strong hands in multiway pots is:
options: No problem — more players means more reason to trap
Giving multiple opponents free cards equals giving multiple outdraw chances, and protection value is rising
Slow-playing is only a problem heads-up
t9-multiway-q4.explanation: The more live opponents, the higher the cumulative free-card outdraw probability and the greater the value of making equity pay — fast-play strong hands to build the pot multiway.

t9-multiway-q5.question: AA's showdown equity against 4 random opponents is about:
t9-multiway-q5.explanation: AA: 1 opponent ≈85%, 2 ≈73%, 3 ≈64%, 4 ≈56%. Each extra opponent drops about 8-12 points, and realizable equity is even lower — the mathematical basis for fast-playing strong hands and valuing nuttiness multiway.

t9-alpha-q1.question: What is Alpha's formula?
t9-alpha-q1.explanation: Alpha = bet / (pot + bet), sharing the same denominator as MDF with a different numerator. It's the fold-rate threshold the opponent needs.

t9-alpha-q2.question: The relationship between Alpha and MDF is:
t9-alpha-q2.explanation: Alpha + MDF = 1; they're complements. Alpha is the fold rate the opponent needs; MDF is your defense frequency.

t9-alpha-q3.question: Alpha's core value lies in:
t9-alpha-q3.explanation: Alpha provides a quantitative view to evaluate whether the opponent's bluff frequency is high enough to justify calling.

t9-alpha-q4.question: Alpha's application steps are:
options: Compute Alpha → observe opponent fold rate → compare Alpha with his fold rate
Observe fold rate → compute Alpha → compare Alpha with fold rate
Compare Alpha with fold rate → compute Alpha → observe fold rate
Observe fold rate → compare Alpha with fold rate → compute Alpha
t9-alpha-q4.explanation: Alpha's application steps: compute Alpha → observe the opponent's fold rate → compare Alpha with his fold rate.

t9-alpha-q5.question: You bet 1/3 pot, Alpha = 1/4. The opponent's C-Bet fold rate is 30%. You should:
t9-alpha-q5.explanation: The opponent's fold rate is below Alpha, so you should fold.

t9-unified-q1.question: The relationship between GTO and exploitation in the unified framework is:
options: Two modes of one system: equilibrium as the floor without information, exploitation by confidence with information
t9-unified-q1.explanation: Decision = equilibrium baseline + directed deviation weighted by information quality. Zero information → pure baseline; complete information → maximal exploitation; in between → scaled by confidence.

t9-unified-q2.question: The magnitude of deviating from equilibrium to exploit should depend on:
options: The information quality of the leak (sample and confidence) and the opponent's adaptation ability
t9-unified-q2.explanation: Deviations are justified by confirmed leaks; their upper bound is the opponent's counter-attack ability. Together they set the direction and magnitude of exploitation.

t9-unified-q3.question: The operating loop of the complete decision framework is:
options: Equilibrium baseline → observe → deviate with evidence → monitor adaptation → retreat/counter
t9-unified-q3.explanation: This loop integrates T5's equilibrium, T7's information and exploitation, and the adaptation arms race — executed with the psychological system's support from T8.

t9-unified-q4.question: The ultimate test of theoretical learning is:
options: How many formulas you can recite
Whether it changed real in-game decisions and can be executed steadily
t9-unified-q4.explanation: The knowing-doing gap is your skill ceiling. Theory must be converted through training into decision habits that survive pressure — exactly the closed loop between the Theory Academy and training modules.

t9-unified-q5.question: You collect 200 hands showing an opponent folds to C-Bets 65%, and start raising your bluff frequency against him. The basis of this deviation is:
options: An observable bias with sufficiently high confidence, the magnitude supported by information quality
t9-unified-q5.explanation: The unified framework requires deviations to be justified: sufficient sample (200 hands), a clear bias direction (folds too much), and continuous adaptation monitoring. Information quality sets deviation magnitude — the unified expression of GTO and exploitation.

t1sd-combinatorics-q1.question: How many cards does Short Deck hold'em use?
t1sd-combinatorics-q1.explanation: Short deck removes 2-5 and uses 36 cards (6-A, 9 per suit). 40 is an old count in some 6+ variants; the mainstream is 36.

t1sd-combinatorics-q2.question: The total number of starting hands in short deck is about:

t1sd-combinatorics-q3.question: The share of pocket pairs among short-deck starting hands is about:
t1sd-combinatorics-q3.explanation: Short deck 54/630 ≈ 8.6%, above full ring's 78/1326 ≈ 5.9%. Pair density is higher.

t1sd-combinatorics-q4.question: Short-deck's "denser" flop draw environment mainly comes from:
options: Fewer ranks (9) make connected flops more frequent and outs hit rates relatively higher
t1sd-combinatorics-q4.explanation: Short deck's smaller rank pool (9 ranks) makes connected flops more common, and fewer remaining cards make outs hit rates (like 8/31) relatively higher than full ring.

t1sd-combinatorics-q5.question: AK's preflop all-in equity against any pocket pair in short deck is about:
t1sd-combinatorics-q5.explanation: Short-deck AK vs any pocket pair preflop all-in is about 43%-45%, usually trailing. AK is the "strongest non-pair" but doesn't beat pairs.

t1sd-outs-q1.question: The correct way to calculate short-deck flush-draw outs is:
t1sd-outs-q1.explanation: Short deck has only 9 cards per suit, so flush outs = 9 − seen cards of that suit. 13 is the full-ring base.

t1sd-outs-q2.question: Holding 2 hearts with 2 hearts on board, your short-deck flush outs are:
t1sd-outs-q2.explanation: 9 − 4 (4 hearts seen) = 5. Using 9 directly is the full-ring error.

t1sd-outs-q3.question: The mental-math baseline for single-street hit rate after a short-deck flop is:
t1sd-outs-q3.explanation: After a short-deck flop, unknown cards = 36 − 2 (hole cards) − 3 (flop) = 31, so single-street hit rate ≈ outs ÷ 31. 47 is full ring.

t1sd-outs-q4.question: A short-deck flush draw (5 outs) has lower absolute equity than full ring but is still valuable, because:
options: A flush is a super-strong hand in short deck (beats full houses), basically locking the pot when made
t1sd-outs-q4.explanation: In short deck a flush beats full houses and is near-nuts when made, with excellent implied odds — few outs but high made value.

t1sd-outs-q5.question: A short-deck straight draw (e.g. open-ended, 8 outs) hits about ___ on one street:
t1sd-outs-q5.explanation: 8 ÷ 31 ≈ 26%. Full ring 8/47 ≈ 17%; short deck hits more because fewer cards remain.

t1sd-variance-q1.question: The main reason short-deck variance exceeds standard hold'em is:
options: Higher flop rate, more common draws, bigger pots — higher single-result uncertainty
t1sd-variance-q1.explanation: Short deck flops more often, draws are more common, and pots are usually bigger — combined, single-result uncertainty far exceeds full ring.

t1sd-variance-q2.question: The recommended bankroll bar for short-deck cash games is about:
t1sd-variance-q2.explanation: Short-deck standard deviation is higher, so the bankroll bar must be more conservative — suggest ≥150 buy-ins. 50-100 is the full-ring magnitude.

t1sd-variance-q3.question: Short-deck all-in equity often lands in which range, causing high single-result uncertainty?
t1sd-variance-q3.explanation: Short-deck draws vs made hands collide constantly, so all-in equity often lands in 45%-55%, making single results highly uncertain.

t1sd-variance-q4.question: Losing multiple 50% all-ins in a row in short deck is correctly understood as:
options: Mathematical normalcy under high-frequency confrontation — maintain decision quality
t1sd-variance-q4.explanation: Short deck has frequent all-ins; 0.5^N losing streaks are mathematical normalcy. Maintain decision quality instead of doubting your level.

t1sd-variance-q5.question: The most important psychological discipline for short-deck players against high variance is:
options: Review only decision EV, never change play because of results
Raise to get even after losses
t1sd-variance-q5.explanation: Separate "process vs result" — review only whether decision EV was correct, never change play by win/loss, to maintain quality through variance.

t2sd-potodds-q1.question: What betting structure does short deck usually use?
options: An ante structure, with the BTN posting an extra ante
t2sd-potodds-q1.explanation: Short deck usually uses an ante structure: everyone posts the same ante and the BTN posts an extra ante — no traditional SB/BB.

t2sd-potodds-q2.question: Short-deck pot 8 ante, opponent bets 4 ante, you need to call 4. Required equity is about:

t2sd-potodds-q3.question: A short-deck flush draw (5 outs) hits about ___ on one street:

t2sd-potodds-q4.question: When short-deck pots are big and odds cheap, the correct basis for a call decision is:
options: Call mindlessly because odds are cheap
Judge with short-deck-corrected equity, combined with high made-hand value
t2sd-potodds-q4.explanation: Short-deck calls must correct equity on 36 cards and rely on the high value of flushes/straights when made. Cheap odds don't mean free.

t2sd-potodds-q5.question: A short-deck straight draw (8 outs) hits about ___ on two streets:
t2sd-potodds-q5.explanation: Short-deck 8-outs straight hits about 44% on two streets (1 − complement), far above the single-street 24%.

t2sd-implied-q1.question: The polarization of short-deck implied odds is shown by:
options: All draws have poor implied odds
Chasing flushes/straights has excellent implied odds; chasing sets has worse implied odds
All draws have good implied odds
t2sd-implied-q1.explanation: Short-deck flushes/straights are nut-tier when made (good implied odds); trips lose to full houses/flushes (poor implied odds).

t2sd-implied-q2.question: Short-deck set mining needs a higher threshold than full ring because:
options: Trips are harder to make in short deck
Short-deck trips rank below full houses/flushes, discounting implied odds
t2sd-implied-q2.explanation: Short-deck trips lose to full houses and flushes, reducing made-hand value and requiring a higher payoff ratio — hence the higher threshold.

t2sd-implied-q3.question: The probability of flopping trips with a pocket pair in short deck is about:
t2sd-implied-q3.explanation: Short deck ≈ 17.6% (full ring ≈ 12%). Though the hit rate is higher, trips lose value, requiring a higher threshold.

t2sd-implied-q4.question: "Making trips in short deck isn't as happy as full ring" because:
options: Trips lose to full houses and flushes, and high pair density makes outdraws more common
t2sd-implied-q4.explanation: Short-deck trips < full house < flush, and pair density is high, so opponent combos like 99/K9 that outdraw you are more common.

t2sd-implied-q5.question: When chasing a short-deck flush draw, the core of judging call value is:
options: Once made, a flush is nut-tier (beats full houses) with excellent implied odds
Too few flush outs to be worth it
t2sd-implied-q5.explanation: Short-deck flushes beat full houses and are near-nuts when made, with excellent implied odds — few outs but high made value.

t2sd-reverse-q1.question: Reverse implied odds (RIO) refers to:
options: Winning more in the future after calling now
Losing more in the future after calling now
t2sd-reverse-q1.explanation: RIO is the extra you may lose after calling. Short-deck's ranking reshuffle and draw density amplify RIO.

t2sd-reverse-q2.question: Why is RIO amplified in short deck?
options: The ranking reshuffle (flush>full house, trips>straight) and high pair density let marginal made hands be dominated more easily
t2sd-reverse-q2.explanation: Short-deck marginal made hands (top pair/straight) are more easily dominated by stronger hands (full houses/flushes), amplifying RIO.

t2sd-reverse-q3.question: Holding top pair on a wet board (K♣9♦8♥), the correct play is:
options: Pot control or stay alert — avoid losing big pots to straights/two pair on later streets
t2sd-reverse-q3.explanation: Top pair on a wet board has high RIO — pot control or cautious calling, avoiding slow-play and outdraws on later streets.

t2sd-reverse-q4.question: The main risk of slow-playing strong hands (like trips of Aces) in short deck is:
options: Handing the opponent a free flush/straight draw; short-deck draw density makes outdraws easy
t2sd-reverse-q4.explanation: Short-deck draw density is high; slow-playing strong hands hands the opponent free draws, and the turn/river can outdraw you with flushes/full houses.

t2sd-reverse-q5.question: The core strategy for avoiding short-deck RIO is:
options: Fast-play the nuts for protection, pot-control marginal hands, avoid slow-plays on wet boards
t2sd-reverse-q5.explanation: Avoid RIO: fast-play nuts for protection, pot-control marginal made hands, and avoid slow-plays on wet boards that hand free draws.

t3sd-rankings-q1.question: The preflop all-in equity of AK vs a pocket pair in short deck is about:
t3sd-rankings-q1.explanation: Short-deck AK vs any pocket pair is about 43%-45%, usually trailing. AK is the "strongest non-pair" but doesn't beat pairs.

t3sd-rankings-q2.question: The fundamental starting-hand reshuffle in short deck is:
t3sd-rankings-q2.explanation: Short deck: any pocket pair > any A-K (trips outrank straights and pair density is high). AK is the strongest non-pair.

t3sd-rankings-q3.question: AK's equity against KK in short deck is about:
t3sd-rankings-q3.explanation: AK vs KK is about 25%; KK dominates AK more easily in short deck (hand rankings and pair value).

t3sd-rankings-q4.question: Why do small pairs rise in short-deck value?
options: Trips outrank straights and flopping trips is more likely (about 17.6%)
t3sd-rankings-q4.explanation: In short deck trips > straights, and flopping trips is about 17.6% (full ring 12%), significantly raising small-pair value.

t3sd-rankings-q5.question: The positioning of suited connectors (JTs) in short deck is:
options: Playable but secondary — can win big pots but weaker preflop than pairs and AK
t3sd-rankings-q5.explanation: Suited connectors are playable in short deck (straight/flush value), but they're a secondary tier, weaker preflop than pairs and AK.

t3sd-suitedness-q1.question: A flush beats a full house in short deck, meaning:
options: A flush is a top-tier made hand — chasing flush draws has excellent implied odds
A flush only beats a straight
t3sd-suitedness-q1.explanation: Short-deck flush > full house; flushes are top-tier made hands with excellent implied odds, basically locking big pots when made.

t3sd-suitedness-q2.question: The positioning of JTs in short deck is:
options: Playable but secondary — a high-reward speculative hand
t3sd-suitedness-q2.explanation: JTs can make nut flushes/straights (high reward) but is weaker preflop than pairs and AK — a secondary speculative hand.

t3sd-suitedness-q3.question: Suited Ax's value in short deck mainly comes from:
options: Flush-draw nut potential + top pair of Aces
t3sd-suitedness-q3.explanation: Suited Ax's value comes from "flush-draw nut potential + top pair A", not Ax itself — pair density is high, so Ax gets dominated more often.

t3sd-suitedness-q4.question: A♥9♥ on a K♥8♦3♣ board in short deck has ___ flush outs:
t3sd-suitedness-q4.explanation: Seen hearts A♥9♥K♥ = 3, so flush outs = 9 − 3 = 6.

t3sd-suitedness-q5.question: The correct attitude for short-deck suited connectors facing a big 3Bet is:
options: Know when to let go — they're speculative hands
t3sd-suitedness-q5.explanation: Suited connectors are speculative; against strong preflop resistance (big 3Bet) they should let go — not top tier.

t3sd-position-q1.question: Why is short-deck position value amplified?
options: High draw density, more frequent decisions, and bigger pots
t3sd-position-q1.explanation: Short deck has high draw density, frequent decisions, and big pots — position (seeing action, controlling pots) is amplified.

t3sd-position-q2.question: The BTN's (IP) tendency when chasing draws in short deck is:
options: Chase aggressively because equity is realized cheaply
t3sd-position-q2.explanation: BTN/IP has position, realizes equity cheaply, and can chase draws more aggressively.

t3sd-position-q3.question: The BB (OOP) holding top pair on a wet short-deck board should:
options: Bet aggressively to seize the initiative
Pot control and stop-loss to avoid high RIO
t3sd-position-q3.explanation: OOP top pair on a wet board has high RIO and poor equity realization — pot control and stop-loss. Aggression tends to build big pots then get outdrawn.

t3sd-position-q4.question: For the same open-ended straight draw, the value difference between IP and OOP is:
options: IP realizes equity cheaply and controls pots; OOP acts first and gets squeezed
t3sd-position-q4.explanation: IP realizes equity cheaply (get paid when hit, fold/see free when miss); OOP acts first and is torn when raised.

t3sd-position-q5.question: The core strategy out of position in short deck is:
t3sd-position-q5.explanation: Short-deck OOP core is pot control and stop-loss to avoid high-RIO spots, not mindless aggression.

t4sd-range-construction-q1.question: The main structural difference between short-deck and standard hold'em range construction is:
options: Higher pair density, higher flush value, offsuit big high cards relatively devalue
t4sd-range-construction-q1.explanation: Short deck has higher pair density (8.6%), higher flush value, and offsuit big high cards relatively devalue — different range structure.

t4sd-range-construction-q2.question: The speculative tier of a short-deck preflop range mainly includes:
options: 99-22 pairs + suited connectors JTs+ + suited Ax
t4sd-range-construction-q2.explanation: The short-deck speculative tier is small pairs (set mining) + suited connectors + suited Ax, exploiting trips and flush value.

t4sd-range-construction-q3.question: Why are short-deck betting ranges more "polarized"?
options: High draw density and large made-hand value, with medium hands better checked due to high RIO
t4sd-range-construction-q3.explanation: Short-deck draw density is high and made-hand value large; betting ranges use value pairs + semi-bluff draws, while medium hands check due to high RIO.

t4sd-range-construction-q4.question: Holding a medium hand (99) on a short-deck 8♦7♣3♠ flop, the correct play is:
options: Check for pot control — high RIO on a wet board
t4sd-range-construction-q4.explanation: Short-deck medium hands (99) have high RIO on wet boards — better to check and control than bet for value.

t4sd-range-construction-q5.question: The relative value of offsuit AK in short deck versus standard hold'em is:
options: Lower (high pair density makes top-pair value worse than standard hold'em)
t4sd-range-construction-q5.explanation: Short-deck pair density is high, so offsuit AK's top-pair value drops — relatively devalued.

t4sd-equity-q1.question: The main manifestation of equity dilution in short-deck multiway pots is:
options: Top pair/two pair win rates get carved up, and draw outs lose cleanliness
t4sd-equity-q1.explanation: Multiway, top pair/two pair win rates are divided among many, and draw outs may feed a stronger hand (losing cleanliness).

t4sd-equity-q2.question: A heads-up top pair is about 65%; three-way it may drop to:
t4sd-equity-q2.explanation: Each extra opponent dilutes equity; three-way top pair may drop to 35%-45%.

t4sd-equity-q3.question: In short-deck multiway pots, the correct handling of strong hands is:
options: Fast-play and bet for protection, avoiding giving multiple opponents free draws
t4sd-equity-q3.explanation: Multiway, multiple opponents may chase draws — strong hands should fast-play and bet for protection, avoiding free chases.

t4sd-equity-q4.question: Why should draw chases be more cautious in short-deck multiway pots?
options: Outs cleanliness drops (may feed a stronger hand) and RIO rises
t4sd-equity-q4.explanation: Multiway, draw outs may give another opponent a stronger hand and reverse implied odds rise — chase more cautiously.

t4sd-equity-q5.question: The correct play for marginal top pair weak kicker in short-deck multiway pots is:
options: Tighten or pot-control — thin value is diluted
t4sd-equity-q5.explanation: Multiway, top pair weak kicker's thin value is diluted — tighten or pot-control.

t4sd-blockers-q1.question: The special value of blockers in short deck comes from:
options: Extremely high flush value (beats full houses) and high pair density
t4sd-blockers-q1.explanation: Short-deck flushes are extremely valuable (beat full houses) and pair density is high — blocking flushes/pairs is amplified.

t4sd-blockers-q2.question: Holding A♠ on a three-spade board affects the opponent's nut-flush combos by:
options: Completely blocking them (A♠X♠ = 0), raising bluff success
t4sd-blockers-q2.explanation: Holding A♠ zeroes the opponent's A♠X♠ nut-flush combos, trimming his strongest call/raise-back hands and raising bluff success.

t4sd-blockers-q3.question: For a preflop 3Bet bluff, why is A5s better than 76s?
options: A5s blocks AA/AK, lowering the 4Bet frequency
t4sd-blockers-q3.explanation: A5s's A blocks the opponent's AA/AK, lowering 4Bet frequency; 76s blocks no strong hands and runs into QQ+ more often.

t4sd-blockers-q4.question: The applicability boundary of short-deck blockers is:
options: A marginal tool on edge spots, requiring a correct base range first
t4sd-blockers-q4.explanation: Blockers adjust combo ratios, not rewrite ranges — icing when the base range is right, unable to save you when the base is wrong.

t4sd-blockers-q5.question: Holding A♦A♣ (no spade A) on a three-spade board facing a bet, the correct tendency is:
options: Be cautious — you block no flushes, so his calling range skews strong
t4sd-blockers-q5.explanation: Without A♠ you block no flushes; he can have A♠X♠ nuts or a smaller flush, lowering your bluff-catching value.

t5sd-gto-short-q1.question: Does the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee apply to heads-up short deck?
options: Yes — heads-up short deck is a two-player zero-sum game
t5sd-gto-short-q1.explanation: Heads-up short deck (ignoring rake) is a two-player zero-sum game, so the Nash unexploitable guarantee applies.

t5sd-gto-short-q2.question: The equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a short-deck river full-pot bet is about:

t5sd-gto-short-q3.question: The main difference between short-deck GTO and standard hold'em is:
options: Higher made-hand value and common draws make betting ranges more polarized and sizes larger
t5sd-gto-short-q3.explanation: Short-deck flushes/straights are highly valuable and draws common, making betting ranges more polarized, sizes larger, and frequency baselines adjusted.

t5sd-gto-short-q4.question: You observe a short-deck opponent calls big river bets only 25% (equilibrium 50%). The correct counter is:
options: Raise bluff frequency, capped at "I still don't lose if he corrects to 40%"
t5sd-gto-short-q4.explanation: He folds too much, so raise bluff frequency — but with a disciplined cap, keeping room to return to baseline.

t5sd-gto-short-q5.question: "Short-deck GTO isn't playing tight" means:
options: Equilibrium includes high-frequency betting and semi-bluffs, just kept at ratios the opponent can't counter
t5sd-gto-short-q5.explanation: Short-deck GTO is full of high-frequency betting, overbets, and semi-bluffs — the key is ratio balance, not "playing tight".

t5sd-bluff-q1.question: The main reason short-deck bluffing rewards rise is:
options: High made-hand value and usually big pots, so successful pot steals pay well
t5sd-bluff-q1.explanation: Short-deck made hands (flushes/straights) are valuable and pots are big, so successful pot steals pay well.

t5sd-bluff-q2.question: The core short-deck bluffing strategy is:
options: Prefer semi-bluffs with strong draws to reduce risk
t5sd-bluff-q2.explanation: Short-deck semi-bluffs (flush/straight draws) have improvement room even when called, converting risk into investment.

t5sd-bluff-q3.question: Why is a semi-bluff's EV higher than a pure-air bluff?
options: Semi-bluffs have improvement room when called (equity E_win > 0)
t5sd-bluff-q3.explanation: A semi-bluff retains equity (flush/straight improvement) when called, giving higher EV.

t5sd-bluff-q4.question: Holding A♠ on a three-spade board matters for bluffing because:
options: It blocks the nut flush, raising bluff success
The opponent definitely has a flush
t5sd-bluff-q4.explanation: Holding A♠ zeros out the opponent's A♠X♠ nut-flush combos, trimming his strongest calling hands and raising bluff success.

t5sd-bluff-q5.question: Why is pure-air bluffing risky in short deck?
options: Opponent draw density is high and calling ranges wide, so you're easily accidentally called into
t5sd-bluff-q5.explanation: Short-deck opponents have high draw density and wide calling ranges — pure-air bluffs easily get accidentally called or even outdrawn.

t6sd-sizing-q1.question: The essence of short-deck "traditional small bets failing" is:
options: Small bets give draws too cheap a price, and short-deck draws get there easily
t6sd-sizing-q1.explanation: Short-deck draw density is high and draws get there easily; small bets give draws too cheap a price and can't protect made hands.

t6sd-sizing-q2.question: Holding an overpair on a wet short-deck board (many draws), the correct size is:
options: 2/3+ pot big bet to protect the made hand
t6sd-sizing-q2.explanation: An overpair on a wet board is easily outdrawn and draw density is high — use a 2/3+ pot big bet to protect and charge draws.

t6sd-sizing-q3.question: Holding top pair on a dry short-deck board (K♠7♦2♣), the correct size is:
t6sd-sizing-q3.explanation: The opponent rarely hits a dry board; a 1/3-pot small thin-value bet works, getting wide-range weak hands to pay.

t6sd-sizing-q4.question: Why do short-deck bet sizes trend larger overall?
options: Big pots + high draw density require big sizes to protect made hands and extract value
t6sd-sizing-q4.explanation: Short-deck pots are big and draw density is high — big sizes are needed to protect made hands, charge draws, and extract value.

t6sd-sizing-q5.question: The equilibrium bluff share of a half-pot bet is about:

t6sd-barrel-q1.question: Why is consecutive value betting more frequent in short deck than standard hold'em?
options: Made-hand value is high and strong made hands need multiple streets to extract
t6sd-barrel-q1.explanation: Short-deck flushes/straights and similar made hands are highly valuable and need consecutive streets of betting to extract full value.

t6sd-barrel-q2.question: Holding top pair on a dry short-deck board (K♠7♦2♣→5♥→9♣), the correct betting line is:
options: Three barrels — the board stays dry and the opponent rarely hits
Big bets on turn and river
t6sd-barrel-q2.explanation: On a dry board the turn/river don't improve the opponent's draws and your top pair stays ahead — three barrels collect full value.

t6sd-barrel-q3.question: When the turn/river completes the opponent's draw in short deck (board changes hands), the correct adjustment is:
options: Lower firing frequency and switch to pot control
t6sd-barrel-q3.explanation: When the board changes hands (completes the opponent's draws), the combos beating you multiply — lower frequency and pot-control.

t6sd-barrel-q4.question: Deep-stacked in short deck, consecutive betting with strong made hands requires:
options: Big sizes so the pot grows geometrically and the shove lands on the river
t6sd-barrel-q4.explanation: Deep-stacked, strong made hands need big sizes to grow the pot geometrically street by street and complete the all-in on the river.

t6sd-barrel-q5.question: "The board changing hands matters more than your hand strength" means:
options: When the turn/river completes the opponent's draws, lower frequency even if you're ahead
No need to watch the board
t6sd-barrel-q5.explanation: When the board changes hands, the combos beating you multiply — lower firing frequency even if you're still ahead.

t7sd-mistakes-q1.question: The most common cognitive bias of short-deck players is:
options: Standard hold'em inertia (wrong outs, underrating flushes, overrating AK)
t7sd-mistakes-q1.explanation: Most short-deck players come from standard hold'em carrying full-ring inertia: wrong outs, underrated flushes, overrated AK, etc.

t7sd-mistakes-q2.question: You find the opponent chases with the full-ring outs table (flush as 9 outs). The correct exploitation is:
options: Bigger value bets and tighter calls — his chases are expensive
t7sd-mistakes-q2.explanation: He overestimates chase equity and chases too loosely — your value bets can be bigger and calls tighter to exploit his errors.

t7sd-mistakes-q3.question: The opponent uses standard hold'em rankings and thinks full house > flush. When you make a flush, the exploitation is:
options: Bet value aggressively — he misjudges strength and keeps calling
t7sd-mistakes-q3.explanation: He mistakenly thinks full house > flush; when you make a flush (which actually beats full houses) he misjudges and calls bigger bets.

t7sd-mistakes-q4.question: The opponent frequently shoves AK (overrating its preflop value). The correct response is:
options: Call with pocket pairs, because short-deck pairs > AK
t7sd-mistakes-q4.explanation: Short-deck pairs > AK (43%-45%), so when he overrates AK, calling his shove with pocket pairs is slightly ahead.

t7sd-mistakes-q5.question: The foundation of short-deck exploitation is:
options: Identifying the opponent's "standard hold'em inertia" cognitive biases
t7sd-mistakes-q5.explanation: Identifying the opponent's full-ring inertia biases (outs/rankings/starting hands) matters more than memorizing more GTO — it's the prerequisite for exploitation.

t7sd-adjustment-q1.question: The most critical mindset shift from NLHE to short deck is:
options: Reshuffle rankings, recalculate outs, re-evaluate starting hands, and be more conservative on variance
t7sd-adjustment-q1.explanation: Short deck requires full shifts: rankings (flush>full house), outs (36 cards), starting hands (pairs>AK), and variance (more conservative).

t7sd-adjustment-q2.question: The correct understanding of chasing a short-deck flush (5 outs) is:
options: Few outs but the made hand is the nuts — look at implied odds
t7sd-adjustment-q2.explanation: Short-deck flushes have few outs (5) but made hands are the nuts (beat full houses) with excellent implied odds — judge by implied odds, not outs count alone.

t7sd-adjustment-q3.question: The correct judgment of AK facing a pocket-pair all-in in short deck is:
options: About 43%-45% trailing — decide by pot odds
t7sd-adjustment-q3.explanation: Short-deck AK vs a pocket pair is about 43%-45% trailing; decide by pot odds (call at 40%, fold at 45%).

t7sd-adjustment-q4.question: Why should short-deck bankroll management be more conservative than standard hold'em?
options: Short deck is easier to win
Short-deck variance is higher and needs a bigger buffer
t7sd-adjustment-q4.explanation: Short-deck standard deviation is higher (flop rate/draws/big pots), so variance is higher and the bankroll bar must be more conservative.

t7sd-adjustment-q5.question: The mark of a short-deck pro is:
options: Always reminding yourself you're in short deck and re-evaluating every hand
t7sd-adjustment-q5.explanation: The mark of a short-deck pro is always reminding yourself you're in short deck and re-evaluating every hand by short-deck rules, not using full-ring memory.

t8sd-variance-q1.question: The core of handling short-deck variance is:
options: Treating variance as an uncontrollable variable and controlling only decision quality
t8sd-variance-q1.explanation: Variance is uncontrollable weather; decision quality is controllable ability. Handling variance means keeping strategy undistorted.

t8sd-variance-q2.question: Losing multiple 50% all-ins in a row in short deck is correctly understood as:
options: Mathematical normalcy under high-frequency confrontation — maintain decision quality
t8sd-variance-q2.explanation: Short deck has frequent all-ins; 0.5^N losing streaks are mathematical normalcy. Maintain decision quality instead of doubting your level.

t8sd-variance-q3.question: The "pause at 50BB" variance budget exists to:
options: Limit the maximum you can lose
Stop and restart, avoiding chase-style re-buying
t8sd-variance-q3.explanation: A variance budget is stop-loss discipline — pause at the budget line, cutting the "get even" impulse and avoiding bad adjustments during violent variance.

t8sd-variance-q4.question: The hardest situation for short-deck variance tolerance is:
options: Letting your guard down after winning (relaxing and playing marginal hands)
t8sd-variance-q4.explanation: Relaxation after winning is the most dangerous — players let their guard down, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. Short-deck discipline must be consistent throughout.

t8sd-variance-q5.question: The best review method for short-deck mental resilience is:
options: Use a decision log recording reasoning, asking only EV not results
t8sd-variance-q5.explanation: Record each key decision's reasoning with a decision log, asking only EV not results, to maintain quality through variance.

t8sd-tilt-q1.question: Why is short deck a tilt hotspot?
options: High variance, high flop rates, big pots, and violent win-loss alternation
t8sd-tilt-q1.explanation: Short deck has high variance, high flop rates, big pots, and violent win-loss alternation — tilt triggers more easily.

t8sd-tilt-q2.question: Tilt's most typical damage to your range is:
options: Opening too loose, calling too wide, chasing too aggressively
t8sd-tilt-q2.explanation: Tilt distorts your range: opening looser, calling wider, chasing harder — systematically deviating from the equilibrium baseline.

t8sd-tilt-q3.question: The core of separating "process vs result" is:
options: Review only decision EV, never change play because of results
t8sd-tilt-q3.explanation: Review only process (decision EV) not results (win/loss) to maintain long-term quality.

t8sd-tilt-q4.question: The short-deck tilt-defense triad is:
options: Emotional red light, preset stop-loss, process attribution
t8sd-tilt-q4.explanation: Self-awareness (emotional red light), preset discipline (stop-loss point), process attribution (only ask EV) — built off the table.

t8sd-tilt-q5.question: The correct statement about when short-deck tilt occurs is:
options: Relaxation after winning is equally dangerous
t8sd-tilt-q5.explanation: Relaxation after winning is equally dangerous — letting your guard down to play marginal hands gives the edge back. Discipline must be consistent throughout.

t9sd-integration-q1.question: The correct order of the short-deck decision loop is:
t9sd-integration-q1.explanation: The loop: range (T4) → math (T2) → betting (T6) → opponent (T7) → psychology (T8) — all five questions, none optional.

t9sd-integration-q2.question: The main strategic difference between deep-stacked and short-stacked short deck is:
options: Deep stacks: wider ranges, aggressive draw chasing; short stacks: more frequent, more direct preflop all-ins
t9sd-integration-q2.explanation: Deep stacks play wider ranges and chase draws aggressively (good implied odds); short stacks shove preflop more, adjust set mining, and play more directly.

t9sd-integration-q3.question: Short-deck review should focus most on:
options: Whether the decision process (range/EV/size/opponent/emotion) was correct
t9sd-integration-q3.explanation: Review only process (decision quality), not results (win/loss), turning every hand into training for continuous improvement.

t9sd-integration-q4.question: Short-deck short stack (20BB) holding AQs, the most reasonable play is:
options: Shove directly or small raise to shorten the decision tree
t9sd-integration-q4.explanation: With a short stack you don't plan multiple streets; AQ has solid equity against wide ranges — shove or small raise is the standard play.

t9sd-integration-q5.question: "System stability" matters more than "every-hand perfection" because:
options: A stable decision loop plus emotional discipline keeps long-term expectation climbing; chasing perfection causes overthinking and tilt
t9sd-integration-q5.explanation: Occasional mistakes are inevitable; a stable loop and discipline keep the long-term expectation curve climbing, while chasing "every-hand perfection" causes overthinking and tilt.

t9sd-case-study-q1.question: The core dividing line between top short-deck players and amateurs is:
options: Decision framework (short-deck thinking + frequency balance + discipline)
t9sd-case-study-q1.explanation: Pros rely on systems (short-deck thinking, frequency balance, discipline); amateurs rely on full-ring intuition.

t9sd-case-study-q2.question: How does a pro short-deck player adjust preflop ranges against a 3Bet-too-much opponent?
options: Narrow the open, reducing marginal hands that only fold after a 3Bet
t9sd-case-study-q2.explanation: Against a 3Bet-too-much opponent, marginal hands only fold after a 3Bet — narrow the opening range.

t9sd-case-study-q3.question: A pro short-deck player holding an overpair on a wet board (9♦8♣3♥) should:
options: 2/3+ pot big bet for protection (short-deck draw density is high)
t9sd-case-study-q3.explanation: Short-deck wet boards have high draw density; small bets give draws too cheap a price, so pros protect overpairs with big sizes.

t9sd-case-study-q4.question: Top short-deck players deciding with the same framework after losing multiple all-ins reflects:
options: Emotional discipline — treating variance as an uncontrollable variable and controlling only decision quality
t9sd-case-study-q4.explanation: Top players treat variance as an external variable and control only decision quality — the ultimate form of "process vs result" separation.

t9sd-case-study-q5.question: The most valuable way to study pro short-deck hands is:
options: Deconstructing layer by layer with the decision loop and distilling reusable principles
Only watching how much they win
t9sd-case-study-q5.explanation: Deconstruction + comparing gaps + distilling principles converts the pro framework into your own system.

t1hu-probability-q1.question: Heads-up, holding AKo vs the opponent's random hole cards, your preflop all-in equity is about:
t1hu-probability-q1.explanation: AKo vs random is about 65.4%. 85% is AA vs random; 55% is near small/medium pair level — treating AKo as 55% undervalues HU high cards.

t1hu-probability-q2.question: Holding two non-Ace hole cards, the probability the HU opponent has at least one Ace is about:
t1hu-probability-q2.explanation: 1 − C(46,2)/C(50,2) = 1 − 1035/1225 ≈ 15.5%. 0.65% is the full-ring magnitude for at least one of 8 opponents holding AA (when you hold AA), a different conditional probability. 30% clearly overestimates the Ace frequency.

t1hu-probability-q3.question: Which statement about the HU blind structure is correct?
options: SB posts 0.5, BB acts last preflop, BB acts first postflop
SB acts last preflop and sees the flop for free
BB posts 0.5 and acts last postflop
SB and BB postflop order is random
t1hu-probability-q3.explanation: In heads-up the SB posts 0.5 (doubling as an ante; the SB is the button): preflop the SB acts first and the BB last; postflop the BB acts first, and the SB (button) acts last with positional advantage. The other options contradict HU rules.

t1hu-probability-q4.question: Compared with a nine-handed table, the probability your AA gets counterfeited by another AA in heads-up is:
t1hu-probability-q4.explanation: After your two Aces, only 2 remain in 50 cards, so a HU opponent has AA 1/1225 ≈ 0.08%; in full ring at least one of 8 opponents has AA about 8/1225 ≈ 0.65%. In heads-up your strongest hand's dominance is less often offset by a crash.

t1hu-outs-q1.question: You're ahead with K♠Q♠ (K-high) vs J♣T♦ (J-high) on a 9♠7♦2♣ flop. The probability the opponent overtakes by the river is about:
t1hu-outs-q1.explanation: The opponent has 6 outs (3 Js + 3 Ts); two-street hit = 6/45 + (39/45)×(6/44) ≈ 25.2%. 13% is the one-card magnitude; 50% clearly overestimates.

t1hu-outs-q2.question: Heads-up, a 15-out combo draw shoving on the flop has exact equity of about:
t1hu-outs-q2.explanation: 1 − (32/47)×(31/46) ≈ 54.1%. The 2/4 rule gives 60%, overestimating by about 6 points; 45% only counts flush outs — exactly why 15 outs needs the corrected formula.

t1hu-outs-q3.question: Why are straight-draw outs usually "cleaner" in heads-up than full ring?
options: Because with only one opponent, the probability that another opponent holds the same draw and discounts your outs is lower
Because HU straights are bigger hands
t1hu-outs-q3.explanation: The multiway risk of "one of my outs gives another opponent a flush" almost disappears in heads-up; the discount relaxes from 70-80% to about 90%. Pot size and dealing don't affect out cleanliness.

t1hu-outs-q4.question: You hold A♥K♥ behind 5♠5♦ on a 9♥7♥2♣ flop. Your equity is about:
t1hu-outs-q4.explanation: Flush 9 outs + overcards 6 outs = 15 outs; two-street ≈ 54.1% — behind yet a coin-flip favorite, the mathematical basis for aggressive combo-draw shoves. 40% only counts flush outs.

t1hu-variance-q1.question: Heads-up, you shove 10 consecutive hands at 55% equity. The probability of losing all 10 is about:
t1hu-variance-q1.explanation: 0.45¹⁰ ≈ 0.00034 ≈ 0.03%. Though rare per event, HU has 200+ hands/hour with 55%-60% all-ins recurring, so losing streaks appear in nearly every session — the variance effect of high-frequency confrontation.

t1hu-variance-q2.question: The typical standard deviation of HU cash games (bb/100) compared with full ring is:
t1hu-variance-q2.explanation: HU participates in every hand and all-in equity often lands in 50%-60%, so single-result uncertainty is strong; the typical standard deviation is 120-180bb/100, clearly above full ring's 80-100.

t1hu-variance-q3.question: Why is the SB's low-cost limp-to-see-flop more common in heads-up than full ring?
options: The SB has already posted 0.5 and only completes 0.5 to see the flop, and the BB acts last preflop
In HU the SB always acts last
HU blinds are smaller than full ring
There is no postflop betting in HU
t1hu-variance-q3.explanation: The SB has already posted 0.5 and only completes 0.5 to 1 to see the flop (odds 1:3, calling 0.5 to contest a 1.5 pot); even if the BB raises preflop, the SB (button) still acts last postflop and keeps positional advantage — so HU nearly every hand sees a flop, with extremely high decision density. The other options contradict HU rules.

t1hu-variance-q4.question: For bankroll management, the suggested buy-in count for HU cash games is about:
t1hu-variance-q4.explanation: HU standard deviation is high and downswings more compressed; Moshman suggests 50+ buy-ins. 20-40 is the full-ring standard and can get blown through by HU variance; 10-15 and 2-3 are far beyond reasonable risk.

t2hu-odds-q1.question: Heads-up, the required equity for the SB to complete 0.5 and see the flop is about:
t2hu-odds-q1.explanation: Pot 1.5BB, SB calls 0.5BB, required equity = 0.5 ÷ (1.5+0.5) = 25%. Option B is correct; the others deviate too much.

t2hu-odds-q2.question: SB opens 3BB; the BB's required equity to call is about:
t2hu-odds-q2.explanation: Pot = 3+1 = 4BB, BB calls 2BB, required equity = 2 ÷ (4+2) = 33.3%. Option B is correct; note this differs from the full-ring BTN call at 40% because HU dead money share is higher.

t2hu-odds-q3.question: The correct meaning of "odds dilution" in heads-up is:
options: The pot-odds formula changes with player count
A half-pot bet needs the same required equity heads-up and full ring, but your win rate gets divided among multiple opponents
Each out loses value in multiway pots
t2hu-odds-q3.explanation: The pot-odds formula is size-independent; a half pot is always 25%. But in multiway pots you face several opponents — a made flush can lose to a bigger flush and top pair to a better kicker. That's the "equity discount" dilution mechanism.

t2hu-odds-q4.question: A wide opponent range (like 60% of starting hands) affects HU call decisions by:
options: Lowering the required-equity threshold, so more hands can call
Not affecting the math, only position
Forcing players to tighten their calling ranges
t2hu-odds-q4.explanation: The wider the opponent's range, the higher your equity with any two cards (e.g. 9-high is ahead about 40% vs a wide range). At the same pot odds, a wide range lowers the call bar — the mathematical basis of HU aggression.

t2hu-ev-q1.question: The EV three branches in heads-up refer to:
t2hu-ev-q1.explanation: The EV three branches are fold/call/raise — the atomic options of every decision node. Options A/C classify bet types, not atomic branches.

t2hu-ev-q2.question: Pot 4BB, opponent bets 2BB, you have 30% equity. The call EV is about:
t2hu-ev-q2.explanation: EV = 0.3×6 − 0.7×2 = 1.8 − 1.4 = +0.4BB. Option B (−0.47) is the single-street −EV of a flush draw, which requires a different 30%-equity context; at 30% here you hold a strong pair, not a draw.

t2hu-ev-q3.question: HU positional value of about 0.5-1BB/hand means:
options: The BB wins 1BB more on every flop
Over the long run the BB earns 0.5-1BB more expected value per hand than the SB
t2hu-ev-q3.explanation: Positional value is a long-run expectation gap: the BB's postflop information advantage averages 0.5-1BB extra per hand. Not a per-hand guarantee, but a statistical expectation.

t2hu-ev-q4.question: SB with Q♠J♠: limp EV = +0.29BB, raise 2.5BB EV = +0.53BB. The correct decision is:
t2hu-ev-q4.explanation: EV maximization is the core principle: raise (0.53) > limp (0.29). Even if limping is +EV, it isn't optimal. A pro's job is to pick the bigger number.

t2hu-risk-q1.question: Heads-up, who acts first postflop?
t2hu-risk-q1.explanation: The SB is the postflop positional-disadvantage side (acts first); the BB is the advantage side (acts last). This basic HU rule decides all the math behind postflop decisions.

t2hu-risk-q2.question: Pot 6BB, opponent bets 3BB. The break-even fold rate for a check-raise to 9BB is:
t2hu-risk-q2.explanation: Under a pure-bluff assumption (must lose at showdown), EV(check-raise) = f×9 − (1−f)×9 = 18f − 9; EV(check-call) = −3 (calling 3 must lose). Set 18f − 9 = −3 → f = 33.3%. Note: if the check-raise has showdown value (W>0), the break-even fold rate is lower. Option B is correct.

t2hu-risk-q3.question: Why might HU implied odds be lower than full ring?
options: Because the opponent's range is wide, so payment density is low
t2hu-risk-q3.explanation: A wide opponent range (60%+) means lots of air — when you make a strong hand (set/two pair), he often lacks strong enough hands to pay. That's "low payment density", lowering implied odds.

t2hu-risk-q4.question: At SPR > 12, the OOP side (SB) should tend toward:
options: Aggressively playing for stacks with top pair
t2hu-risk-q4.explanation: High SPR amplifies the positional disadvantage: you risk deep-pot tough decisions (especially when raised). The OOP side should pot-control, avoiding committing too many chips with marginal hands.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q1.question: The SB's 0.5 blind in heads-up is described as "also acting as an ante". The most accurate understanding is:
options: It's invested dead money that stays in the prize pool whether or not the SB participates, giving limp and steal their mathematical basis
It's automatically returned to the SB at the end of preflop
It only applies when the BB also limps
It lets the SB see the flop for free without further investment
t3hu-sb-strategy-q1.explanation: The SB's 0.5 enters the pot whether or not he participates, with ante-like dead-money properties: limping completes 0.5 to see a 1.5 pot (25% required equity), and stealing contests it as a prize. Option B contradicts the rules, C confuses the ante's condition, and D ignores that the SB still completes the blind difference.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q2.question: SB min-raises to 2BB; assuming the EV when called or 3Bet is zero, at what BB fold rate does the SB auto-profit with any two cards?
t3hu-sb-strategy-q2.explanation: SB extra risk 1.5BB, target prize 1BB: f×1 = (1−f)×1.5 → f = 1.5/2.5 = 60%. 40% is the BB's minimum defense frequency (MDF); 50% and 75% don't match the derivation.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q3.question: Why is the SB limp a GTO-reasonable option in heads-up but almost never in full ring?
options: The HU SB acts last preflop; after a limp the BB can only check or raise, so a limp doesn't additionally lose position
HU pots are smaller, so limping's loss is negligible
In HU the SB also acts last postflop, so limping has no postflop cost
Full-ring rules forbid the SB from limping
t3hu-sb-strategy-q3.explanation: The core is structural: the HU SB acts last preflop and has posted 0.5 dead money (25% odds), so a limp isn't punished by "losing position after a raise"; the full-ring SB acts second-to-last, and after a limp faces a multiway raise losing both position and initiative. B ignores the odds structure, C contradicts the HU rule that the SB acts first postflop, and D doesn't exist.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q4.question: The BB isolates your limp at 70% frequency; you (SB) hold K♠8♠ deep. The optimal adjustment is:
options: Keep limping normally and rely on postflop
Drastically reduce limping — switch marginal hands to min-raise or direct fold, leaving only strong hands in the limp pile
Increase limping to fight back with more hands
t3hu-sb-strategy-q4.explanation: A 70% isolate frequency means your limp almost always gets attacked: the 25%-odds plan to see a flop fails, and marginal hands are forced OOP into big pots. The correct adjustment is narrowing the limp pile and using min-raise to reclaim initiative; continuing to limp is being exploited, limping more amplifies the leak, and 4x sizes only make the BB fold weak hands and keep strong ones.

t3hu-bb-defense-q1.question: The typical HU BB defense frequency vs an SB open is about:
t3hu-bb-defense-q1.explanation: Solvers show the HU BB defends about 60%-70% (calls 35%-50% + 3Bets 15%-25%). 15%-25% is the full-ring vs a tight open magnitude, and 85%-95% is a passive calling station's magnitude — neither is GTO.

t3hu-bb-defense-q2.question: SB opens 3BB (total 3). By the dead-money perspective, the BB's minimum defense frequency (MDF) is about:
t3hu-bb-defense-q2.explanation: MDF = 1 − 3/(1.5+3) = 1 − 66.7% ≈ 33.3%. 67% is the BB fold rate the SB needs to auto-profit (f*); 20% and 50% don't match the derivation. Note MDF is only the floor; GTO actually defends 60%-70%, far above it.

t3hu-bb-defense-q3.question: Why is the GTO HU BB defense frequency (60%-70%) far above the MDF floor (33%-38%)?
options: Because the BB's cards are better than the SB's
Because the BB is postflop IP with equity realization over 100%, making calls themselves +EV
Because the MDF formula doesn't apply preflop
Because the BB must stop the SB from stealing with any cards
t3hu-bb-defense-q3.explanation: MDF only guarantees "stopping pure-bluff auto-profit"; the BB's call +EV comes from postflop position (equity realization >100%), the SB's 0.5 dead money, and the SB's wide range — allowing defense above the floor while still profiting. A contradicts dealing randomness, C is wrong (MDF applies to any betting scenario), and D confuses the floor with the optimum.

t3hu-bb-defense-q4.question: After an SB limp, you (BB) hold A♠8♠ and the SB folds to a raise about 55%. The optimal action is:
options: Check, letting the flop come free
t3hu-bb-defense-q4.explanation: Isolate EV ≈ 0.55×1.5 + 0.45×0.5 ≈ +1.05BB, clearly above checking's ~+0.7BB. Raising to 10BB over-pressures — the SB only continues with strong hands and your A8s's postflop equity crashes; checking lets the SB realize a weak range for free; folding wastes IP showdown value.

t3hu-position-reversal-q1.question: The most accurate meaning of "position reversal" in heads-up is:
options: The SB acts last preflop but first postflop; the BB acts second preflop but last postflop
The SB and BB swap the button every hand
The BB bets first after the flop
Positional advantage disappears on the river
t3hu-position-reversal-q1.explanation: Heads-up: the SB acts last preflop (has preflop position) and first postflop (no postflop position); the BB is the opposite — heads-up's unique position reversal. B misreads the button rule, C contradicts the rule (the SB acts first postflop), and D contradicts "river position matters most".

t3hu-position-reversal-q2.question: In the street-by-street positional model (flop/turn/river contributions 0.05/0.10/0.20BB), the river accounts for about what share of total positional value?
t3hu-position-reversal-q2.explanation: Total value = 0.05 + 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.35BB; river share = 0.20/0.35 ≈ 57%. 33% is the three-street average (1/3); 67% wrongly compares the river against the flop alone.

t3hu-position-reversal-q3.question: Why does postflop OOP usually avoid donk betting?
options: Donk betting is prohibited by the rules
The donk range is naturally strong, can't balance when raised, and gives up the check-raise lever
Donk betting only works in small pots
t3hu-position-reversal-q3.explanation: A donk range is strong-heavy and can't balance when IP raises; it also forfeits the x/r lever, freely exposing range strength. It only appears as an exception on boards where OOP's range dominates (e.g. high two-pair/straight density in limp pots). A contradicts the rules, C is too absolute (OOP has the x/r lever), and D has no basis.

t3hu-position-reversal-q4.question: You (SB) min-raised preflop and hold K♠Q♠ on a K♦9♣3♠ flop; the BB (IP) is an aggressive high-float player. The optimal tendency is:
options: Bet 2/3 pot immediately to take it down
Mix checks with small (about 1/3 pot) c-bets, keeping the check-raise lever and pot control
Shove directly to protect top pair
t3hu-position-reversal-q4.explanation: OOP vs a float-happy player, big bets are extremely costly (you must fold to a raise), shoving is overkill, and 100% checking makes your range transparent and exploitable. Mixing checks with small c-bets: small bets make marginal hands pay to see cards, checks keep the x/r lever, and the frequency balance keeps IP from pinning down your top-pair strength — the combined application of OOP compensation tools.

t4hu-range-width-q1.question: The typical HU SB opening frequency is about:
t4hu-range-width-q1.explanation: The HU SB opens about 80%: only one opponent to beat, any two cards keep about 35% equity vs random, and completing 0.5 sees a 1.5BB pot. 20% is a tight full-ring magnitude and 40% a full-ring BTN-vs-many magnitude.

t4hu-range-width-q2.question: Why can the HU BB defend 60%+ while the full-ring BB only defends about 25%-40%?
options: The HU BB is the postflop positional-advantage side with equity realization over 100%
The HU BB gets good cards every hand
The HU BB doesn't need to defend
Full-ring rules forbid wide BB defense
t4hu-range-width-q2.explanation: The position reversal makes the HU BB act last postflop (IP) with equity realization over 100%, and the SB's 0.5 dead money makes calls cheap (33.3%). The full-ring BB is permanently OOP postflop and must tighten defense.

t4hu-range-width-q3.question: The most accurate understanding of the SB's ~80% opening range is:
options: Enter with 80% of hands, but many give up quickly postflop, relying on position and board fit
Raise after opening with 80% of hands
Only play the top 80% of strong hands
t4hu-range-width-q3.explanation: A wide range means "participate a lot, invest little": about 80% enter, but half give up postflop. The real error is playing a wide range as "never fold any street" — that's a calling station.

t4hu-range-width-q4.question: Against an aggressive BB who 3Bets at 25%, you (SB) should adjust range width by:
options: Narrowing the opening range, reducing marginal hands that only fold after a 3Bet
t4hu-range-width-q4.explanation: High 3Bet frequency erodes steal EV, and marginal hands only fold after a 3Bet. Narrowing is correct; stopping entirely overreacts and opening 100% is suicide.

t4hu-range-width-q5.question: The difference between range width and "playing loose" is:
options: Width realizes value through postflop position and board fit rather than mindless investment
t4hu-range-width-q5.explanation: Wide-range pros bet for money on the right boards and fold fast on the wrong ones; stations are wide AND over-invest on every street. The key is whether you expand and contract with board and position.

t4hu-polarization-q1.question: The meaning of a polarized range is:
options: A range arranged linearly from strong to weak
A range containing only strong and weak hands (bluffs), with the middle given to checking
A range containing only strong hands
t4hu-polarization-q1.explanation: Polarized = strong value + weak bluffs, middle hands check. Only a linear range is arranged continuously by strength.

t4hu-polarization-q2.question: The equilibrium value:bluff ratio for a river full-pot bet is about:
t4hu-polarization-q2.explanation: f = 1/3, so 2/3 value and 1/3 bluffs, value:bluff = 2:1. Exactly equals the opponent's required call equity of 33%.

t4hu-polarization-q3.question: Why does top pair weak kicker (like KQ) usually stay out of the HU betting range?
options: Because it isn't strong enough — check for pot control and bluff-catching
Because it's a strong hand that must bet
Because it affects the value:bluff ratio
t4hu-polarization-q3.explanation: KQ is a middle hand: it can't beat AK/AA but loses to any bigger K kicker. Betting and being raised leaves it torn; checking and pot control spare KQ from awkward decisions.

t4hu-polarization-q4.question: "Draw converting to bluff" means:
options: Continuing to value-bet after the draw hits
When a draw misses, using blockers and board structure to convert it into a pure bluff
Giving up the draw and checking
t4hu-polarization-q4.explanation: When the turn misses, a draw shifts from "showdown-improvement potential" to "pure bluff", double-barreling with blockers (like an A high) to represent strength — the dynamic core of the polarized range.

t4hu-polarization-q5.question: Regarding polarized bluff share on the turn/flop vs the river, the correct statement is:
options: Bluff share is highest on the river
Turn/flop can carry higher bluff share because later streets remain
Flop bluff share is the lowest
t4hu-polarization-q5.explanation: Earlier streets have later streets to convert or abandon, so bluff share can be higher; on the river, the last street, bluffs must precisely match pot odds (1/3 for a full pot).

t4hu-blocking-q1.question: The mechanism of a blocker is:
options: Cards you hold reduce the count of specific opponent combos
Hiding your range from the opponent
t4hu-blocking-q1.explanation: Each card you hold removes every opponent combo containing that card — your hole cards become information about the opponent's range.

t4hu-blocking-q2.question: Holding a lone A♠ (no flush) on a three-spade board matters for bluffing because:
options: It doesn't matter since you have no flush
You block the opponent's nut-flush combos, raising bluff success
The opponent definitely has no flush
t4hu-blocking-q2.explanation: Holding A♠ zeroes the opponent's A♠X♠ nut-flush combos, trimming his strongest calling hands and raising your bluff's fold equity.

t4hu-blocking-q3.question: Holding A♦A♣ (no spade blocker) on a three-spade board facing an all-in, the correct tendency is:
options: Be cautious — you block no flushes, so his calling range skews strong
t4hu-blocking-q3.explanation: Without A♠ you block no flushes; he can have the A♠X♠ nut flush or a smaller flush, lowering your bluff-catching value.

t4hu-blocking-q4.question: For a preflop 3Bet bluff, why is A5s better than 76s?
options: A5s blocks AA and AK, lowering the 4Bet probability, and folds cleanly to a 4Bet
t4hu-blocking-q4.explanation: A5s's A blocks the top of the opponent's range (AA/AK), lowering 4Bet frequency, and A5s folds cleanly to a 4Bet. 76s blocks no strong hands and runs into QQ+ more often.

t4hu-blocking-q5.question: The correct statement about the applicability boundary of blockers is:
options: Blockers can overturn any base range analysis
Blockers are a marginal tool for edge spots, requiring a correct base range first
Blockers only work on the river
Blockers are only for calling decisions
t4hu-blocking-q5.explanation: Blockers adjust combo ratios rather than rewrite ranges. They're icing when the base range is right and can't save you when it's wrong — the line separating them from a "master key".

t5hu-gto-he-q1.question: The Nash "unexploitable" guarantee strictly applies in:
options: Pots of any size in player count
t5hu-gto-he-q1.explanation: In games with three or more players the equilibrium floor weakens under coalition effects. Heads-up is the strict domain of the Nash "unexploitable" guarantee.

t5hu-gto-he-q2.question: Against a leaky weak opponent, the HU GTO strategy:
options: Doesn't lose, but earns less than targeted exploitation
Is identical to the exploitative strategy
t5hu-gto-he-q2.explanation: GTO guarantees expectation at or above the game value (a floor) but doesn't actively exploit opponent errors; exploitation extracts more, at the cost of opening your own leaks.

t5hu-gto-he-q3.question: The main difference between HU GTO and full-ring GTO is:
