options: HU ranges are extremely wide, so GTO means very high betting frequency and bluff density
t5hu-gto-he-q3.explanation: HU ranges are wide (SB 80%, BB 60%+), so the equilibrium comes with high betting frequency and polarized ranges — not "playing tight".

t5hu-gto-he-q4.question: "Minimum necessary deviation" means:
options: Using GTO as the baseline and deviating with direction and a magnitude cap based on observable biases
t5hu-gto-he-q4.explanation: Deviations need direction (targeting the opponent's leak) and magnitude discipline (still not losing if he corrects), keeping room to return to baseline anytime.

t5hu-gto-he-q5.question: When studying solver outputs, you should focus more on:
t5hu-gto-he-q5.explanation: Memorizing frequencies is worse than understanding structure: why this size, why this hand enters the betting range, why the frequency changes on the turn. Understand the structure and the frequencies remember themselves.

t5hu-frequency-q1.question: Facing a half-pot bet, MDF (Minimum Defense Frequency) is about:
t5hu-frequency-q1.explanation: MDF = 1/(1+0.5) = 2/3 ≈ 67%. Continue with about the strongest two-thirds, or any opponent bluff becomes profitable.

t5hu-frequency-q2.question: In equilibrium, a hand is mixed across multiple actions only if:
options: The hand is too hard to decide
All actions have exactly equal EV
It was chosen randomly to confuse the opponent
t5hu-frequency-q2.explanation: Indifference Principle: when EV differs, a rational strategy picks the higher one. Mixing only occurs on critical hands with equal EV.

t5hu-frequency-q3.question: You only defend 30% against full-pot bets (MDF should be 50%). The opponent's correct exploitation is:
options: Raise bluff frequency with any two cards
t5hu-frequency-q3.explanation: A 70% fold rate far exceeds the 50% a full-pot bluff needs to break even — the opponent auto-profits betting any two cards and should aggressively add bluffs.

t5hu-frequency-q4.question: "Defense isn't only calling" in heads-up means:
options: Raises also count toward defense frequency — compute the total, then allocate
The tighter the defense, the better
t5hu-frequency-q4.explanation: Defense consists of calls plus raises; the BB's 60%+ includes 3Bet value and bluffs. Against high-frequency bluffers, substitute some calls with raises.

t5hu-frequency-q5.question: For live players, the most pragmatic attitude toward mixed-strategy nodes is:
options: Recognize that either side loses almost nothing, and invest effort in high-EV-difference decisions
t5hu-frequency-q5.explanation: Both sides of a mixed node have equal EV, so a single "wrong choice" costs ≈0; what actually separates results is pure-strategy nodes and range construction on earlier streets.

t6hu-sizing-optimal-q1.question: As bet size increases, the equilibrium bluff share:
t6hu-sizing-optimal-q1.explanation: f = b/(1+2b) rises monotonically with b: full pot bluffs 33%, 2× pot 40%. The bigger the size, the worse the opponent's calling price, allowing higher bluff density.

t6hu-sizing-optimal-q2.question: On a dry high board (like K♠7♦2♣), the optimal sizing tendency for top pair is:
options: 1/3-pot small thin-value bet, avoiding a wide range only continuing with strong hands
t6hu-sizing-optimal-q2.explanation: The opponent rarely hits a dry board; a small bet already realizes thin value from weak hands and controls the pot. A big bet only leaves the BB with stronger hands, wasting the K's thin value.

t6hu-sizing-optimal-q3.question: At SPR ≈ 19.5 (deep stacks) with a strong draw on the flop, the correct sizing strategy is:
options: Big bets to build the pot, paving the way for a turn/river all-in
t6hu-sizing-optimal-q3.explanation: At high SPR the pot must grow geometrically with big bets to complete an all-in on the river. Small bets grow the pot too slowly to get a deep stack in.

t6hu-sizing-optimal-q4.question: Medium-strength hands (like top pair with a straight draw) tend toward:
options: Small bets for pot control, limiting risk exposure
t6hu-sizing-optimal-q4.explanation: Medium hands don't seek to play for stacks; a small bet both realizes thin value and controls the risk of being raised. Overbets/full pots drag medium hands into awkward big pots.

t6hu-sizing-optimal-q5.question: The equilibrium bluff share of a half-pot bet is about:
t6hu-sizing-optimal-q5.explanation: f = 0.5/(1+1) = 0.25, value:bluff = 3:1. 33% is full pot, 20% is 1/3 pot, and 40% is 2× pot.

t6hu-barrel-q1.question: On a dry high board (like K♠7♦2♣→5♥→9♣), the correct betting line for top pair is:
options: High-frequency triple barrel, because the opponent's range rarely hits and the board stays dry
Big bets on both turn and river
t6hu-barrel-q1.explanation: On a dry board the opponent rarely hits and the board never improves draws — top pair keeps its full lead and a triple barrel collects all the value.

t6hu-barrel-q2.question: On a wet connected board (9♠8♥4♣→7♦→6♣), the correct turn/river firing frequency is:
options: Cut sharply, because the board changes hands and the opponent's straight combos multiply
Must fire the turn, must fold the river
t6hu-barrel-q2.explanation: Wet boards easily complete straights/flushes; the turn/river board change weakens made hands like AA, so firing frequency must drop accordingly.

t6hu-barrel-q3.question: Pot 5BB, high SPR. To shove all the chips by the river, the flop size should be:
options: About 2/3 pot to grow the pot geometrically
t6hu-barrel-q3.explanation: High SPR needs about 2/3 pot to grow the pot geometrically street by street and complete the all-in on the river; 1/3 pot grows too slowly to get a deep stack in.

t6hu-barrel-q4.question: AA bet the 9♠8♥4♣ flop; the turn brings 7♦. The correct adjustment is:
options: Lower turn betting frequency, because the opponent's range was improved by the new card
t6hu-barrel-q4.explanation: 7♦ completes QT, 65, and other straights; the BB's wide range holds plenty of straight combos, weakening AA's lead — pot control rather than continuing to fire.

t6hu-barrel-q5.question: "Semi-bluff closes on the turn" means:
options: Bet a draw on the flop, and on a favorable turn convert to a pure bluff to take the pot
t6hu-barrel-q5.explanation: A semi-bluff bets the flop with a draw; when the turn misses but the card is favorable (like an A blocker), it converts to a pure bluff so the opponent folds and you win the pot directly.

t7hu-patterns-q1.question: The correct way to "read people" in heads-up is:
options: Inferring the opponent's range from frequencies (open rate / fold rate, etc.)
t7hu-patterns-q1.explanation: Reading is estimating ranges, not guessing hands. Cross the four key frequencies (open / fold / 3Bet / showdown) to infer the opponent's portrait.

t7hu-patterns-q2.question: An opponent opens 85% and folds to C-Bets 60%. The correct judgment is:
options: He's "wide range + weak defense" — C-Bet at high frequency to steal
t7hu-patterns-q2.explanation: Wide open + many folds = wide range with weak defense. As IP, C-Bet at high frequency to steal, and the BB can widen defense — harvest two leaks at once.

t7hu-patterns-q3.question: Against a calling station who almost never folds postflop, the correct exploitation is:
options: Value-bet thin value and reduce bluffs
t7hu-patterns-q3.explanation: A station doesn't fold, so pure bluffs are useless; switch to thin value bets because he calls with worse hands.

t7hu-patterns-q4.question: When identifying an opponent type, the sufficient sample size is about:
t7hu-patterns-q4.explanation: A single all-in win/loss is noise; only 50-100 hand frequency statistics form a reliable signal. Concluding from single-hand impressions is exploitation's biggest enemy.

t7hu-patterns-q5.question: An opponent opens only 30% and over-folds to raises (nit). The exploitation direction is:
t7hu-patterns-q5.explanation: A nit folds too much, so the fold rate on steals and raises is automatic profit. But note he's usually strong once in a pot — avoid being re-raised by his occasional strong hands.

t7hu-exploit-q1.question: The discipline of "minimum necessary deviation" is:
options: Aiming at the opponent's leak with minimal magnitude, ready to return to baseline anytime
t7hu-exploit-q1.explanation: Deviations open your own leaks, so keep the magnitude controlled; aim at the leak, keep it minimal, and return to baseline when the opponent adjusts.

t7hu-exploit-q2.question: Against an opponent with a 60% fold rate (equilibrium 40%), the steal EV is:
t7hu-exploit-q2.explanation: EV = 0.6×1.5 − 0.4×1.5 = +0.3BB, pure stealing already profits. The higher the opponent's fold rate, the more your steal frequency should rise.

t7hu-exploit-q3.question: The purpose of node locking is:
options: Locking your own strategy to prevent misclicks
Fixing the opponent's strategy to the observed tendency and solving the maximally exploitative response
t7hu-exploit-q3.explanation: Node locking feeds "how the opponent actually plays" into the solver and outputs the optimal harvest scheme for that deviation — turning exploitation from feel into calculation.

t7hu-exploit-q4.question: Against a station who calls too loosely postflop, the exploitation adjustment is:
options: Increase value bets and put thin-value hands into the betting range
t7hu-exploit-q4.explanation: The station calls with weak hands, so your wide value range gets overpaid — increase value-bet sizes and include thin-value hands in the betting range.

t7hu-exploit-q5.question: After you raise steal frequency, the opponent starts 3Betting frequently. The correct move is:
options: Return to the GTO baseline and narrow the range
t7hu-exploit-q5.explanation: The opponent detected your deviation, and your newly opened leaks will be harvested in reverse. You must return to baseline — exploitation is a "deviate → get detected → return" dynamic game.

t8hu-pressure-q1.question: Losing multiple 60%-equity all-ins in a row in heads-up is mainly because:
options: Mathematical necessity under high-frequency confrontation (0.4^N streaks appear often)
t8hu-pressure-q1.explanation: 0.45^8 ≈ 0.17% losing streaks are rare per event, but HU has 200+ hands/hour with 55%-60% all-ins recurring — losing streaks are steadily present background noise.

t8hu-pressure-q2.question: The core meaning of separating "process vs result" is:
options: Only winning counts as playing right
Review only whether decision EV was correct, never change play because of results
t8hu-pressure-q2.explanation: A shove of AK vs 55 is +EV even when it loses. Review process (EV) rather than results (win/loss) to maintain long-term quality.

t8hu-pressure-q3.question: Tilt's most typical damage to strategy is:
options: Opening looser, calling wider, chasing harder — all deviating from baseline
t8hu-pressure-q3.explanation: Tilt distorts your range: opening too loose, calling too wide, chasing too aggressively — systematically deviating from the equilibrium baseline.

t8hu-pressure-q4.question: The role of a "preset variance budget" in a HU session is:
options: Limiting the maximum you can lose
Pausing for review at the stop-loss point, avoiding chase-style re-buying
t8hu-pressure-q4.explanation: A variance budget is stop-loss discipline: pause and review at the preset point, cutting the "get even" impulse rather than continuing to chase into tilt.

t8hu-pressure-q5.question: The correct statement about when tilt occurs is:
options: Relaxation after winning is equally dangerous
t8hu-pressure-q5.explanation: After winning, players often relax, play marginal hands, and give the edge back. HU discipline must be consistent throughout — no relaxation in either direction.

t8hu-reads-q1.question: The most reliable HU read is:
options: Cross-verifying action narrative with frequency statistics
t8hu-reads-q1.explanation: A single action or rhythm has insufficient samples to be reliable. Combining "whether the action sequence is self-consistent" with "50+ hand frequency statistics" is the reliable read.

t8hu-reads-q2.question: The core of "counter-reading (Balanced Play)" is:
options: Making actions not leak range information, keeping rhythm consistent
Making the opponent unable to guess hand strength
t8hu-reads-q2.explanation: Counter-reading requires actions not to leak range: no "bet fast with strong, bet slow with weak" — deliberately keep rhythm consistent or break it to avoid being cracked.

t8hu-reads-q3.question: The correct attitude toward HU reads is treating them as:
options: A probability (like "60% sure") folded into decisions
t8hu-reads-q3.explanation: Reads carry uncertainty; pros convert them into probabilities rather than certainties, then fold them into equity and pot-odds calculations — the sustainable strategy.

t8hu-reads-q4.question: An opponent bets the flop and turn then checks the river. The most likely reading is:
options: Combined with frequency and size, it may be thin value or giving up
t8hu-reads-q4.explanation: The narrative is "strength on flop/turn, giving up on the river", but you must combine the river size and frequency statistics — it may be thin value rather than pure giving up; cross-verify.

t8hu-reads-q5.question: The classic betting leak is:
options: Betting fast with strong hands and slow with weak hands
t8hu-reads-q5.explanation: "Fast with strong, slow with weak" is the classic leak. Counter-reading keeps rhythm consistent or deliberately breaks it so the opponent can't crack your range strength.

t9hu-mastery-q1.question: The correct order of the HU decision loop is:
t9hu-mastery-q1.explanation: The loop: range (T4) → math (T2) → betting (T6) → exploitation (T7) → psychology (T8) — all five questions, none optional.

t9hu-mastery-q2.question: The main difference between deep-stacked (100BB) and short-stacked (15BB) HU is:
options: Deep stacks: wider ranges, more polarized betting, multi-street planning; short stacks: more frequent, more direct preflop all-ins
t9hu-mastery-q2.explanation: Stack depth changes strategy: deep stacks have high SPR requiring multi-street planning and polarized betting; short stacks shove preflop more and play more directly.

t9hu-mastery-q3.question: HU review should focus most on:
options: Whether the decision process (range/EV/size/exploitation/emotion) was correct
t9hu-mastery-q3.explanation: Review only process (decision quality), not results (win/loss), turning every hand into training for continuous improvement.

t9hu-mastery-q4.question: Short-stacked (15BB) HU holding KQs, the most reasonable play is:
options: Shove directly or small-raise to induce, shortening the decision tree
t9hu-mastery-q4.explanation: Short stacks skip multi-street planning; KQs has about 60% equity vs a wide range, so shoving or small-raising to induce is the standard play.

t9hu-mastery-q5.question: "System stability" matters more than "every-hand perfection" because:
options: A stable decision loop plus emotional discipline keeps long-term expectation climbing; chasing perfection causes overthinking and tilt
t9hu-mastery-q5.explanation: Occasional mistakes are inevitable; a stable loop and discipline keep the long-term expectation curve climbing, while chasing "every-hand perfection" triggers overthinking and tilt.

t9hu-pro-study-q1.question: The core dividing line between top HU players and amateurs is:
t9hu-pro-study-q1.explanation: The gap between pros and amateurs is the "decision framework" — pros rely on systems (range construction, frequency balance, discipline), amateurs on feel.

t9hu-pro-study-q2.question: A pro facing a BB who folds too much adjusts preflop strategy by:
options: Raising opening frequency toward 100% and lowering sizes (min-raise) to maximize steal EV
t9hu-pro-study-q2.explanation: The opponent's fold-rate statistics support "wide range + small sizes" to maximize steal EV — a computable decision, not feel.

t9hu-pro-study-q3.question: On a dry high board A♠8♦3♣, the raiser's C-Bet frequency should:
options: Bet the whole range at high frequency and small size
t9hu-pro-study-q3.explanation: The raiser's range advantage is clear (lots of Ax) and the caller rarely hits an A, so a high-frequency small C-Bet over the whole betting range is correct.

t9hu-pro-study-q4.question: Top players deciding with the same framework after losing multiple 60% all-ins reflects:
options: Emotional discipline — treating variance as an uncontrollable variable and controlling only decision quality
t9hu-pro-study-q4.explanation: Top players treat variance as an external variable and control only decision quality — the ultimate form of "process vs result" separation.

t9hu-pro-study-q5.question: The most valuable way to study pro hand examples is:
options: Deconstructing layer by layer with the decision loop and distilling reusable principles
Only watching how much they win
t9hu-pro-study-q5.explanation: Layer-by-layer deconstruction (range/math/betting/exploitation/psychology) + comparing gaps + distilling principles converts the pro framework into your own system.
